Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build U.S. factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:50:01 UTC
01:50:01 KST

Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.
The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.
The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.
The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.
6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

GPU-Accelerated Weight Teleportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:49:00 UTC
01:49:00 KST

Introduction#
Large-scale RL is different from either large-scale pretraining or large-scale inference. A key difference is that the training weights and the sampler weights should ideally match as closely as possible, which requires the trainers sending weight updates to the samplers. This creates a bottleneck: one must either use high speed intra-cluster networking to send weight updates or accept the often-meaningful delay that comes with attempting to communicate terabytes of model weights, not to mention blocking on the samplers. We introduce a faster weight update paradigm, in most cases allowing better-than-intra-cluster speeds, regardless of whether the samplers and trainers are co-located within the same cluster.
The design starts from the widely adopted idea of delta weight sync1Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training, §4.3 Disk-Delta Updates.. We co-designed an entire Blackwell-native compression/decompression pipeline combining the following techniques:
- Massively parallel GPU compression, with distributed ownership and fault tolerance.
- A curated double compression algorithm with heterogeneous CPU-GPU decompression.
- Blackwell Decompression Engine (DE) and hardware-native decompression algorithms, fully overlapping DE with ordinary GPU compute.
- Tiny memory buffer overheads across trainers and samplers, CPUs and GPUs.
As a result, we bring the sampler pause time below 0.23 s and the end-to-end weight sync time below 4 s in our Ampersand production RL configuration, fully saturating the Blackwell Decompression Engine pipeline and making the decompression ASIC the bottleneck for sampler pause time. The implementation is so fast in terms of both end-to-end weight sync time and sampler pause time that even intra-cluster P2P RDMA is slower for most real-world workloads.
For the rest of this article, we use the following as a consistent workload proxy. The model is NVFP4 GLM-5.3, with 445 GB of canonical weight tensors. RL training signals are sparse, with only a tiny portion of weights being updated during each training step, so we mutate 0.085% of the checkpoint as a proxy for one steady-state update. The trainer has 8 nodes with 64 B300 GPUs. Each rollout receiver has two TP4 NVFP4 GLM-5.3 engines on one 8-GPU B300 node. The diagrams use fewer GPUs and model layers for clarity.
CPU disk delta weight sync#
To explain our design progression, we need to understand the foundations of delta weight sync and why a naive implementation is not enough.
Delta update algebra#
# trainer
mask            = weights_old ⊕ weights_new
# rollout
weights_updated = weights_old ⊕ mask
                = weights_new
The core of delta weight sync is the bitwise XOR (⊕) operation. Before a training step, the rollout engines and trainer hold identical weights. The trainer finishes a training step and advances from weights_old to weights_new. The trainer performs a bitwise XOR between weights_old and weights_new to obtain a mask with exactly the same shape as the weights. The 1s in the mask indicate that the weight bit at that location has flipped, and 0s mean unchanged. The rollout engines need weights_new to sample from the new policy for the next RL step. To obtain them, the engines only need to flip the same weight bits. Thus, we transfer the mask to the rollout engines and apply bitwise XOR between their weights_old and the mask. Since the weights are viewed as a long contiguous sequence of bits, their specific data types do not matter and floating-point arithmetic or rounding is not involved.
But masks have the same size as the weights, so directly transferring masks does not save anything versus transferring the full weights. What truly makes the delta sync approach attractive is the following insight. In RL, training signals are sparse, so only a tiny portion of weights are updated during each training step. That means the masks contain mostly 0s and only a tiny portion of 1s. A lossless compression algorithm can then compress the masks into a tiny transfer payload.
Model checkpoint as a handoff#
Now let’s look at a naive but clean delta weight sync design within the RL loop. The trainer and rollout engines need to sync their checkpoints, so let’s use model checkpoints as the handoff. The trainer performs a training step, computes the mask, compresses it into a small payload, and sends the compressed mask to the rollout engines. The rollout engines load and decompress the mask, patch the checkpoint to match the new trainer weights, and reload weights from that checkpoint. Since the checkpoint is the handoff, the rollout engines reuse the same code path as server startup. We don’t need to handle how the rollout engines re-shard or map the weights.
The existing disk-delta implementation in Miles1Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training, §4.3 Disk-Delta Updates. largely follows this design:
From the measurement above, the compressed payload is only 0.876 GB, matching our expectations. However, this benefit has been completely offset by other significant overheads:
- Trainer compression adds latency.
- Checkpoint patching requires a disk round trip.
- Rollout engines need to reload the entire checkpoint from disk.
GPU accelerated (de)compression#
The RL stack already runs on distributed GPU clusters, so the intuitive next step is to make this pipeline GPU-accelerated, using their powerful parallel compute and high-bandwidth HBM.
A strong baseline with Blackwell-native DE#
Blackwell has a fixed-function Decompression Engine (DE) 2Decompression Engine FAQ. that performs certain supported decompression algorithms extremely efficiently. To make our baseline sufficiently strong, we directly codesign the GPU-accelerated pipeline with GPU-native (de)compression algorithms and Blackwell-native dedicated hardware.
The table below compares (de)compression algorithms on GPUs3NVIDIA nvCOMP Quick Decision Matrix, qualitative ratings.:
Table 1. GPU codec trade-offs and Decompression Engine support.
As shown in Fig. 4 above, the major overheads are on the receiver side, including decompression, checkpoint patching, and engine reload. Therefore, we prioritize receiver-side decompression performance, starting with LZ4/Snappy for a fast GPU codec pipeline.
LZ4 and Snappy are from the same algorithm family 4LZ4 and Snappy are byte-oriented LZ77 codecs: both encode literals and backward copies, without an entropy-coding stage. See the Snappy format and LZ4 block format., with one noticeable difference in how the copy commands are encoded. A single Snappy copy command can cover at most 64 bytes. LZ4, however, can encode a much longer region directly with fewer copy commands. Because the RL update masks are mostly filled with long sequences of zeros, LZ4 tends to compress the final payloads more compactly than Snappy. Note that the exact results can be implementation specific. Our experimental results support this intuition. On the same proxy mask, nvCOMP LZ4 compressed more compactly than Snappy. The LZ4 baseline produces a complete publication of 5.36 GB. Therefore, we choose LZ4 as the codec for this design.
Since we have decided to use GPUs for decompression, the decompressed masks are already resident in GPU HBM, and paying for a disk round trip for checkpoint patching does not make sense. Therefore, we implemented Triton kernels to apply the bitwise XOR in place in GPU HBM. The tiling and address mapping between model layers and decompressed masks can be complicated, so we prepare this metadata on the CPU and let the Triton kernel read from the prepared plan. As a result, the XOR application stage can be done extremely efficiently by a single Triton kernel launch for the entire model.
On the trainer side, we employ all the existing GPUs used by distributed training to compress the masks in parallel. Distributed training already means distributed tensor ownership, but it may still duplicate some model weights, especially with context parallelism (CP) and data parallelism (DP). For compression, we remap weight ownership so that the GPU ranks collectively cover the entire model checkpoint exactly once, with each rank owning only a subset of the weights it holds for distributed training. This has three major advantages:
- Compression is greatly accelerated by parallelizing it across the existing training GPUs.
- Weight-gathering traffic is greatly reduced because we only need to gather rank-local compressed payloads instead of the original model weights.
- The memory pressure from holding earlier versions of the weights is greatly mitigated across all the existing ranks.
Putting the design together: all trainer GPUs compress concurrently, rollout GPUs decompress LZ4 directly using DE, and a single Triton kernel launch updates all model weights in HBM. All weight-sync network traffic carries compressed payloads, and disk checkpoints are completely out of the hot path. This is already an extremely strong baseline: for the same proxy payload, trainer-side preparation and compression take 0.834 s, and receiver-side work takes 6.041 s.
Working with low-precision RL#
Since compression, decompression, and bitwise XOR all treat model weights as a contiguous buffer of bits, delta weight sync works losslessly with low-precision RL.
Low-precision weights can even absorb small high-precision updates, such as changes to low mantissa bits, making the delta payload even smaller.
An interesting detail is how to work with high-performance MoE kernels like the one we described in Faster-than-light NVFP4 decode—with precision. To achieve aggressive fusion, high-performance kernels may reorder the logical weights into a different physical layout. See the example below of pairing gate and up weights in groups of 64. Using model checkpoints as handoffs dodged this complexity earlier, but we have to solve it when we want to update the weights in place.
Since the decompressed masks have the same shapes as the model weights, we can remap the masks the exact same way so they become pointwise aligned with the remapped model weights again. This adds another layer of complexity to the tiling and address mapping between model layers and decompressed masks, but all of this metadata is prepared on the CPU. The Triton kernel for XOR application only needs to read the prepared plan.
The remaining trade-offs#
We already have an extremely strong baseline: for the same proxy payload, trainer-side preparation and compression take 0.834 s, and receiver-side work takes 6.041 s. However, two critical flaws remain:
- Payload size. On the same proxy workload, the nvCOMP LZ4 payload size is 5.36 GB, while the CPU Zstd baseline is only 0.876 GB, so LZ4 transfers 6.1x as many bytes. GPU-friendly compression algorithms do not necessarily optimize for a high compression ratio. According to Table 1, there is no single compression algorithm that combines a high compression ratio, fast decompression, and DE support.
- GPU buffer size. GPU decompression also means GPU input and output buffers. To fit the large decompressed masks in HBM, we must evict the KV cache. First, this complicates memory lifetime management. More importantly, evicting the KV cache effectively makes overlapping rollout decoding with decompression impossible, since the KV cache is gone.
From accelerator to teleporter#
We now show how to turn GPUs from accelerators into teleporters, reducing the rollout pause for weight sync to under 0.23 s.
Double compression with heterogeneous decompression#
Compressed payloads can still contain repetition, especially with GPU-friendly algorithms that do not necessarily optimize for compression ratio. We therefore consider adding a round of Zstd compression on top of GPU-friendly codecs such as LZ4 or Snappy:
Table 2. Payload sizes before and after outer Zstd compression.
Empirically, Snappy + Zstd produces a meaningful reduction in payload size compared with the LZ4 baseline. Adding Zstd to LZ4, however, provides a smaller improvement. One possible explanation is that Snappy’s simpler copy commands are easier for Zstd to compress, even though Snappy is less efficient than LZ4 at encoding long runs of zeros in a single pass.
Double (de)compression unlocks receiver-side design opportunities beyond reducing payload size. Since the outer Zstd stage operates on small, already compressed payloads, the CPU can handle this decompression efficiently without using GPU compute or HBM. Rollout decoding can continue normally while the CPU receives the delta update payload, prepares metadata, performs the outer decompression, and stages the resulting Snappy payload in pinned CPU RAM buffers for the GPUs to consume later.
DE can directly consume pinned CPU RAM and output to GPU HBM5CUDA Driver API cuMemCreate, using CU_MEM_LOCATION_TYPE_HOST_NUMA and CU_MEM_CREATE_USAGE_HW_DECOMPRESS in allocFlags.usage. Ordinary pinned allocations are not sufficient; see NVIDIA’s DE memory requirements., which fits seamlessly into this CPU-GPU decompression pipeline. This also eliminates the need for input staging buffers in HBM, slightly reducing GPU memory pressure. We also found empirically that this approach achieves higher host-device transfer bandwidth than our own ring-buffer implementation.
Overlapping DE and SM#
To fully saturate DE, we use one final feature. Since DE is a fixed-function hardware block for decompression, its work can overlap with GPU compute on the streaming multiprocessors (SMs). For our use case, this means overlapping DE decompression with the Triton bitwise XOR kernel on the SMs. We designed a double-buffered software pipeline in which DE decompresses into one slot while the SMs read from the other. We stream all model weights through these buffers, layer by layer:
As the Nsight Systems profiling trace above shows, the DE pipeline is fully saturated, and Triton kernels are completely hidden by the DE setup-decompression loop, bringing the pause below 0.23 s.
This double-buffered streaming design also eliminates the need for a decompression output buffer for the full model. The two buffers only need to hold two model layers at a time, so they fit within the GPU memory outside the KV cache, typically reserved for activations during inference. No KV cache eviction or changes to the inference engine’s GPU memory pool are needed.
Assembling the weight teleporter#
Now it is time to assemble the complete GPU weight teleporter in our RL stack:
Since Snappy is a more GPU-friendly compression algorithm, the combined trainer-side preparation and compression time falls from 0.834 s with LZ4 to 0.789 s, even with an extra round of Zstd compression. The rollout engines take 2.355 s to pull the payload, prepare metadata, decompress the outer Zstd layer, and stage the Snappy payload. Rollout inference can continue normally because preparation uses neither GPU compute nor GPU memory. Only DE-SM streaming blocks inference, for just 219.6 ms.
Beyond the steady-state RL loop#
So far, we have mainly focused on steady-state trainer-rollout weight updates, the core RL hot path. However, this approach also provides general-purpose infrastructure for other use cases:
Eval, fault tolerance, and resuming from trained checkpoints#
Unlike steady-state trainer-rollout weight updates, where the version always increments by one, several use cases in the RL loop require updating from different weight versions:
Table 3. Base versions for evaluation, recovery, and resumed training.
These use cases require maintaining deltas against at least two additional versions: the last eval version and the rollout/eval engines’ base version. Due to our fully distributed ownership design on the trainer side, the weights are sharded and distributed across the entire training engine. Each CPU only needs to hold the extra versions of its assigned shards, without adding significant memory overhead. Also, the processing for these auxiliary deltas can be easily overlapped with the payload transmission or preparation phase on the trainer-rollout hot path, without lengthening the rollout pause, which remains below 0.23 s.
Another important detail about resuming from a trained checkpoint is that the resumed checkpoint may have advanced many steps beyond the base version and accumulated a decent amount of delta. How do we make sure the rollout engines still have enough memory buffers for staging the larger delta? The LZ4 + Zstd codec we previously did not adopt becomes a good fit here. It has a larger final payload size, but the startup transfer only happens once and can overlap with other startup work. The smaller inner payload size helps to keep the staging buffer small even with a larger accumulated delta. The trainer-rollout hot path can still use the Snappy + Zstd codec to benefit from the small final payload size.
Inference deployment and beyond#
This infrastructure also greatly simplifies inference serving and deployment. Whenever a new trained checkpoint comes out, we only need to send its tiny compressed delta across data centers instead of a full model checkpoint. The inference engine launches from a base checkpoint and simply makes a single call to /update_weights_from_gpu_delta to pull and apply the latest delta. To release resources that are no longer needed in a pure inference use case, we have implemented an opt-in release_state argument that will automatically clear any staging buffers, GPU kernels, and CPU threads related to delta updates after the delta is applied.
We also treat this infrastructure as a superior alternative to LoRA adapters to some extent. Our approach compresses full-parameter deltas into tiny final payloads, while LoRA keeps the payload small by limiting the ranks of the updates. What’s more, our approach can swap different deltas on and off during serving with just one API call and a pause of less than 0.23 s, completely imperceptible to end users.
Speeding up research iterations#
Together, these capabilities let us iterate on research experiments much more rapidly. During each training checkpoint export step, we always export the auxiliary compressed delta against the base version and save it to disk. We can immediately move it across data centers and conduct experiments without waiting for checkpoint conversion or inter-cluster checkpoint transfer. The inference endpoints can immediately pull the refreshed delta on the fly with just one API call and do not need to restart.
We have also removed a major source of network traffic both between clusters and within our cluster. As a small bonus, this also helps relieve network congestion and improve stability.
Open source#
We have open-sourced the implementation across the stack:
- Orchestration, distributed GPU compression, fault tolerance, and delta checkpointing in Miles6Miles GPU-delta publication and receiver coordination..
- The heterogeneous decompression pipeline with full DE-SM overlap, optimized Triton kernels, and the one-shot /update_weights_from_gpu_delta API in SGLang7SGLang GPU-delta decompression and in-place weight updates..
This effort uses nvCOMP heavily. We thank the NVIDIA nvCOMP team for their high-performance implementations of compression and decompression algorithms.
Conclusion#
We do not foresee further work on RL weight sync because we believe this is the optimal solution for existing hardware. The rollout pause time is so short, the CPU/GPU memory footprint is so small, and the support for fault tolerance is so complete that even the best intra-cluster P2P RDMA implementation becomes obsolete. We have used one of the fastest GPU-native codecs, fully saturated the DE pipeline, and overlapped SM work; the bottleneck for weight sync has become hardware throughput.

How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:34:39 UTC
01:34:39 KST

inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more, has decided to embrace the modding community. In an interview with The Verge, inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell said, “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want.” That “toolbox” includes making the code for devices like the recently teased MPC Sample Key open source, but also offering developers an SDK to make modifications easier and lessen the risk of bricking your beloved sampler.
How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
inMusic is making open-source MPCs, hackable synths, and mod-friendly DJ decks.
While Akai is eager to see what the modding community cooks up, and has started seeding devices to developers ahead of the official release of the Sample Key, the company takes reliability seriously. O’Donnell said the company wants to “make sure that our official software is completely stable and good for an artist on stage.” He can’t have Fred Again going on stage and discovering his MPC is riddled with bugs. But he also wants people to feel comfortable tinkering. “We’ll try to give them a reset button,” he said so “They can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”
The company is planning to make a big splash NAMM, the annual convention of music manufacturers in Anaheim, with Creator Lab, where it will let technically curious musicians get some hands-on time hacking 22 new products from across its brands. That includes products from Moog, that might not seem like a natural pairing for vibe coding because of its analog design. But O’Donnell thinks it can be, “if we open it up correctly.” That will involve building a platform for devs to work around the analog parts of the circuit.
Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, Polyend open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes, and Behringer has also announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller.
The change in the industry has been quick and seismic. O’Donnell said of the need to provide developers tools for hacking inMusic’s products, “I can tell you it wasn’t on our task list five weeks ago. It just all of a sudden has to be on a task list now.”
Of course, not everyone is thrilled. Elektron has expressed mixed feelings about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned linking to hacks and modified firmware from its official forums, though not discussing them generally, citing concerns about the possibility of damaging instruments. A statement posted on its forums says: “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”
While Elektron doesn’t want people posting links to hacked Digitone firmware on its forums, it’s not actively trying to thwart the modding community. The consensus is there’s no going back now that vibe coding has upended the music gear world, and trying to stand in the way would be a mistake. inMusic’s O’Donnell told the Verge, “you can try to wall them off, which is just a losing battle one … and so we want to embrace them.”

Rune: A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:31:32 UTC
01:31:32 KST

A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, with its own renderer, text, layout and springs.
Every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive it with scripted input.
fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let label = text(if s.on { "Lights on" } else { "Lights off" })
        .font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text);
    let knob = el().key("knob").size(18.0, 18.0).radius(9.0).fill(t.knob)
        .absolute(if s.on { 18.0 } else { 2.0 }, 2.0);
    let switch = el().key("switch").role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on)
        .focusable(true).size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
        .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
        .motion(motion::SNAPPY)
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on)
        .child(knob);
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(16.0).fill(t.bg).child(label).child(switch)
}
Give your coding agent this repo. Have it start from examples/hello and crates/rune/README.md, then check its own work headlessly by rendering PNGs and inspecting the element tree.

Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
Vincent Bernat
To optimize the performance metrics of this blog, I relied on Amazon CloudFront to serve the assets,1 and Route 53 for the geo-aware DNS2 to direct readers to the closest host serving the content. But Route 53 is expensive: US$0.50 per zone per month, US$0.70 per million geolocation queries, and US$0.75 per healthcheck per month[1], plus US$1 per month for the KMS key[2] needed to sign zones with DNSSEC. When I discovered that Bunny DNS is almost free[3] for up to 500 domains and features scriptable answers, I made the jump! Plus, it’s a European company based in Slovenia.
Bunny CDN#
Bunny.net[4] started as BunnyCDN in 2015[5]. They added IPv6
support in 2017[6]. Switching was uneventful. I don’t bring a custom domain: I
serve the content from the b-cdn.net domain. As I depend on content
negotiation to serve AVIF and WebP images[7], I configure the CDN to cache
each image format separately[8].
I disable logging[9] to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page[10] promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.
The only downside of the bunny.net CDN offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no ETA to share.
Bunny DNS#
Bunny.net introduced their DNS offering in 2022[11] and recently reduced its cost to almost zero[3]. They support geographical routing[12], but a very cool feature is the scriptable DNS[13]: it runs a piece of user-supplied JavaScript on each query to compute the answer.
I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny’s scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the two nearest servers. The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.
const servers = [
  {
    ipv4: "45.90.160.60",
    ipv6: "2a0c:8881:5:100::1",
    latitude: 48.88,
    longitude: 2.22,
  },
  /* […] */
  {
    ipv4: "139.180.162.114",
    ipv6: "2001:19f0:5800:1855:5400:6ff:fef0:4c0a",
    latitude: -33.87,
    longitude: 151.21,
  },
];
const families = { A: "ipv4", AAAA: "ipv6" };
const records = { A: ARecord, AAAA: AaaaRecord };
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const type = String(query.request.queryType).toUpperCase();
  const family = families[type];
  if (!family) return [];
  // Get user location
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  // Build a list of candidates
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s[family], s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest alive servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Return their IP addresses
  return selected.map((s) => new records[type](s.ip, 3600));
}
The above script relies on the
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer()[14] helper, which returns the
closest alive3 server to the user.4 Thanks to Doggo[15], we can
check it works as expected, at least for A:5
$ doggo --gp-from="Amsterdam" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Amsterdam, NL
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  45.90.160.60
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  116.203.18.48
$ doggo --gp-from="Texas" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Houston (TX), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
The most annoying drawback of this method is that a user from Buenos Aires gets both São Paulo (1000 mi, 30 ms RTT) and Ashburn (5200 mi, 140 ms RTT). Most resolvers randomize the order, so the user may pull the web page from Ashburn. We could return only the nearest server—and swap the scripted record with the built-in geographic routing instead. But if the server becomes unavailable, the browser has no alternative until the DNS cache expires. It leaves a short window of unavailability, even with a short TTL.
The HTTPS record solution#
The HTTPS DNS record[19], defined in RFC 9460[20], solves both the availability and the latency issues. Modern browsers query this record to get additional information to reach an HTTP server, including an alternative port and the application layer protocol—HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Each record has a priority. We can ask browsers to contact the nearest server first and fall back to the next one if the first is unavailable:
vincent    HTTPS  1 first.geo  alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  2 second.geo alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  3 .          alpn="h3,h2"
; Bunny DNS must provide the two closest servers as "first.geo"
; and "second.geo" with geographic or latency routing.
first.geo  A      45.90.160.60
first.geo  AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
second.geo A      116.203.18.48
second.geo AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
vincent    A      45.90.160.60
vincent    A      116.203.18.48
vincent    AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
vincent    AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
This looks like the ideal solution! Unfortunately, Chrome ignores any record
whose target is not .[21], hence the last record at priority 3.
Moreover, unlike with a CNAME, Bunny DNS does not return the IP addresses for
first.geo and second.geo in the additional section. The resolver needs to
send a first request to get the HTTPS record, and a second to resolve
first.geo.
HTTPS records are still too new[22] for this use case. Back to the drawing board! 📐
The hybrid solution#
As a compromise, the script returns the two nearest servers if they are at a similar distance from the user. Otherwise, it returns only the nearest one with a lower TTL of 2 minutes.
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s.ipv4, s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Compute the distance to the user for each of them
  const [first, second] = selected.map((s) =>
    GeoDistance.calculate(s, location),
  );
  // If the second one is at twice the distance and at more than 1000 miles
  // from the first, return only the first one with a TTL of 2 minutes.
  if (second > 2 * first && second - first > 1000) {
    return [new ARecord(selected[0].ip, 120)];
  }
  // Otherwise, return both with a TTL of 1 hour.
  return selected.map((s) => new ARecord(s.ip, 3600));
}
We can check it with Doggo. From Chicago, we get only the Ashburn server with a TTL of 2 minutes, while from Mexico, we get both Ashburn and San Jose.
$ doggo --gp-from="Chicago" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Chicago (IL), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     120s   5.161.44.145
$ doggo --gp-from="Mexico" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Queretaro, MX
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
$ doggo --reverse 5.161.44.145 149.28.219.155
NAME                          TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
145.44.161.5.in-addr.arpa.    PTR   7187s  web05.luffy.cx.
155.219.28.149.in-addr.arpa.  PTR   3600s  web07.luffy.cx.
Note
On the live page[23], the map below is interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.
Note
Enable JavaScript to make the map below interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.
This page was brought to you by ???. Check on the map below whether it matches your
location!
The complete code[18] is a bit more complex. It works around
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() supporting only IPv4, and it handles the case
where there are not enough alive servers to build an answer.
Bunny.net has a comprehensive Terraform provider[24]. I leverage CDK Terrain[25] to build the target state in TypeScript and OpenTofu[26] to deploy it. Have a look at “Managing infrastructure with Terraform, CDKTF, and NixOS[27]” for more details.6
ACME DNS with Hickory DNS#
Route 53 covered one additional use case of mine: serving acme.luffy.cx to
solve DNS-01 ACME challenges[29]. Unlike Route 53, Bunny DNS cannot
restrict access to a single zone with a fine-grained access policy. As this
usage requires neither high availability nor low latency, I replaced Route 53
with Hickory[30], a memory-safe DNS server written in Rust. It supports
automatic DNSSEC signatures[31] and dynamic updates[32]. Its
configuration is simple:
[[zones]]
zone = "acme.luffy.cx"
zone_type = "Primary"
[zones.stores]
allow_update = true
type = "sqlite"
journal_path = "acme.luffy.cx.sqlite"
zone_path = "acme.luffy.cx.zone"
# Private key to sign the zone with DNSSEC. Generated with:
#  openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256
[[zones.keys]]
algorithm = "ECDSAP256SHA256"
key_path = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.pem"
# TSIG key to sign zone updates. Generated with:
#  openssl rand 32
[[zones.stores.tsig_keys]]
algorithm = "hmac-sha256"
key_file = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.update.acme.luffy.cx.tsig"
name = "update.acme.luffy.cx."
The provided zone file[33] only seeds the database on first start. I delegate
DNS-01 challenges to this zone with CNAME records:
_acme-challenge          CNAME bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
_acme-challenge.vincent  CNAME vincent.bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
Lego[34], the ACME client I use to get certificates from Let’s Encrypt[35], answers the DNS-01 challenge by pushing entries with the DNS UPDATE protocol[36].
Unfortunately, Bunny DNS cannot publish a DS record in a zone.7 I need one
to secure the acme.luffy.cx zone and certificate delivery. Therefore, I host
the luffy.cx zone on deSEC[37],8 a free DNS hosting service run by a
non-profit organization based in Berlin. I derive the DS record to publish in
luffy.cx from the DNSKEY record of acme.luffy.cx:
$ ZONE=acme.luffy.cx
$ dig @nsupdate.luffy.cx $ZONE DNSKEY +noall +answer \
>   | dnssec-dsfromkey -a SHA-256 -f - $ZONE
acme.luffy.cx. IN DS 55628 13 2 4946E7508F20E15F1B577A231104B029A1A82E04699A80CD46ADCE31227EE81F
Overall, I am quite happy with the switch to bunny.net. There are still a few
rough edges, like the inability to publish DS records, the lack of HTTP/3, and
the IPv4-only RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper. The bill went from US$5
per month to US$1. So far, performance is on par with AWS[39], but I
only finalized the current setup, including the server in Sydney, in late
October. I need a bit more time to gather more data, and I’ll post a short update. 📈
Update (2026-11)
This post was briefly discussed on Hacker News[40].

Promethevs: Full DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017, locally, on 12GB of VRAM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:14:47 UTC
01:14:47 KST

The original model, not a smaller copy · 64 GB of RAM and one 12 GB NVIDIA card · free and open source
PROMETHEVS runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, one of the strongest open models, from all 510 GB of its original weights, on an ordinary PC that cannot even load it: a Ryzen 9 3950X with 64 GB of DDR4, an RTX 3060 with 12 GB and two NVMe drives.
The PROMETHEVS engine gets there with compress-then-correct, a method devised by Ryan Flavell. Every word is first computed on a 2-bit copy of the model's experts. When the model itself is unsure (its top two choices are close), that word is recomputed with the original weights, rebuilt exactly from a stored correction plane. You get close to the speed of the compressed copy and close to the answers of the full model.
- Full-model quality, counted. On 960 audited words the output picks the full model's word 98.3% of the time (the 2-bit copy alone: 97.4%).
- Up to 7.4 tokens/s on a code prompt (warm cache, best case), against 2.14 for running the full model exactly on the same PC. Server runs: 5 to 8 on code, 4.5 to 5.4 on reasoning and agent prompts.
- Fast follow-ups. Only the first read of a long prompt is slow; the engine keeps what it has read, so the next message in a conversation starts in about 2 seconds.
- Works with your tools. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on localhost, with streaming and tool calls, so apps and coding agents that speak the OpenAI API can use it.
- Private. The model runs on your PC; your chats stay there.
- Built from the original weights, on your machine. The installer downloads DeepSeek's weights and builds every store itself, checked against published hashes, so you do not have to trust our files.
- Free. Engine Apache-2.0; report, figures and logs CC BY 4.0.
New here? Check what you need, then install.
The hardware check in the bundle tests all of this and tells you up front if anything falls short. The full list is in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md.
- Download PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip from the latest release and extract it, for example to C:\promethevs_pkg.
- In PowerShell, from that folder:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\check_hardware.ps1        # checks the PC, picks the drives
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_stores.ps1 --run    # downloads the weights, builds the stores (resumable)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\start_engine.ps1          # starts the engine (about 1 minute)
python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed                                # checks it and measures the speed
- Point any OpenAI-compatible app at http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1, model deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-promethevs, any non-empty API key. Close other programs that use the graphics card first.
Every step, the time and disk each one takes, and the known gaps are in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md. Release notes: engine-0.2/RELEASE_NOTES_0.2.md.
Measured on the build machine, 160 new tokens per prompt, two passes per run. Cold is a pass that starts with an empty expert cache. Warm is the second pass of the same prompt with the cache kept from the first, which is the best case for a cache; a real session that sends a different prompt lies between the two. Every individual run is in RESULTS.md.
Agreement is measured word by word against the word the exact path would choose given the same history. A slip is a difference the engine did not check, because the model was confident; the unchecked count counts those. Counting every difference also includes the words the engine checked and deliberately kept at a near-tie (both words almost equally likely). On its own the 2-bit copy picks the full-weight word on 97.4 percent of words; with the corrections, 98.33 percent counting every difference (99.17 percent by the unchecked count). The engine differs from the baseline build in two ways: it holds the draft head's experts in the 2-bit format too, and it keeps the expert cache from the first pass into the second. Keeping the cache lifted the code prompt but not the reasoning or agent prompts (the report gives the round timers behind this). In all three warm code passes no correction overturned a word, so the cache, the 2-bit draft head and the absence of an overturn are not separated, and 7.4 is a best case, not a typical session.
The PROMETHEVS engine does four things at once.
A 2-bit copy answers every word. The experts are stored in a 2-bit format that is smaller than the original FP4, so each word needs fewer bytes from disk. That is what makes the machine fast enough to be useful.
The model's own confidence picks the words to redo. For each word the engine looks at the gap between the model's top two candidates. When the gap falls below a threshold, the gate (0.45 here), the word is flagged.
Flagged words are corrected exactly. A stored correction plane turns an expert's 2-bit copy back into the exact FP4 expert, so a correction is the full model's answer for that word.
A draft head proposes several words at a time. DeepSeek ships a draft head with the model. The engine checks its guesses together in parallel lanes, which spreads the cost of reading experts across several words. The experts the model uses most sit in GPU memory; the rest live in RAM and on the two drives.
The method is compress-then-correct, devised by Ryan Flavell; the PROMETHEVS engine is built around it. Speculative decoding, quantised drafts and offloaded mixture-of-experts inference are the work it builds on; the report sets the method beside the closest references.
The build machine is a Windows 11 desktop with 64 GB DDR4, an RTX 3060 12 GB, and two NVMe drives (2 TB and 1 TB). The stores need about 1,009 GiB: 475 GiB of raw weights plus 534 GiB of derived stores (2-bit copies, correction planes, and FP4 copies of the first layers). Disk is the largest barrier for anyone repeating this. We kept each drive below about 90 percent full.
Every number above comes from one PC. If you run release 0.2 on your own machine, please send the output of python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed and your engine log as a benchmark report. Reports are added here as they arrive.
Frontier-level AI today needs either a cloud subscription or hardware costing tens of thousands of pounds. Open-weight models are closing the gap with the closed frontier models, but running them still means someone else's server. PROMETHEVS, named after Prometheus, who in the myth brought fire to people, sets out to change that: frontier capability, at a speed close to the cloud, within 97 percent of what the original full weights would say, on a computer people already own. Release 0.1 published the method and every measurement; release 0.2 lets you run it.

We measured agreement against our own exact path; we have not yet run DeepSeek's reference implementation side by side. Speeds vary by prompt and by run, so we give every run. No prompt reaches the 8 tokens/s milestone we set, and the reasoning and agent prompts run below 5.3. First-word time on long prompts is read-bound: on a 1,163-token prompt the first word arrives after about 126 s (98 s with a candidate prompt-reading setting whose effect on quality we have not fully measured). The 99.17 percent figure covers three prompts of 30, 76 and 1,163 tokens. On a further 1,101-token agent prompt the engine scores 97.80 percent and the baseline build 97.16 (9 slips in 317 words), 0.16 points above our 97 percent contract at the gate we use (at gate 0.30 it falls to 96.21 percent); on a 4,288-token prompt the engine scores 100 percent and the baseline build 99.69. Counting every difference, both builds fall below 97 percent on the 1,101-token prompt (95.91 and 95.58 percent). Each long-prompt audit is one run. The chat template matches DeepSeek's encoder on six plain conversations; tool results and thinking mode are unchecked. All numbers come from one machine, one model and one prompt family.
REPRO.md outlines the steps we ran: download and verify the weights, build the stores, set the profile, run the benchmark. The scripts themselves ship in release 0.2 (PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip, see engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).

Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:05:36 UTC
01:05:36 KST

Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.
Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.
“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”
For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.
Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.
The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.

How the S-1 talks about existential risk
Zvi: Yeah. So as usual, when I look at anything from Anthropic, I want to see their attitude towards existential risk, alignment, whether or not they're going to potentially kill everyone.
So in this case, they mention existential risk only in passing, only in the passive voice. They're clearly trying to have it both ways. When they talk to the investors, they want to say, "Oh, look at our big mission, but our big mission is to build this super profitable hypercomputing thing." And then other times they want to say, "Our geniuses in the data center actually might kill everyone," and these two things have to coexist.
Similarly, pacing the frontier is something they do talk about here, but then they make clear to investors, "Don't worry. When we said pacing the frontier, we did not mean not making incredibly fast AI progress. We did not mean voluntarily let someone else go first. We just meant it would be great if everybody could collectively agree to go only at super speed and not at ludicrous speed." But they will do the embedded evaluations.
Similarly, we're all worried about recursive self-improvement. And here they call that "closing the loop" to be more business-friendly, but they say that their entire business model is they want to close the loop. They are worried that if someone else closes the loop before they close the loop, they will be out of the loop and they will lose.
So they intend to close the loop as fast as possible and as much as possible.
Patrick: I feel like there is an interesting tension around S-1s, because we largely have this culture in the tech industry of, necessarily, Zuck speaks for Facebook and Facebook speaks for Zuck. Tech has done complicated innovations with share classes that enable the founder/company relationship to be relatively durable over a period of years and decades.
[Patrick notes: Facebook was not the first company to issue super-voting founder shares but it popularized the model. Pattern matching goes both ways with Silicon Valley investors: you should believe your new investment is the second coming of Facebook. If you don’t, stop now; returns in venture are heavily weighted towards a handful of generational companies, and the entire game is spreading out your fund such that you are definitely in them and persuading the founder that you will be easy to work with (and so please don’t cut your allocation in any round). If you believe you are investing in the next Facebook, you affirmatively want the next Zuck at the helm durably regardless of how diluted their economic stake gets as they raise capital. Public market investors, seeing a company which grew from a dorm room to a global power, largely seem to accept precedent on provisions guaranteeing founder control. If founders have them at IPO, they keep them.]

But when you get the quote-unquote "responsible adults" in the room — S-1s are largely drafted by external counsel and counsel working for the banks that are the underwriters of the S-1.
Responsible adults say: "We all understand that everyone in the tech industry thinks that the CEO runs the company. However, managerial capitalism says that the CEO only runs the company to the extent that they're not fired by the board on behalf of the shareholders.

Founder control and Anthropic's share classes
Patrick: Cool. Shall we go to the second part of your takeaways, which was on control, I think?
Zvi: Anthropic has long had an attitude, like many tech companies, as you point out, that the founders should continue to control the company, and that the worst thing that could happen to Anthropic would be to have the likes of Google and Amazon suddenly having them maximize shareholder value and then thinking about only corporate things. And then their company would probably go out there and increase the risk that the world is destroyed, and lose their unique company culture, and this would be extremely bad.

Anthropic's anticipation is this will last until long after the fate of the world has been decided one way or another. And this seems rather likely, because there are something like nine of them, and only three of them have to keep showing up.

Patrick: I don't think I've ever heard of another company explicitly privileging employees with share classes. Generally, it's something of the reverse.
[Patrick notes: Employees most typically get stock options or restricted stock units which are designed to convert into common stock, or into a second class of common that is economically identical and differs only in voting, with the distinction typically disappearing after IPO or sale. Companies sometimes offer employees inducements to impair their stock in some way, such as accepting a voting proxy agreement (ceding their votes to the founders) in return for e.g. better-than-market exercise terms for their options.
Common shares vote like Republicans in Chicago: mathematically you have no say in outcomes, but you do have a right to have your opinion tallied.]

The traditional thing to do in the tech industry is to have the employees proxy their votes to the founders, and the founders literally get to vote them in whichever way they want. And you're, in doing this, suggesting, "No, I think the employees are sufficiently philosophically aligned with management that they will proxy without a proxy agreement being in place," which is an interesting point of view.
And I'm not saying "interesting" as a way of saying I don't think it is well-calibrated. [Patrick notes: Many companies experience, after hypergrowth, discontent among long-time employees (and sometimes founders) that the company has lost something special in the culture. You then intentionally, as a mechanical consequence of hypergrowth and with your eyes open, hired 10 people with impeccable credentials from AppAmaGooBookSoft for every one who previously worked with you. You will always find your culture drawn to the median culture of AppAmaGooBookSoft as a result of this choice. You will be warned about it in advance, and you will say “It will not happen here!” It will happen to you. It happened to AppAmaGooBookSoft, too.]
Patrick continues: Not that there is another company at that revenue growth rate to point to, but we will get to that in a moment, I think.
Zvi: Well, so before we move on, I would say Anthropic has long cultivated a very special company culture that has a large awareness of safety, but also of altruistic goals and charity and making the world a better place.
The founders have famously pledged 80% of their shares to charity, and they've offered very, very generous matching donations for those who want to give their stock away. And in fact, how much stock you gave away determines how many Class E shares you have to vote. So they're, on several levels, determining, no, these are the preselected people who have very, very costly signaled that they want to influence the future in generally good ways, rather than build personal wealth and maximize profits.
Those are the people who will ultimately make the tie-breaking vote in this situation, and that is exactly what that was selected for.
Anthropic's uncapped donation matching
Patrick: I couldn't find if this was explicitly called out in the S-1, and I will edit the transcript if I missed it in my first two readings. But their matching program for employees might be one of the most expensive single corporate decisions ever made in the history of capitalism.
The matching program for employees was, I hear, calibrated to essentially allow employees to do something similar to what the founders were doing, and give away 80% of their economic stake. And to make those numbers work, they said that the corporation will basically match employee donations on a 3:1 basis, which is unheard of in the rest of capitalism.
And additionally, typically a corporate matching program is: okay, we will match on a one-to-one basis up to, let's say, $7,000 a year. And so you say, okay, well, optimally executed, that option is worth $7,000 to charity, and perhaps $10,000, $11,000 or so in pre-tax income. The Anthropic matching program is uncapped.
And so there are employees that will donate $20 million to charity and have it get backed by $60 million of Anthropic money in the wake of the IPO and their continued operation and similar. And when you sum that over extremely charitably minded employees, times thousands of them, times many of them that have presumptively eight- and nine-figure equity values, which they will quickly be giving away, that is just going to be an extremely expensive decision.
Zvi: Yeah, but they got what they wanted out of it. You want to strongly differentiate yourself as an employer and attract aligned employees.
If you're not committed to the mission, it sounds expensive, but if you are mission-aligned, the expense is a positive. And when you turn out to be the fastest-growing company in history, and the stock is worth close to $2 trillion, it will be a larger line item than you thought.
But at the same time, you'll be able to afford it conditional on success, so it works both ways.
Postscript: what the matching program will actually cost
Patrick injects via new recording: I failed at Ctrl+F prior to recording. The S-1 does indeed mention the donation matching program in a few places. For example, it says that the Class N shares are reserved against the need to make good on these commitments, and the company took a $2 billion non-cash charge in Q3 related to it.
So in terms of cash, the matching program will be close to free. Shareholders as a class, inclusive of donors, pay for it through dilution. In terms of accounting, though, when you promise people compensation worth billions of dollars, we want to record the fact that you have promised billions of dollars.
When you promise them compensation based on future world states, we update the cost of that promise as we learn more about the future. I suspect the Q3 charge is very far from the last non-cash charge attributable to the matching program. Future charges will happen as employees make new pledges, as past pledges not yet settled get remarked from a 409A valuation to the public price, and, probably the dominant factor, as currently pledged equity continues to vest and gets matched at public market prices rather than the private ones.
The S-1 suggests there is presently about $24 billion in unvested equity compensation, with that calculation being made as of the day the equity was granted. When the cost of the match is calculated, it is calculated the day the equity vests, which will probably be at a higher valuation.
And then you assume that much of the equity is going to employees eligible for three-to-one matching at the new mark, and much of the remainder to employees eligible for one-to-one matching at the new mark, and that probably tens of percent of it will be donated. And so, yep, that is almost certainly the most expensive perk in the history of capitalism.
I suspect the magnitude of the first post-IPO charges is going to surprise people. Much has been written, including by my former colleague Nan, of the coming tidal wave of charitable donations. A large portion of that tidal wave flows through Anthropic's P&L.
Revenue growth and cohort economics
Zvi: So the next section of questions is about money, of course.
So Anthropic is one of the fastest-growing companies in history. We're talking about 10x year over year for several years in a row. We're talking, in some places, even greater than that. First two quarters this year were completely nuts.
Patrick: About 15x in the first half, right?
[Patrick notes: $1.16 billion in H1 2025 to $16.3 billion in H1 2026, so about 14x, though what is one entire prior-year half between friends.]
Zvi: Right. Approximately, something like that, 15x in the first half, from a very large baseline to begin with, rather than from very small amounts.
I mean, in the beginning it was like, okay, you're 10x-ing, but this is not unheard of because it's a very small company. Now it's a relatively large company, and people are asking questions like, how many times can you 10x? The entire economy is only so big. There are only so many Fortune 500 companies.
It's just 500. At some point you're going to run out of targets. But that's not necessarily something we're getting close to. Quarter three, they did slow their growth. So their growth was still the envy of almost every company on Earth, but by their own standards, it was reasonably small.
We have a variety of explanations for this. Anthropic was relatively badly positioned in terms of the quality of their available models and their appeal to business, compared to how they had been in the previous period or in the later period that we're in now. So that's probably my guess as to the main reason.
There's also some talk about quarter three just being a slow period for growth, relatively speaking, due to the calendar. But my expectation is that quarter three was relatively slow, but that quarter four has picked up again, and you will see some very, very large growth numbers out of Anthropic.
Patrick: In analysis of securities, we have to pretend that the gross quarter-to-quarter revenue results matter. But in this case, I think Anthropic is properly modeled more or less as a software company, where what you are doing is stacking cohorts together. And for reasons, we do not require software companies to break out their cohort numbers in S-1s and similar.
[Patrick notes: This is extremely well-understood among the best managers in the world, and relatively well-understood among investors. One classic articulation of it is Bezos’ in 2017, referencing a much slower-moving business which was once the fastest growing business of all time: “Those quarterly results were fully baked three years ago. So today I'm working on a quarter that will happen in 2020, not next quarter. Next quarter is done already and it's probably been done for a couple years.”]
If we did, that would be a fascinating window into the growth of the business. And so the cohorts are often heterogeneous with each other, and so the customers that you recruited in Q3 2026 are at a different point in their ramp of spend than the customers you recruited in Q3 2025, than in 2024.
And the very interesting thing that you would want to see on those graphs is: do they asymptote at any point? And finger to the wind, my guess is the answer is no. The S-1 says they have a net revenue retention of 900%, which is silly for any other SaaS business. If you were doing 110%, that would be wonderful.
[Patrick notes: Slight exaggeration; that’s workmanlike execution for an IPOable SaaS company selling on annual contracts.]
But my guess is their "early adopter customers," the ones that were there in the ancient history of two years ago, have not figured the limits of cognition in their businesses yet, and are continuing to pour money at tokens and get business results out. And if you were hypothetically in a world where a cohort graph would show that, okay, after the first two years of adoption, the growth pace goes to that of a normal software business, then you would be much more bearish on Anthropic and labs generally as a business.
I suspect we are not in that world. I suspect the line for people that have been on two years continues to be vertical, and it will look less vertical in the first three months of a customer's life, as they do things like internal pilots, IT starts to get involved, yada, yada, yada, all that fun stuff for the absorption of this technology in the world.
And so I suspect quarter-to-quarter softness in the number is more an artifact of how the cohort graphs stack up than it is an artifact of the total corporate positioning relative to competitors in that quarter. But I do not have internal numbers on this. Obviously, if I had internal numbers, I would not be able to share them.
Postscript: Q3 was a supply story, not a demand story
Patrick: After recording the episode, I thought through this a bit more, including with Claude assisting, and have a better hypothesis.
As I mentioned, it is useful to have lenses available, like being a SaaS-y guy, because it lets you see the world in terms of cohorts. It sometimes impairs your vision, though, because you imagine every business as having arbitrarily high margins and the ability to scale to customer demand as quickly as DevOps can type into their terminal.
Anthropic is, importantly, less like a software business in those respects. Anthropic says in the S-1, "We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us." Their ability to service revenue from fully bought-in customers is limited by the contracted, racked, powered GPUs available to them.
The S-1 says historically they make these arrangements 12 to 18 months in advance. And so, in roughly Q1 or Q2 of 2025, they had to make a guess as to how compute efficient a yet-to-be-released Opus 5.5 would be, and how much customers would be willing to use it.
Anthropic seems to have underestimated or —in Zvi's parlance elsewhere—perhaps simply not to have been aggressive enough.
Their Q3 revenue softening isn't a demand story. It's a supply story. They're running all the GPUs they have, and it just isn't enough. Supporting evidence: they talk about hitting the spot market for GPUs for $5 billion, at substantially more than their multi-year commitments typically run, in such a way as to eat 10% of the margin just from the shift in the mix.
You'd assume low tens of percent of revenue is served by spot compute, but that spot compute made up 50% of their compute spend for the quarter. The S-1 says "short-term commitments," which might not line up one-to-one with, for example, how AWS will sell you a spot instance. Roll with me here on the lingo.
The important bit is that you're paying through the nose for availability as a trade-off for not contracting for that capacity in advance. And so why has the revenue softened? Either because you want to make the principled decision that you don't want to climb the cost curve in the spot market and sell at wafer-thin margins or for a loss just to inflate your top-line metrics, or perhaps because you just tapped all the spot that capitalism had available in Q3 2026.
I think analysts who read this as softening demand would need to explain tapping spot for 50% of one's spend. I frankly don't think there is an explanation available there. These analysts are just straightforwardly wrong. Even if one allocates all of the spot compute to training runs for Opus 6.x or whatever, that's still saying they fully saturated the long-term contracted chips, and their customers still had tokens waiting.
Is it a bubble?

And they say this every time the number 10xes, which has been a remarkably large number of times. And yes, at some point, number has gone up, and estimates of the future rate of number going up will go down, and therefore stock price will go down even as the token usage and the revenue numbers go up. And at that point, people will talk about the bubble bursting, and they will be wrong.
That is the default. Obviously, nothing I say is investment advice. As per usual, nothing you say is investment advice. But it's very easy to predict who will continuously predict these things happening and who will not.

Sizing the market for tokens
Patrick: Five years ago, I thought there is a reasonable chance that LLMs asymptote “just a bit higher than where we are today” on the capabilities curve. We'd have to hit an incredibly narrow bullseye for that to happen.

The commodification bear case
Zvi: The bear case is essentially the expectation by many of commodification. It's the idea that, well, the cheaper, faster, open-weight, competitive models are going to be good enough for whatever you want to do.
You will choose to use them instead. If Anthropic's models don't get better, then a year from now, they would think, well, okay, at that point, the DeepSeek model or the Qwen model will be almost as good, and it will be cheaper and faster. So if all that Anthropic does is make their own model cheaper and faster, this will destroy their revenue margins, and their business will no longer function.
But there's no longer a case of, oh, AI doesn't do much, and the economy will adopt almost no AI. Again, even if AI is the minimum it could possibly be, and we never see another release that's any good again, and Carbon turns out to be terrible, and Fable 5.5 turns out to be a disappointment, and we go from there, and so on and so forth.
Cash efficiency and $800 billion in compute commitments
Zvi: The other thing to know about Anthropic's financials is that Anthropic's financials are actually incredibly good for a startup that is growing at this kind of rate, especially one that just eats capital in various ways. Not on net. And they are directly profitable in the first half: cash flow of $3.9 billion positive.
Now, if you adjust for the convertible notes not having been converted yet, and therefore they have to be considered as losses every time the stock price goes up, they post an $80 billion loss from that. They've sold that stock. Amazon has not converted to stock, but for all practical purposes, Amazon just has stock in Anthropic. Patrick: The one thing I would say with regards to them being incredibly cash efficient — and they have been incredibly cash efficient — is that there are ways to trade off cash and future promises in ways that matter, and they've done some excellent corporate finance.
And I'm not saying that as a criticism at all. This is just someone who enjoys the game looking at a team of people that are very, very good at the game. They have locked up compute for the next couple of years in a trade where both parties get something they want. Anthropic says, "We want a price, and we want availability," and the other party says, "Okay, we want a guaranteed spend over a number of years."
And so a way in which they keep their cash expenses in the current period low is to say, "Okay, we're going to smear out a very large commitment over the next couple of years," and they're up to, I think the number is about $800 billion in commitments going forward. I think a midwit way to look at that is, well, that's equivalent to having $800 billion of debt, just like it would be if you had $800 billion of real estate leases. [Patrick notes: The conventional way to round $895 billion is to $900 billion but what is $95 billion between friends.]

Zvi: So Anthropic has been incredibly conservative, in my opinion, on its forward commitments and its acquisition of compute. OpenAI has been much, much more aggressive. And still, OpenAI proved to be more conservative than it would have been optimal to have been, as things played out.
But you are trying to guard the downside option. And Anthropic has basically been saying, "Oh, we don't want to go broke and suddenly be in this position if growth is only very good and not insane." That didn't happen. But if it had, it is not clear to me that not having bought enough compute would have saved things that were that valuable. Obviously, there are reasons to want to be risk-averse, but I do think they played it too conservatively, even though from an outside perspective, oh, $800 billion of forward commits, that's completely insane.
That's over a number of years. Compute is growing rapidly. AI is growing rapidly. Postscript: what happens if the commits go bad
Patrick: Hideho, folks. So, a bit of a post-interview riff on this topic. There's an old saw: if you owe the bank $900, you have a problem. If you owe the bank almost $900 billion, the bank has a problem.
What does a future look like in which the buyer is unhappy about the $900 billion in forward commits? The most likely future is one with globally soft compute prices. You get there via some combination of: A, a supply glut of powered and racked GPUs because of capital overshooting demand.
B, major improvements in inference-time compute efficiency. C, a saturation of current approaches to intelligence, such that new training runs don't improve economic impact and are therefore shelved. D, policy restrictions on the amount of compute that can be put into training, or perhaps, less likely, inference.
Or E, a large decrease in global demand for cognition. I think you need to imagine some improbable world states to get there, but perhaps one gets there. Okay. What does one do with the commits then? Does one proceed straight to bankruptcy, like, for example, WeWork eventually did to get out from under many billions of dollars of now-uneconomic leases? No.
[Patrick notes: I had WeWork bonds, believing that they could refinance their way through unattractive leases using excellent access to the Japanese capital markets.
