Chomsky and the Two Cultures of Statistical Learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
08:18:36 UTC
17:18:36 KST

derided researchers in machine learning who use purely
statistical methods to produce behavior that mimics something in the
world, but who don't try to understand the meaning of that
behavior. 
It's true there's been a lot of work on trying to apply statistical models to
various linguistic problems. I think there have been some successes, but a lot of failures.
There is a notion of success ... which I think is novel in the history of science.
It interprets success as approximating unanalyzed data.
Chomsky's remarks were in response to Steven Pinker's question about the success of probabilistic models trained with statistical methods. This essay is a response to Pinker and Chomsky, and will address these questions:
For example, a decade before Chomsky, Claude Shannon proposed probabilistic models of communication based on Markov chains of words. If you have a vocabulary of 100,000 words and a second-order Markov model in which the probability of a word depends on the previous two words, then you need a quadrillion (1015) probability values to specify the model. The only feasible way to learn these 1015 values is to gather statistics from data and introduce some smoothing method for the many cases where there is no data. Therefore, most (but not all) probabilistic models are trained. Also, many (but not all) trained models are probabilistic.
As another example, consider the Newtonian model of gravitational attraction, which says that the force between two objects of mass m1 and m2 a distance r apart is given by
F = G m1 m2 / r2
(This example brings up another distinction: the gravitational model is continuous and quantitative whereas the linguistic tradition has favored models that are discrete, categorical, and qualitative: a word is or is not a verb, there is no question of its degree of verbiness. For more on these distinctions, see Chris Manning's article on Probabilistic Syntax.)
A relevant probabilistic statistical model is the ideal gas law, which describes the pressure P of a gas in terms of the the number of molecules, N, the temperature T, and Boltzmann's constant, K:
P = N k T / V.
The equation can be derived from first principles using the tools of statistical mechanics. It is an uncertain, incorrect model; the true model would have to describe the motions of individual gas molecules. This model ignores that complexity and summarizes our uncertainty about the location of individual molecules. Thus, even though it is statistical and probabilistic, even though it does not completely model reality, it does provide both good predictions and insight—insight that is not available from trying to understand the true movements of individual molecules.
Now let's consider the non-statistical model of spelling expressed by the rule "I before E except after C." Compare that to the probabilistic, trained statistical model:
P(IE) = 0.0177 P(CIE) = 0.0014 P(*IE) = 0.163 P(EI) = 0.0046 P(CEI) = 0.0005 P(*EI) = 0.0041
Accuracy("I before E") = 0.0177/(0.0177+0.0046) = 0.793
Accuracy("I before E except after C") = (0.0005+0.0163)/(0.0005+0.0163+0.0014+0.0041) = 0.753
A more complex statistical model (say, one that gave the probability of all
4-letter sequences, and/or of all known words) could be ten times more
accurate at the task of spelling, but does not offer concise insight into how spelling
works. Insight would require a model that knows about phonemes,
syllabification, and language of origin.  Such a model could be trained (or not) and
probabilistic (or not).
As another example of insight, consider the Theory of Supreme Court Justice Hand-Shaking: when the supreme court convenes, all attending justices shake hands with every other justice. The number of attendees, n, must be an integer in the range 0 to 9; what is the total number of handshakes, h for a given n? Here are three possible explanations:
Now let's look at some components that are of interest only to the computational linguist, not to the end user:
Clearly, it is inaccurate to say that statistical models (and probabilistic models) have achieved limited success; rather they have achieved an overwhelmingly dominant (although not exclusive) position.
Another measure of success is the degree to which an idea captures a community of researchers. As Steve Abney wrote in 1996, "In the space of the last ten years, statistical methods have gone from being virtually unknown in computational linguistics to being a fundamental given. ... anyone who cannot at least use the terminology persuasively risks being mistaken for kitchen help at the ACL [Association for Computational Linguistics] banquet."
Now of course, the majority doesn't rule -- just because everyone is jumping on some bandwagon, that doesn't make it right. But I made the switch: after about 14 years of trying to get language models to work using logical rules, I started to adopt probabilistic approaches (thanks to pioneers like Gene Charniak (and Judea Pearl for probability in general) and to my colleagues who were early adopters, like Dekai Wu). And I saw everyone around me making the same switch. And I didn't see anyone going in the other direction. We all saw the limitations of the old tools, and the benefits of the new.
And while it may seem crass and anti-intellectual to consider a financial measure of success, I note that the intellectual offspring of Shannon's theory create several trillion dollars of revenue each year, while the offspring of Chomsky's theories generate well under a billion.
This section has shown that one reason why the vast majority of researchers in computational linguistics use statistical models is an engineering reason: statistical models have state-of-the-art performance, and in most cases non-statistical models perform worst. For the remainder of this essay we will concentrate on scientific reasons: that probabilistic models better represent linguistic facts, and statistical techniques make it easier for us to make sense of those facts.
A dictionary definition of science is "the systematic study of the structure and behavior of the physical and natural world through observation and experiment," which stresses accurate modeling over insight, but it seems to me that both notions have always coexisted as part of doing science. To test that, I consulted the epitome of doing science, namely Science. I looked at the current issue and chose a title and abstract at random:
Chlorinated Indium Tin Oxide Electrodes with High Work Function for
Organic Device Compatibility
In organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), a stack of multiple organic layers facilitates charge flow from the low work function [~4.7 electron volts (eV)] of the transparent electrode (tin-doped indium oxide, ITO) to the deep energy levels (~6 eV) of the active light-emitting organic materials. We demonstrate a chlorinated ITO transparent electrode with a work function of >6.1 eV that provides a direct match to the energy levels of the active light-emitting materials in state-of-the art OLEDs. A highly simplified green OLED with a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 54% and power efficiency of 230 lumens per watt using outcoupling enhancement was demonstrated, as were EQE of 50% and power efficiency of 110 lumens per watt at 10,000 candelas per square meter.
It certainly seems that this article is much more focused on "accurately modeling the world" than on "providing insight." The paper does indeed fit in to a body of theories, but it is mostly reporting on specific experiments and the results obtained from them (e.g. efficiency of 54%).
I then looked at all the titles and abstracts from the current issue of Science:
I said that statistical models are sometimes confused with probabilistic models; let's first consider the extent to which Chomsky's objections are actually about probabilistic models. In 1969 he famously wrote:
But it must be recognized that the notion of "probability of a sentence" is an entirely useless one, under any known interpretation of this term.
His main argument being that, under any interpretation known to him, the probability of a novel sentence must be zero, and since novel sentences are in fact generated all the time, there is a contradiction. The resolution of this contradiction is of course that it is not necessary to assign a probability of zero to a novel sentence; in fact, with current probabilistic models it is standard practice to do smoothing and assign a non-zero probability to novel occurrences. So this criticism is invalid, but was very influential for decades. Previously, in Syntactic Structures (1957) Chomsky wrote:
I think we are forced to conclude that ... probabilistic models give no
particular insight into some of the basic problems of syntactic structure.
This criticism is correct, but it is a criticism only of Markov-chain models, not of probabilistic models (or trained models) in general. Since 1957 we have seen many types of probabilistic language models beyond the Markov-chain word models. Examples 1-4 above can in fact be distinguished with a finite-state model that is not a chain, but other examples require more sophisticated models. The best studied is probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG), which operates over trees, categories of words, and individual lexical items, and has none of the restrictions of finite-state models. We find that PCFGs are state-of-the-art for parsing performance and are easier to learn from data than nonprobabilistic categorical context-free grammars. Other types of probabilistic models cover semantic and discourse structures.
Every probabilistic model is a superset of a deterministic model (because the deterministic model could be seen as a probabilistic model where the probabilities are restricted to be 0 or 1), so any valid criticism of probabilistic models would have to be because they are too expressive, not because they are not expressive enough.
In Syntactic Structures, Chomsky introduces a now-famous example that is another criticism of finite-state probabilistic models:
Neither (a) 'colorless green ideas sleep furiously' nor (b) 'furiously
sleep ideas green colorless', nor any of their parts, has ever occurred
in the past linguistic experience of an English speaker. But (a) is
grammatical, while (b) is not.
But regardless of what is meant by "part," a statistically-trained finite-state model can in fact distinguish between these two sentences. Pereira (2001) showed that such a model, augmented with word categories and trained by expectation maximization on newspaper text, computes that (a) is 200,000 times more probable than (b). To prove that this was not the result of Chomsky's sentence itself sneaking into newspaper text, I repeated the experiment, using a much cruder model with Laplacian smoothing and no categories, trained over the Google Book corpus from 1800 to 1954, and found that (a) is about 10,000 times more probable.
Furthermore, the statistical models are capable of delivering the judgment that both sentences are extremely improbable, when compared to, say, "Effective green products sell well." Chomsky's theory, being categorical, cannot make this distinction; all it can distinguish is grammatical/ungrammatical.
Another part of Chomsky's objection is "we cannot seriously propose that a child learns the values of 109 parameters in a childhood lasting only 108 seconds." (Note that modern models are much larger than the 109 parameters that were contemplated in the 1960s.) But of course nobody is proposing that these parameters are learned one-by-one; the right way to do learning is to set large swaths of near-zero parameters simultaneously with a smoothing or regularization procedure, and update the high-probability parameters continuously as observations comes in. Nobody is suggesting that Markov models by themselves are a serious model of human language performance. But I (and others) suggest that probabilistic, trained models are a better model of human language performance than are categorical, untrained models. And yes, it seems clear that an adult speaker of English does know billions of language facts (a speaker knows many facts about the appropriate uses of words in different contexts, such as that one says "the big game" rather than "the large game" when talking about an important football game). These facts must somehow be encoded in the brain.
It seems clear that probabilistic models are better for judging the likelihood of a sentence, or its degree of sensibility. But even if you are not interested in these factors and are only interested in the grammaticality of sentences, it still seems that probabilistic models do a better job at describing the linguistic facts. The mathematical theory of formal languages defines a language as a set of sentences. That is, every sentence is either grammatical or ungrammatical; there is no need for probability in this framework. But natural languages are not like that. A scientific theory of natural languages must account for the many phrases and sentences which leave a native speaker uncertain about their grammaticality (see Chris Manning's article and its discussion of the phrase "as least as"), and there are phrases which some speakers find perfectly grammatical, others perfectly ungrammatical, and still others will flip-flop from one occasion to the next. Finally, there are usages which are rare in a language, but cannot be dismissed if one is concerned with actual data. For example, the verb quake is listed as intransitive in dictionaries, meaning that (1) below is grammatical, and (2) is not, according to a categorical theory of grammar.
Steve Abney points out that probabilistic models are better suited for modeling language change. He cites the example of a 15th century Englishman who goes to the pub every day and orders "Ale!" Under a categorical model, you could reasonably expect that one day he would be served eel, because the great vowel shift flipped a Boolean parameter in his mind a day before it flipped the parameter in the publican's. In a probabilistic framework, there will be multiple parameters, perhaps with continuous values, and it is easy to see how the shift can take place gradually over two centuries.
Thus it seems that grammaticality is not a categorical, deterministic judgment but rather an inherently probabilistic one. This becomes clear to anyone who spends time making observations of a corpus of actual sentences, but can remain unknown to those who think that the object of study is their own set of intuitions about grammaticality. Both observation and intuition have been used in the history of science, so neither is "novel," but it is observation, not intuition that is the dominant model for science.
Now let's consider what I think is Chomsky's main point of disagreement with statistical models: the tension between "accurate description" and "insight." This is an old distinction. Charles Darwin (biologist, 1809–1882) is best known for his insightful theories but he stressed the importance of accurate description, saying "False facts are highly injurious to the progress of science, for they often endure long; but false views, if supported by some evidence, do little harm, for every one takes a salutary pleasure in proving their falseness." More recently, Richard Feynman (physicist, 1918–1988) wrote "Physics can progress without the proofs, but we can't go on without the facts."
On the other side, Ernest Rutherford (physicist, 1871–1937) disdained mere description, saying "All science is either physics or stamp collecting." Chomsky stands with him: "You can also collect butterflies and make many observations. If you like butterflies, that's fine; but such work must not be confounded with research, which is concerned to discover explanatory principles."
Acknowledging both sides is Robert Millikan (physicist, 1868–1953) who said in his Nobel acceptance speech "Science walks forward on two feet, namely theory and experiment ... Sometimes it is one foot that is put forward first, sometimes the other, but continuous progress is only made by the use of both."
After all those distinguished scientists have weighed in, I think the most relevant contribution to the current discussion is the 2001 paper by Leo Breiman (statistician, 1928–2005), Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures. In this paper Breiman, alluding to C. P. Snow, describes two cultures:
First the data modeling culture (to which, Breiman estimates, 98% of statisticians subscribe) holds that nature can be described as a black box that has a relatively simple underlying model which maps from input variables to output variables (with perhaps some random noise thrown in). It is the job of the statistician to wisely choose an underlying model that reflects the reality of nature, and then use statistical data to estimate the parameters of the model.
Second the algorithmic modeling culture (subscribed to by 2% of statisticians and many researchers in biology, artificial intelligence, and other fields that deal with complex phenomena), which holds that nature's black box cannot necessarily be described by a simple model. Complex algorithmic approaches (such as support vector machines or boosted decision trees or deep belief networks) are used to estimate the function that maps from input to output variables, but we have no expectation that the form of the function that emerges from this complex algorithm reflects the true underlying nature.
It seems that the algorithmic modeling culture is what Chomsky is objecting to most vigorously. It is not just that the models are statistical (or probabilistic), it is that they produce a form that, while accurately modeling reality, is not easily interpretable by humans, and makes no claim to correspond to the generative process used by nature. In other words, algorithmic modeling describes what does happen, but it doesn't answer the question of why.
Breiman's article explains his objections to the first culture, data modeling. Basically, the conclusions made by data modeling are about the model, not about nature. (Aside: I remember in 2000 hearing James Martin, the leader of the Viking missions to Mars, saying that his job as a spacecraft engineer was not to land on Mars, but to land on the model of Mars provided by the geologists.) The problem is, if the model does not emulate nature well, then the conclusions may be wrong. For example, linear regression is one of the most powerful tools in the statistician's toolbox. Therefore, many analyses start out with "Assume the data are generated by a linear model..." and lack sufficient analysis of what happens if the data are not in fact generated that way. In addition, for complex problems there are usually many alternative good models, each with very similar measures of goodness of fit. How is the data modeler to choose between them? Something has to give. Breiman is inviting us to give up on the idea that we can uniquely model the true underlying form of nature's function from inputs to outputs. Instead he asks us to be satisfied with a function that accounts for the observed data well, and generalizes to new, previously unseen data well, but may be expressed in a complex mathematical form that may bear no relation to the "true" function's form (if such a true function even exists). Chomsky takes the opposite approach: he prefers to keep a simple, elegant model, and give up on the idea that the model will represent the data well. Instead, he declares that what he calls performance data—what people actually do—is off limits to linguistics; what really matters is competence—what he imagines that they should do.
In January of 2011, television personality Bill O'Reilly weighed in on more than one culture war with his statement "tide goes in, tide goes out. Never a miscommunication. You can't explain that," which he proposed as an argument for the existence of God. O'Reilly was ridiculed by his detractors for not knowing that tides can be readily and concisely explained by a system of partial differential equations describing the gravitational interaction of sun, earth, and moon (a fact that was first worked out by Laplace in 1776 and has been considerably refined since; when asked by Napoleon why the creator did not enter into his calculations, Laplace said "I had no need of that hypothesis."). (O'Reilly also seems not to know about Deimos and Phobos (two of my favorite moons in the entire solar system, along with Europa, Io, and Titan), nor that Mars and Venus orbit the sun, nor that the reason Venus has no moons is because it is so close to the sun that there is scant room for a stable lunar orbit.)
But O'Reilly realizes that it doesn't matter what his detractors think of his astronomical ignorance, because his supporters think he has gotten exactly to the key issue: why? He doesn't care how the tides work, tell him why they work. Why is the moon at the right distance to provide a gentle tide, and exert a stabilizing effect on earth's axis of rotation, thus protecting life here? Why does gravity work the way it does? Why does anything at all exist rather than not exist? O'Reilly is correct that these why questions can only be addressed by mythmaking, religion or philosophy, not by science.
Chomsky has a philosophy based on the idea that we should focus on the deep whys and that mere explanations of reality don't matter. In this, Chomsky is in complete agreement with O'Reilly. (I recognize that the previous sentence would have an extremely low probability in a probabilistic model trained on a newspaper or TV corpus.) Chomsky believes a theory of language should be simple and understandable, like a linear regression model where we know the underlying process is a straight line, and all we have to do is estimate the slope and intercept.
For example, consider the notion of a pro-drop language from Chomsky's Lectures on Government and Binding (1981). In English we say, for example, "I'm hungry," expressing the pronoun "I". But in Spanish, one expresses the same thought with "Tengo hambre" (literally "have hunger"), dropping the pronoun "Yo". Chomsky's theory is that there is a "pro-drop parameter" which is "true" in Spanish and "false" in English, and that once we discover the small set of parameters that describe all languages, and the values of those parameters for each language, we will have achieved true understanding.
The problem is that reality is messier than this theory. Here are some dropped pronouns in English:
From the beginning, Chomsky has focused on the generative side of language. From this side, it is reasonable to tell a non-probabilistic story: I know definitively the idea I want to express—I'm starting from a single semantic form—thus all I have to do is choose the words to say it; why can't that be a deterministic, categorical process? If Chomsky had focused on the other side, interpretation, as Claude Shannon did, he may have changed his tune. In interpretation (such as speech recognition) the listener receives a noisy, ambiguous signal and needs to decide which of many possible intended messages is most likely. Thus, it is obvious that this is inherently a probabilistic problem, as was recognized early on by all researchers in speech recognition, and by scientists in other fields that do interpretation: the astronomer Laplace said in 1819 "Probability theory is nothing more than common sense reduced to calculation," and the physicist James Maxwell said in 1850 "The true logic for this world is the calculus of Probabilities, which takes account of the magnitude of the probability which is, or ought to be, in a reasonable man's mind."
Finally, one more reason why Chomsky dislikes statistical models is that they tend to make linguistics an empirical science (a science about how people actually use language) rather than a mathematical science (an investigation of the mathematical properties of models of formal language, not of language itself). Chomsky prefers the later, as evidenced by his statement in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965):
Linguistic theory is mentalistic, since it is concerned with
discovering a mental reality underlying actual behavior. Observed use of language ... may
provide evidence ... but surely cannot constitute the subject-matter
of linguistics, if this is to be a serious discipline.
 Plato's answer was that the knowledge is 'remembered'
from an earlier existence. The answer calls for a mechanism: perhaps
the immortal soul ... rephrasing Plato's answer in terms more
congenial to us today, we will say that the basic properties of
cognitive systems are innate to the mind, part of human biological
endowment. 
It was reasonable for Plato to think that the ideal of, say, a horse, was more important than any individual horse we can perceive in the world. In 400BC, species were thought to be eternal and unchanging. We now know that is not true; that the horses on another cave wall—in Lascaux—are now extinct, and that current horses continue to evolve slowly over time. Thus there is no such thing as a single ideal eternal "horse" form.
We also now know that language is like that as well: languages are complex, random, contingent biological processes that are subject to the whims of evolution and cultural change. What constitutes a language is not an eternal ideal form, represented by the settings of a small number of parameters, but rather is the contingent outcome of complex processes. Since they are contingent, it seems they can only be analyzed with probabilistic models. Since people have to continually understand the uncertain, ambiguous, noisy speech of others, it seems they must be using something like probabilistic reasoning. Chomsky for some reason wants to avoid this, and therefore he must declare the actual facts of language use out of bounds and declare that true linguistics only exists in the mathematical realm, where he can impose the formalism he wants. Then, to get language from this abstract, eternal, mathematical realm into the heads of people, he must fabricate a mystical facility that is exactly tuned to the eternal realm. This may be very interesting from a mathematical point of view, but it misses the point about what language is, and how it works.

Gold proved a result in formal language theory that
  we can state (with some artistic license) as this: imagine a game
  between two players, guesser and chooser.  Chooser says to
  guesser, "Here is an infinite number of languages. I'm going to
  choose one of them, and start reading sentences to you that come
  from that language. On your N-th birthday there will be a True-False
  quiz where I give you 100 sentences you haven't heard yet, and you
  have to say whether they come from the language or not."  There are
  some limits on what the infinite set looks like and on how 
  the chooser can pick sentences (he can be deliberately
  tricky, but he can't just repeat the same sentence over and over,
  for example). Gold's
  result is that if the infinite set of languages are all generated by
  context-free grammars then there is no strategy for guesser that
  guarantees she gets 100% correct every time, no matter what N you
  choose for the birthday. This result was
  taken by Chomsky and others to mean that it is impossible for
  children to learn human languages without having an innate "language
  organ."  As Johnson (2004) and others show, this was an invalid
  conclusion; the task of getting 100% on the quiz (which Gold called
  language identification) 
  really has nothing in common with the task of language acquisition
  performed by children, so Gold's Theorem has no
  relevance.
Where Gold found a negative result—that
  context-free languages were not identifiable from examples, Horning found a positive result—that probabilistic
  context-free languages are identifiable (to within an arbitrarily
  small level of error).  Nobody doubts that
  humans have unique innate capabilities for understanding language
  (although it is unknown to what extent these capabilities are
  specific to language and to what extent they are general cognitive
  abilities related to sequencing and forming abstractions). But
  Horning proved in 1969 that Gold cannot be used as a convincing
  argument for an innate language organ that specifies all of language
  except for the setting of a few parameters.
The best article I've seen on what Gold's Theorem
  actually says and what has been claimed about it (correctly and
  incorrectly).  Concludes that Gold has something to say about formal
  languages, but nothing about child language
  acquisition.
An excellent article discussing the poverty of the
  stimulus, the fact that all models have bias,  the difference
  between supervised and unsupervised learning, and modern (PAC or VC)
  learning theory. It provides
  alternatives to the model of Universal Grammar consisting of a fixed
  set of binary parameters.
A compelling introduction to probabilistic syntax,
  and how it is a better model for linguistic facts than categorical
  syntax. Covers "the joys and perils of corpus
  linguistics."
Shows working code to implement a probabilistic,
  statistical spelling correction algorithm.
Expands on the essay above; shows how to implement
  three tasks: text segmentation, cryptographic decoding, and spelling
  correction (in a slightly more complete form than the previous essay).
When I set out to write the page you are reading now,
  I was concentrating on the events that took place in Cambridge,
  Mass., 4800 km from home.  After doing some research I was surprised
  to learn that the authors of
  two of the three best articles on this subject sit within a total of
  10 meters from my desk: Fernando Pereira and Chris Manning. (The
  third, Steve Abney, sits 3700 km away.) But perhaps I shouldn't have
  been surprised. I remember giving a talk at ACL on the corpus-based
  language models used at Google, and having Fernando, then a
  professor at U. Penn., comment "I feel like I'm a particle physicist
  and you've got the only super-collider."  A few years later he moved
  to Google. Fernando is also famous for his quote "The older I get, the
  further down the Chomsky Hierarchy I go." His article here covers
  some of the same ground as mine, but he goes farther in explaining
  the range of probabilistic models available and how they are useful.
Cited here for the allegory of the cave.
An enormously influential article that started the
  field of information theory and introduced the term "bit" and the noisy
  channel model, demonstrated successive n-gram approximations of
  English, described Markov models of language, defined entropy with
  respect to these models, and enabled the growth of the
  telecommunications industry.

About the bubbles and this research sample
Who is included: employers with more than 1,000 worldwide employees in at least one sourced year and a documented Bay Area workplace. All records includes unresolved and outside-tech cases; use the scope and industry filters to narrow the sample.
Reading the map: bubbles show workplaces or approximate city presence, not employee totals. Hollow bubbles are city-level records; cluster numbers count distinct employers. Click a bubble for dated evidence and sources. The dashed rectangle marks the study extent, not complete coverage.
Gaps are not closures: supported presence intervals remain visible; short carry-forwards are labeled estimated. Older observations appear only with “Show last-known locations,” and remain unverified. Confirmed closures or departures suppress the affected locations. All recorded years combines observations from different dates.
Navigation: drag to pan; use +/− or Ctrl+scroll to zoom. Keyboard: arrows, +/− and Home. The timeline advances in five-year steps; Latest shows 2026. Roads and boundaries are US Census 2024 geography, not historical reconstructions. City positions remain approximate at every zoom.
San Francisco · government employment statistics
San Francisco tech employment share
High-tech industry jobs as a percentage of all QCEW-covered jobs in San Francisco County. Census's high-tech industry definition, applied to BLS county data; this is a separate calculation from the employer map.
▲ Published minimum: the true share may be higher. ● Complete published basket. Lines connect annual published values within each industry definition, not estimates of missing employment. Gaps and definition changes break the line.
1960–1989 has no comparable series here; 2026 has no full-year observation. The 2022 industry-code change alters the basket, so values across that boundary are not directly comparable. Missing industry cells can change the published minimum without employment actually changing.
Definition, industry codes and sources
Jobs are counted at workplaces, not by where workers live. QCEW excludes many self-employed workers and is not a count of all people working. San Francisco County is the fixed statistical unit. No employer-size cutoff applies.

App Store 2026 in numbers: AI, pricing, abandoned apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
07:59:19 UTC
16:59:19 KST

Research · Data as of November 6, 2026
App Store 2026 in numbers
We looked at 178,637 apps that appeared in the App Store top charts of 173 countries and regions since October 9, 2026. Here are the answers to five questions.
Key findings
- About 1 in 10 apps in the charts mention AI in their store listing (9.8%); in Graphics & Design it is 43%.
- Apps that sell in-app purchases or subscriptions are 3 times as likely to mention AI as plain free apps (19.9% vs 6.6%).
- 26.7% of free-to-download apps sell in-app purchases or subscriptions; most in Graphics & Design (60.2%), fewest in Shopping (11.5%).
- 20.3% of apps in the charts have not been updated for a year or more; 9.8% for over three years.
- In 1-2 star reviews the most common complaint is subscription & price (12.7%), ahead of bugs & broken features (10.9%) and login & account (10%).
1. How many apps talk about AI
17,456 apps (9.8%) mention AI, GPT, machine learning, generative or chatbot in their name or the start of their description. They cluster in Graphics & Design, Photo & Video and Developer Tools. Ratings barely differ: among apps with at least 50 ratings, those mentioning AI average 4.49 stars and the rest 4.4.
Show the numbers
2. How free apps make money
Of 164,056 free-to-download apps, 26.7% say in their description that they offer in-app purchases, a subscription, a trial or a Pro unlock. Graphics & Design and Photo & Video lead; Shopping and News come last; many of those are apps of businesses that most likely earn their money outside the app.
Show the numbers
3. How much of the charts independent developers hold
By our definition (see the notes below), 67.3% of apps in the charts come from independent developers. Their ratings match the larger publishers': 4.41 against 4.41 stars for apps with at least 50 ratings. The share is highest in Developer Tools, Sports and Navigation and lowest in Games.
Show the numbers
4. How many apps are no longer maintained
70.9% of apps in the charts were updated in the last six months, yet 20.3% have gone a year or more without an update and 9.8% more than three years. Books, Reference and News have the most apps left alone; Finance the fewest (10.9%).
Show the numbers
5. What bad reviews complain about
We read 165,735 US App Store reviews of 3,912 apps. Among 1-2 star reviews, 12.7% complain about subscription & price, 10.9% about bugs & broken features and 10% about login & account. One review can fall under several themes.
Next edition
We will refresh this report every quarter. From the next edition it will show change over time: which apps moved to subscriptions, how fast the AI share grows, and whether abandoned apps come back.
How to read these numbers
- Scope: 178,637 iPhone, iPad and Mac apps that appeared in an App Store top chart since October 9, 2026. In 12 large markets that means the overall and category charts for free, paid and top grossing apps; elsewhere the overall free chart. Apps never seen in a chart are left out.
- Categories: the app's primary App Store category, with names in other languages merged. Categories with fewer than 1,500 apps have no row of their own.
- Mentions AI: the name or the first 1,500 characters of the description contain AI, GPT, artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative, LLM or chatbot. It shows the app markets itself with AI, not that its features depend on it.
- Sells in-app purchases or subscriptions: free to download, and the description mentions a subscription, in-app purchase, premium, trial, unlock, Pro or a monthly or yearly price. Apps that say nothing may still sell something, so this share is on the low side.
- Independent developer: at most 5 of the developer's apps seen in the charts, no app with 30,000 ratings or more, and a seller name that does not read as a company (Inc, Corp, GmbH and the like). We only see apps that charted, so this share may run high.
- Last update: the release date of the current version on the US App Store.
- Reviews: recent public reviews on the US App Store. Themes come from keywords (for example subscription, ads, crash); shares are of 1-2 star reviews, except feature requests, which are of all reviews. Recent reviews lean negative, so we do not publish the overall share of bad reviews.
- Ratings: only apps with at least 50 ratings count.
Cite and download
The charts and data are free to use, commercial use included (CC BY 4.0). Please credit “Obelisk Club” and link to this page.
Suggested citation
Obelisk Club, “App Store 2026 in numbers”, November 6, 2026, https://obelisk.club/research/app-store-2026

Kugelblitz – Mac-Native Google Earth Alternative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
07:47:38 UTC
16:47:38 KST

Maps
Drawn maps on real terrain
A library. A spaceship. A time machine.
App for macOS
The Earth and its neighbors as a 3D globe and atlas for the Mac – maps and open geodata on real terrain.
Kugelblitz shows the Earth and its neighbors as a globe and as an atlas you fly over smoothly like a pilot, even on an M1. Imagery, road map and topographic map lie on real terrain, joined by thousands of open maps from the Library. Everything comes from freely available geodata, straight from its publishers, OpenStreetMap from the Kugelblitz tile server; you need no account.
Everything loaded stays in the cache, and Kugelblitz instances in the same network share it with each other if you wish. Status windows tell how far the view has loaded, where you are looking and where its data comes from, and every source is listed with its license in “Sources and Licenses”. Kugelblitz speaks German and English and uses the units of your choice.
The Earth on three kinds of map, as a globe and as an atlas: Imagery, road map and topographic map. The two drawn ones do not lie flat beside it but on the globe's terrain, with buildings in 3D. A scene brings back a ready-made view in one move.
Beside the globe Kugelblitz shows every body as an atlas: the same data flat in five projections, from the whole sheet to the finest images. You switch in the title bar or with ⇧⌘A.
The Library (⇧⌘B) opens directories and geoportals with map services from all over the world: aerial images, satellite images, elevation models, maps and buildings in 3D. “On the Globe” shows any service at once, and one click adds it to “My Places”.
OpenStreetMap comes from Kugelblitz's own tile server: the whole planet, prepared for Kugelblitz, in tiles only for the area you see, at the level the distance asks for. No regions, no large download, the same everywhere on Earth.
Aerial image, terrain, buildings, roads and names at once, and the flight stays smooth. Kugelblitz is made and measured on a Mac mini with M1 and 16 GB.
The Mac draws, the headset shows: View → “Show on Vision Pro…” (⌥⌘V) brings the globe all around you, without an app on the headset, from an M1 too. Checked with Mac and headset on 27.2.
Eclipses over 5,000 years, computed rather than read from tables, as well as earthquakes, eruptions, tsunamis and fireballs at their place and time. Let the time shuttle run and you see them come and go.
Every body flat as a printed map
One move instead of many switches
Search, view and add the world's open geodata
Your places, your data
All of OpenStreetMap, without a download and without regions
Cities in three dimensions
Fly like a pilot with a SpaceMouse
Smooth, even on an M1
The Mac streams the globe into the headset
Earth, Moon, Mars and more
The Sun stands where it really is

Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
07:40:35 UTC
16:40:35 KST

Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui.
People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat!
Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord
This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or
jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in
docs/ or on the website when there's
more to say.
BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU.
At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it.
What BUI is not:
- Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it.
- Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network.
- Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's
interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui.
Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and
drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit
the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You
type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have
these habits in their hands.
That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency.
- You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged.
- You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect.
- You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser.
- You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag.
- You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words.
Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations: no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system.
You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions:
Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest.
- Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap.
- Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y.
- Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets.
- Drag across checkboxes to set them all.
- Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first.
- Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields.
- Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation.
- The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser.
- Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time.
- tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI.
- Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers.
- Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates.
- Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style.
- One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything.
- All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (<NumberSlider>, <Button>, <ColorSwatch> ...) are real Blender widgets.
- Modern CSS: flexbox, grid with named areas, tables, calc() and every math function, var(), oklch() and color-mix(), :has(), nesting, @layer, @media ranges, @container, ::before/::after, counters.
- Effects and motion: @keyframes animations and transitions, filters, backdrop-filter, blend modes, clip-path, masks, 2D transforms, border-image.
- Tailwind CSS v4: class="md:hover:bg-sky-500/50" or bare attributes (<div p-4 bg-[#4772b3]>), with "did you mean" compile errors.
- rsx! / view! HTML-like markup, #[component], and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style (use_state, signal, Memo, Effect, context).
- gpui-compatible syntax too: div().flex().gap_2(), Render, cx.listener.
- On crates.io: cargo add blenderui.
- Damage rendering: an idle UI costs 0% CPU, and a hover redraws only the widget it touches.
- Opt-in GPU renderer (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux), modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing. It draws the same pixels as the CPU raster.
- In the benchmark, 2–4× less CPU per frame than gpui-fast, with less RAM and a ~5 ms first frame.
- Blender's text: Inter (Blender's UI font) is embedded and rendered with FreeType the way Blender renders it, so text looks the same on every platform. On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug, falling back to a per-glyph atlas like Blender's.
- One decoder set for every language, in C: PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA, QOI (Wuffs, memory-safe), JPEG (libjpeg-turbo), WebP including animated (libwebp), Radiance HDR, PNM and SVG. The design is Blender's imbuf: one image type and a format table.
- Decoded at the size it is drawn, off the UI thread: JPEG thumbnails use DCT scaling (a 4K photo becomes a 256 px thumbnail in ~12 ms), visible images first, scrolled-away requests cancelled, and only the image's rectangle redraws when it arrives. The page never jumps: sizes come from the file header.
- One memory-budgeted cache (256 MiB by default). Scrolling 1,000 photo thumbnails: 2.9 ms p99 frames and 100 MB, against 96 ms and 2.5 GB when decoding on the UI thread; 0 allocations in a settled frame, every block freed at exit. Images.
- Animated GIF and WebP play everywhere an image shows, decoded one frame at a time at the size drawn (two frames held per animation), each frame for its own delay, only the image's rectangle repainting. Off screen, scrolled away or in a hidden window they pause: 200 animations at once take 0.76 ms p50 / 1.5 ms p99 render frames, and nothing at all once off screen. frame holds one frame; reduced motion holds them all.
- Large images on the GPU: images over 2047 px get a texture of their own on Direct3D 11 and OpenGL (tiled only past the device limit), freed with the image.
- Video: <video> in every language, decoded by the OS (Media Foundation with DXVA, GStreamer, AVFoundation; loaded at run time) at the size drawn, frames in one GPU texture per player updated in place, YCbCr converted in the shader, and nothing decoded off screen. 1080p plays at 0.99 ms render frames and 9 % of a core on the GPU renderer, five at once at 28 %, with 0 allocations per frame. Play, pause, seek, rate, loop, poster, state events, and Blender-style controls. Video.
- <img>, CSS background-image, object-fit, Blender Image components, tkinter PhotoImage (now also JPEG, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI, HDR, SVG), canvas items, data-table image columns, chat-list media and Dear ImGui textures (animated ones too).
- React 19.3 renders to BUI: HTML host components, CSS and Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and Blender components (<NumberSlider>, <Button> ...). BUI draws them, on the CPU or the GPU; there's no browser and no webview.
- React's hooks, by React's names, holding signals: pass one into JSX ({count}) and a change updates that one node without re-rendering; read it while rendering (count.value) and the component re-renders, as with React. A conformance suite checks each hook against React's own.
- Svelte 5 (@blender-ui/svelte): components with runes, snippets, bindings and scoped styles, mounted into native windows; Svelte's compiled code runs on BUI's DOM, so a $state change updates the one node that shows it.
- @blender-ui/native: a DOM-like API (createElement, appendChild, addEventListener) with the same signals, for apps without a framework, and the shared layer the React and Svelte bindings are thin adapters over.
- Node.js and Bun, through a napi-rs addon, with headless mode for tests.
- bui build app.jsx produces one executable of 6.3 to 6.9 MB (by the features it uses): BUI with an embedded QuickJS engine.
- First frame in ~70 ms, at 19 MB of RAM, with nothing to install. There's no browser and no webview.
- --bun builds a Bun executable instead, with Node's APIs and a JIT.
- Builds take under a second: the app's bundle is appended to a prebuilt runtime.
- Pay for what you use: one feature table (features.json) drives CMake options, cargo features and bui build, which links the smallest runtime an app needs: 6.3 MB for hello world, 6.9 MB with images or video. Binary size.
- The real Dear ImGui 1.93: every function of imgui.h works, including ShowDemoWindow().
- Four languages: C++ (drop-in imgui.h), C (cimgui.h, all 399 functions), Python and Rust (generated from imgui.h).
- Blender's look: Blender's theme colors and metrics with Inter; or, with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON, Blender's actual widgets and interaction, pixel-identical to BUI's own.
- Idle costs nothing: frames run only on input and while something animates.
- Native windows on Windows (Win32) and Linux (X11, Wayland through XWayland), and an experimental Cocoa host for macOS ported from Blender's GHOST.
- HiDPI: per-monitor DPI on Windows, Xft.dpi on Linux, Retina on macOS.
- Headless mode for tests and screenshots, with a virtual clock that steps animations exactly.
- On Linux, libX11 and libGL are loaded at run time, so BUI imports on servers without them.

Python. You need CPython 3.11 or newer. Wheels are published for Windows, Linux and macOS, so there's nothing to compile. One package gives you all four Python APIs (tkinter syntax, Qt syntax, the Blender components and Dear ImGui):
pip install blenderui
python -c "import blenderui; print(blenderui.__version__)"
Import it as blenderui. You'll also see import bui in older examples: it's
the same code under its original name, but an unrelated project owns bui on
PyPI, so prefer blenderui in anything you publish.
Rust. The crate is blenderui on crates.io:
cargo add blenderui
The first build compiles BUI's C kit for you, so you need Rust 1.88 or newer,
CMake and a C compiler (on Windows, the Visual Studio Build Tools for the
default MSVC target), and on Linux the X11 headers (libx11-dev or
libX11-devel; no GL headers are needed).
JavaScript. You need Node.js 18 or newer, or Bun:
npm install @blender-ui/react react     # or: bun add @blender-ui/react react
npm install @blender-ui/svelte svelte   # Svelte 5
npm install @blender-ui/native          # the DOM-like API, without React
The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64. On Linux, build the
addon from a clone (npm install then npm run build in bindings/, with
Rust, CMake and a C compiler); windows are native X11 windows there. On
macOS, JavaScript runs headless for now (see Platforms).
C and C++. Build from source with CMake 3.20+ and a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC or MinGW-w64, or Clang); on Linux, also the X11 headers:
git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j 2
ctest --test-dir build            # optional: run the test suites
In your own CMake project, add BUI as a subdirectory and link bui::kit (or
bui::imgui for Dear ImGui):
add_subdirectory(BUI)
target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE bui::kit)
Dear ImGui. Python gets it with pip install blenderui
(import blenderui.imgui). C++ links bui::imgui, C links bui_cimgui.
Rust uses the blenderui-imgui crate:
cargo add blenderui-imgui

blenderui-tk my_app.py          # same as: python -m bui.tksyntax my_app.py

run. Or opt in from code:
import blenderui.tksyntax as tk
from blenderui.tksyntax import ttk, messagebox
root = tk.Tk()
name = tk.StringVar(value="Cube")
ttk.Entry(root, textvariable=name).pack(fill="x", padx=8, pady=8)
ttk.Button(root, text="Greet",
           command=lambda: messagebox.showinfo("Hi", "Hello " + name.get())).pack()
root.mainloop()

Write Qt-style Python. The import is the only line that differs from PySide or PyQt, and neither is needed:
import sys
from blenderui.qtsyntax import (QApplication, QWidget, QVBoxLayout, QFormLayout,
                                QLineEdit, QComboBox, QSlider, QProgressBar,
                                QPushButton, QLabel, Qt)
app = QApplication(sys.argv)
window = QWidget()
window.setWindowTitle("Export")
layout = QVBoxLayout(window)
form = QFormLayout()
kind = QComboBox()
kind.addItems(["glTF", "FBX", "OBJ"])
quality = QSlider(Qt.Horizontal)
quality.setRange(0, 100)
form.addRow("Format:", kind)
form.addRow("Quality:", quality)
layout.addLayout(form)
bar = QProgressBar()
quality.valueChanged.connect(bar.setValue)
layout.addWidget(bar)
status = QLabel("Ready.")
go = QPushButton("Export")
go.clicked.connect(lambda: status.setText("Exporting as " + kind.currentText()))
layout.addWidget(status)
layout.addWidget(go)
window.show()
sys.exit(app.exec())
A bigger program in the same syntax, a material editor (not the output of the snippet above):
Qt syntax (examples/site/qt_material.py)
Qt syntax is partial (about 24% of Qt's method names on the main widget
classes); anything missing raises AttributeError. Guide:
docs/qt.md.
BUI's Rust crate has two first-class syntaxes, and they draw the same window:
- rsx! is HTML-like markup inside a macro, with #[component] functions
and hooks for state.
- gpui builders are plain method chains: div().flex().gap_3().child(...).
State lives in your view struct, and cx.listener updates it. gpui code
compiles against BUI too.
In rsx! (this is
bindings/rust/blenderui/examples/hello.rs;
run it with cargo run --release --example hello in bindings/rust):
use blenderui::prelude::*;
#[component]
fn counter(label: &str) {
    let (count, set_count) = use_state(0);
    rsx! {
        <div flex items-center gap-3 p-4 rounded-xl bg-zinc-800>
            <span text-zinc-300>{label.to_string()} ": " {count().to_string()}</span>
            <div px-3 py-1 rounded-md bg-sky-700 hover:bg-sky-500 onClick={move || set_count(count() + 1)}>
                "Add one"
            </div>
        </div>
    }
}
struct Hello;
impl Render for Hello {
    fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, _: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
        rsx! {
            <body m-0 p-6 min-h-screen flex flex-col gap-4 bg-zinc-900 text-white>
                <h1 text-2xl font-bold>"Hello, BUI"</h1>
                <counter label="Clicks" />
                <NumberSlider min={0.0} max={10.0} value="5" />   // a real Blender slider
            </body>
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    Application::new().run(|cx| {
        cx.open_window(WindowOptions::default(), |_, cx| cx.new(|_| Hello)).unwrap();
    });
}
In gpui builders, the same window:
use blenderui::prelude::*;
struct Hello { count: i32 }
impl Render for Hello {
    fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, cx: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
        let counter = div().flex().items_center().gap_3().p_4().rounded_xl().bg(rgb(0x27272a))
            .child(span().text_color(rgb(0xd4d4d8)).child(format!("Clicks: {}", self.count)))
            .child(div().px_3().py_1().rounded_md().bg(rgb(0x0369a1))
                .hover(|s| s.bg(rgb(0x0ea5e9))).cursor_pointer()
                .child("Add one")
                .on_click(cx.listener(|this, _, _, cx| {
                    this.count += 1;
                    cx.notify();
                })));
        body().m_0().p_6().css("min-height", "100vh").flex().flex_col().gap_4()
            .bg(rgb(0x18181b)).text_color(white())
            .child(h1().text_2xl().font_bold().child("Hello, BUI"))
            .child(counter)
            .child(NumberSlider().min(0.0).max(10.0).value("5"))   // a real Blender slider
    }
}
fn main() {
    Application::new().run(|cx| {
        cx.open_window(WindowOptions::default(), |_, cx| cx.new(|_| Hello { count: 0 })).unwrap();
    });
}
Two small things that trip people up in rsx!:
- Text children are text (&'static str, String, SharedString) or
elements. Numbers and borrowed &str props aren't, so write {count().to_string()} and {label.to_string()}.
- A component's body is a normal block that ends in markup, usually an
rsx!.
Here's a bigger example, a render-farm dashboard, written once in each syntax. The two programs draw identical pixels:
site_dashboard.rs (rsx!) and site_dashboard_builder.rs (gpui builders)
Guide: docs/rust.md, and the Rust tutorial on the website.
/** @jsxImportSource @blender-ui/react */
import { render, useState, NumberSlider } from "@blender-ui/react"
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0) // React's hook, holding a signal
  return (
    <main styled className="p-6 flex flex-col gap-3">
      {" "}
      {/* `styled`: Blender's look */}
      <span>Clicks: {count}</span>
      <button onClick={() => setCount((c) => c + 1)}>Add one</button>
      <NumberSlider min={0} max={10} /> {/* a Blender component */}
    </main>
  )
}
render(<Counter />, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })bun app.jsx                    # run it (Bun reads JSX directly)
npx bui build app.jsx          # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file
Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API:
const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native")
const app = new App({ gpu: true })
const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 })
win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]"
const clicks = signal(0)
const label = win.createElement("span")
label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal
const button = win.createElement("button")
button.textContent = "Add one"
button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++)
win.body.appendChild(label)
win.body.appendChild(button)

The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged.
C++:
#include "imgui.h"
#include "imgui_impl_bui.h"     // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp
static void frame(void*) {
    ImGui::ShowDemoWindow();
    ImGui::Begin("Hello");
    static float v = 0.5f;
    ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f);
    ImGui::End();
}
int main() {
    ImGui::CreateContext();
    ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr);
    ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app);
    ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app);
    ImGui::DestroyContext();
}
Python:
import blenderui.imgui as imgui        # C: cimgui.h  ·  Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate
state = {"value": 0.5}
def frame():
    imgui.show_demo_window()
    imgui.begin("Hello")
    _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0)
    imgui.end()
imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800))
C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and
the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the
same way:
use blenderui_imgui as imgui;
fn main() {
    let mut value = 0.5f32;
    imgui::run("Hello", [1280, 800], move || {
        imgui::show_demo_window();
        imgui::begin("Hello");
        imgui::slider_float("Value", &mut value, 0.0, 1.0);
        imgui::end();
    });
}
Build with -DBUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON (or the Rust feature
blender-widgets) and ImGui's widgets become Blender's own: DragFloat is
Blender's drag-to-scrub number field (Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap),
SliderFloat Blender's number slider, checkboxes drag-toggle, menus and combos
get Blender's menus. The rest of the ImGui API is unchanged. (The PyPI wheel
is built without it, so from Python you get ImGui's own widgets in Blender's
theme unless you build from source.)

Guide, coverage and the stock look: docs/imgui.md.
The kit's API is one header, kit/include/BUI_kit.h, and it doubles as the
reference: every function has a one-line comment. This is a shortened
examples/kit_hello.c: a slider and a button in a
native window.
#include <stdio.h>
#include "BUI_kit.h"
static void on_event(void *data, BKNode *node, int kind, void *ref, double a, double b)
{
  if (kind == BK_EV_CLICK) printf("clicked %s\n", BK_get_str(node, "text"));
  else if (kind == BK_EV_CHANGE) printf("%s = %g\n", BK_get_str(node, "label"), BK_get_num(node, "value"));
}
int main(void)
{
  BKNode *root = BK_node_new("frame");          /* everything is a node */
  BK_set_num(root, "padding", 8);               /* configured by property name */
  BKNode *size = BK_node_new("slider");
  BK_set_str(size, "label", "Size");
  BK_set_num(size, "max", 10);
  BK_set_num(size, "value", 2.5);
  BK_node_add(root, size, -1);
  BK_geom_set_manager(size, BK_GEOM_PACK);      /* Tk's packer, in C */
  BK_geom_set(size, "fill", 1);
  BKNode *apply = BK_node_new("button");
  BK_set_str(apply, "text", "Apply");
  BK_node_add(root, apply, -1);
  BK_geom_set_manager(apply, BK_GEOM_PACK);
  BKContext *ctx = BK_context_new(root);        /* input, focus, popups, undo */
  BKHost host = {0};
  host.emit = on_event;                         /* the window fills in the rest */
  BK_context_set_host(ctx, &host);
  if (BK_window_supported()) {                  /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */
    BKWindow *win = BK_window_new(ctx, "BUI from C", 320, 120);
    BK_window_show(win);
    BK_window_run();
    BK_window_free(win);
  }
  BK_context_free(ctx);
  BK_node_free(root);
  return 0;
}cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello

Without a window system, render into a raster instead
(BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full)), which is also how tests and

 your code:   tkinter   Qt   components   Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust)   Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks   JS / React
                  │      │        │                │                                  │                                    │
                  └──── Python: options, signals    │ ImGui core + BUI backend          └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘
                                  │                │                                  │
 C kit (kit/):   node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr
                                         │
 renderer:       damage-driven software raster (parallel)   or   GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in)
                                         │
 window:         native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window   ·   stdlib Tk window   ·   headless (tests, screenshots)
- Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change.
- The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules.
- The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask.
- Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all.
What's under the hood:
- Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's
interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape
tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects,
text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo,
float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the
kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's
own.
- One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation.
- Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen.
- Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs.
More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works.
These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender
widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and
JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's
Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget.
- Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value.
- Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10.
- Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator
(expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and
sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text.
- Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates,
Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy,
Paste and Reset.
- Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke.
- Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder.
- Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer.
- Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first.
- Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step.
- Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need.
- Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay.
Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets.
In Rust and JavaScript you pick the look per element:
The components are Button, Checkbox, Radio, NumberField, NumberSlider,

is the HTML element it stands for, so every attribute, style and event works on
it:

        <input type="range" />                             // Chrome's slider
        <NumberSlider min={0.0} max={10.0} value="2.5" />  // Blender's slider
        <div styled><button>"Apply"</button></div>         // Blender's look inside
    </main>
}
