BUI_GPU=1 / BUI_GPU=0 to pick the renderer. More:
Profiling.
Works means it works and is tested. Experimental means it's written but has had little hands-on testing on real hardware (macOS: two Apple Silicon Macs so far, plus CI).
macOS. The macOS window host is new: it's a port of Blender's Cocoa code
(GHOST). So far it has been checked by CI and tried by hand on two Apple Silicon
Macs: by Krish Kalaria, who reported issue #3 and fixed it in pull request #4, and by DanNoby (17/17 tests; issue #6 added a toolchain note to the guide). If you have another Mac, especially an Intel one, please try it and
tell us what happens: docs/macos-testing.md. Python
can still use the stdlib Tk window there (BUI_HOST=tk; this needs Python's
tkinter, for example from python.org or brew install python-tk). Node runs
BUI on its own UI thread and macOS only allows windows on the main thread, so
JavaScript stays headless on macOS for now.
Linux. libX11 and libGL are loaded when the first window opens, so BUI also
imports and renders headless on servers and in containers without them, and
falls back to the CPU raster where OpenGL is missing. Building from source needs
the X11 headers (libx11-dev / libX11-devel); no GL headers are needed. The
C, Python, window and GPU parity tests pass on Linux, on Mesa's software OpenGL
and on an NVIDIA GPU.
Packages:
Most are read by the C library, so they work the same from every language.
On/off variables look at the first character: 1, y, Y, t or T is on.
Where a variable and an app-wide API call set the same thing, the variable
wins.
Every variable, with defaults and where it's read: Environment variables and docs/getting-started.md.
You need CMake 3.20+, a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC/MinGW or Clang) and Python 3.11+ with headers. On Linux, also the X11 headers.
git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j 2
ctest --test-dir build                      # C, C++, ImGui and Python test suites
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/bindings/python      # Windows: set PYTHONPATH=%CD%\bindings\python
python examples/components_demo.py
cd bindings/rust && cargo test              # Rust: CSS, Tailwind, rsx!, hooks, effects, headless windows
Rebuild the docs screenshots with python tools/gen_doc_images.py (and the
website's dark and light shots with --site). More:
CMake options.
How each was counted: Coverage, SYNTAX_COVERAGE.md, docs/rust.md, docs/imgui.md.
Known limitations. Read these before you pick BUI for something you will ship. The tables below have the details.
- No accessibility support. BUI draws its own widgets and does not talk to the platform's accessibility APIs (UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS), so screen readers can't see them. Don't use it for software that has to be accessible. Accessibility is planned.
- Text. Blender's bundled Inter font only (system fonts only with the Windows GDI option). No per-glyph font fallback (missing characters show as boxes), no input methods (IME), right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, and no OpenType features.
- It doesn't look native. BUI looks like Blender: its Dark and Light themes (other Blender theme files can't be loaded yet). It doesn't follow your operating system's theme, accent color or fonts.
- Rendering. The CPU rasterizer is the default and works everywhere. The optional GPU renderer is Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL 3.3 on Linux. There is none on macOS (no Metal): macOS always draws on the CPU. Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends don't exist yet.
- Platforms. Windows and Linux (X11; Wayland through XWayland) are the supported ones. macOS is experimental: checked by CI and tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs, and JavaScript windows are headless there. The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 only.
- Retained mode, no visual editor. BUI keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI; it is not an immediate-mode library. There is no drag-and-drop UI designer: you write the UI in code.
- Performance numbers come from one machine, a Windows 11 laptop (Ryzen 7 5800U). Linux and macOS haven't been measured yet.
- The home page demos are browser sketches, not the native engine (the page says so). Run the Python, Rust or JavaScript examples to feel the real widgets. A WebAssembly build is planned.
- It's a port, not Blender unchanged. Widget drawing and interaction are
ported from Blender's UI sources, with edits (each marked BUI:), and the rest
of Blender (its data system, window manager and operators) isn't included.
There is no automated sync with Blender's releases.
- Partial areas: Qt syntax (about 24%), CSS (261 of 745 properties render), video has no audio, and image formats such as AVIF, EXR, TIFF, JPEG XL and HEIC aren't supported.
- License. GPL: a program that includes BUI is distributed under the GPL too (why).
Done
Partial or in progress
Planned (coming soon)
Our roadmap has no dates on it. Like a good render, it's done when the noise goes away.
Do I need Blender installed?
No. BUI contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own.
Is it really my unchanged tkinter app?
Yes.blenderui-tk app.py makes import tkinter return BUI's
implementation, which covers every public tkinter and ttk name. Nine real
programs are tested to behave identically on the standard library and on BUI.
See the limitations for the few
differences.
Is it a web browser in Rust?
No. There's no browser engine and no network. BUI takes HTML elements and CSS as a UI language: they are laid out with taffy and drawn by BUI's engine, with Blender's widgets where you ask for them, in a native window. JavaScript is optional: the Rust crate needs none, and the JavaScript packages drive the same engine.
Is the Dear ImGui support a re-implementation?
No. It's the real Dear ImGui (vendored, MIT), running on a BUI backend, so every function behaves as upstream. The optional Blender-widgets build swaps only how ImGui's widgets are drawn and how they react to the mouse, by compiling an edited copy ofimgui_widgets.cpp.
How is it different from Electron, Electrobun or GPUIX?
- Electron ships Chromium with every app: on the order of 100 MB or more.
- Electrobun runs on Bun and renders in the system's webview. It's small to download, but the UI is still a browser page.
- GPUIX, like BUI, renders React natively: React drives Zed's GPUI.
BUI also renders natively, with Blender's widgets, a much larger part of CSS, Tailwind, and hooks backed by signals.
bui build makes a 5 MB
executable that reaches its first frame in about 70 ms.
Do the macros cost performance?
rsx!, #[component], css! and tw!
expand at compile time into the same builder calls you would write by hand.
Tailwind classes are compiled to CSS once, on first use. Hooks are a few
nanoseconds per read or write.
Can I change the colors?
Yes. Switch between Blender's Dark and Light themes at run time (Themes), color individual widgets in every API, and use full CSS on plain HTML elements in Rust and JavaScript. Loading any other Blender theme file is coming soon.
Does it run on my Mac?
Yes, with caveats. The Cocoa host is experimental, but it has been tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs (the bugs they found are fixed) and CI builds and tests it on Apple Silicon and Intel runners. Nobody has tried an Intel Mac by hand yet, it draws on the CPU (there is no Metal renderer), and JavaScript windows are headless there. Python can always fall back to the Tk window (BUI_HOST=tk). If you try it, the notes in
docs/macos-testing.md say what to report.
Can I use BUI from Vue, Angular, Ruby, Go or Lua?
Not yet, but people have asked and they are on the roadmap. Vue and Angular would be thin adapters over@blender-ui/native, the layer React and Svelte already
share (how to add a framework). Ruby and Go
(through cgo) would call the C kit, BUI_kit.h, which has been
versioned since 0.4.1. A Lua binding is in review as a community pull request. If
you want one sooner, open an issue or a pull request:
CONTRIBUTING.md says how.
Is it ready for production?
Much of it is complete and tested (the C kit, tkinter, the components, Rust, Dear ImGui, JavaScript), and some parts are partial or experimental (Qt syntax, parts of CSS and text, macOS). Status and roadmap shows which is which. Pin your version, and test on the platforms you ship.
Who wrote it?
LLMs. Not in the way you think. Instead of porting it, we asked an LLM to remove everything that isn't UI logic, and then ported the drawing and interaction code from Blender's sources. Turns out LLMs are better at removing than at generating. We call it Vibe-Pruning.
Why GPL?
BUI is derived from Blender's source code, so it follows Blender's licensing: the whole is under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later, and individual files keep their own compatible license (`GPL-2.0-or-later` for the files that come from Blender).
Is it immediate mode? Is there a visual UI editor?
BUI is retained-mode: it keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI, and redraws only what changed. There is no visual UI editor yet; you write the UI in code (tkinter, Qt-style, Blender components, Rust, JavaScript or C).
Is the C API stable?
Not before 1.0, but it is versioned:BUI_kit.h has BUI_KIT_VERSION_* macros
and BK_version() reports the library's version, the same number as the Python, Rust and
npm packages. Every change that breaks existing code is listed under "C API changes" in the
changelog. Pin a release number, not a commit. From 1.0 it follows semantic versioning
(details).
Is BUI accessible to screen readers?
Not yet. See the known limitations.
Can I use BUI in a commercial app?
The GPL allows commercial use. What it asks is that when you distribute a program that includes BUI, you distribute it under the GPL too, with its source code available. If that doesn't fit your project, talk to a lawyer before you ship. (This is a summary, not legal advice.)
Contributions are welcome: bug reports, missing tkinter/Qt behavior, CSS features, platform hosts and docs. If you have a Mac, running the Cocoa host and reporting what happens is one of the most useful things you can do right now. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, and please follow the Code of Conduct. Report security issues privately, as SECURITY.md describes.
Releases go to PyPI (blenderui, wheels built by CI on a v* tag), crates.io
(the eight Rust crates, in dependency order) and npm (@blender-ui/native, @blender-ui/react). The steps are
in docs/publishing.md.
License. BUI follows Blender's licensing. BUI as a whole is licensed under
the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (the text is in
LICENSE). Individual files may have a different, but compatible license: the
files that come from Blender keep Blender's SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header, and new files carry the same one. Third-party parts
keep their own licenses:
The Rust and JavaScript bindings also depend on crates and packages such as taffy, napi-rs, React and QuickJS, each under its own license.
The full license texts of everything above, and of every Rust crate BUI's packages are
built from, are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. It ships inside the
Python wheels, the npm packages and the crates, and python tools/gen_notices.py regenerates it.
Acknowledgments. Thank you to:
- Blender and its community: the UI this project is built from, including its GHOST window code and blenlib.
- Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut: the immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI.
- taffy: flexbox, grid and block layout for the Rust crate.
- Tailwind CSS: the v4 theme behind the Tailwind support.
- FreeType: glyph rendering, as in Blender.
- stb_truetype: font metrics and the fallback rasterizer.
- NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen: the icon rasterizer, via Blender's edited copy.
- Inter by Rasmus Andersson: the embedded UI font, as in Blender.
- Slug by Eric Lengyel: the GPU glyph coverage algorithm.
- gpui, zopra and Leptos: the APIs the Rust syntax follows.
BUI is Blender's UI, minus the default cube. You're free to add your own.

At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
07:18:44 UTC
16:18:44 KST

At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since this summer to curb, restrict, or end their use of Flock Safety technology as concerns about mass surveillance and data privacy continue to grow. The backlash is part of a broader pushback against the rapid adoption of advanced AI technology, including the data center buildout, facial recognition, and other uses of AI.
Flock, founded in 2017, sells surveillance software that can help solve crimes, such as finding missing people or stolen cars. Its products include license plate readers, drones, and microphone-based edge-computing devices to pick up gunshots and other sounds. More than 100,000 Flock cameras are in use nationwide.
But in the past three months, Monroe, Ohio; Newburgh, New York; Richmond, Virginia; Hopkinton, Massachusetts; New Bedford, Massachusetts; and Lansing, Michigan, have all moved to end their contracts with Flock. Meanwhile, police in East Bridgewater and Grafton, Massachusetts, also announced plans to stop using Flock cameras. Just this week, residents of League City, Texas, voted against their police department’s continued use of Flock’s license plate readers, and the cameras are now set to be removed.
The concerns range from privacy to how data is shared (and with whom) to procurement concerns.
In Asheville, North Carolina, police lost access to Flock after the city voted to terminate its contract in August, and the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office in Colorado announced in September that it would stop using Flock cameras. When asked for comment, the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office redirected TechCrunch to its press release, where Sheriff Joseph Roybal said that discontinuing the use of Flock was the right decision for the county.
“We have the tools, training, and experience to locate and apprehend criminals without relying on Flock cameras,” he said in the press release.
Tatiana Rice, a senior director for U.S. legislation at The Future of Privacy Forum, told TechCrunch that the backlash to Flock isn’t surprising and only further represents the “growing public skepticism toward technology.” Flock is a target because people can see the sensors and cameras as they drive along roads; data centers have also become physical embodiments of the resentment growing against emerging technology. “A camera at the end of your street is tangible in a way that everyday sharing and selling of personal data online is not,” Rice said.
At the state level this summer, for example, Florida barred license plate readers from state highways, while Texas paused state funding for Flock. The issues again range from data privacy concerns to misuse of the technology.
Misuse has been a real problem. In August, for example, an officer in Brentwood, Missouri was accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his ex-wife during their divorce. In September, an officer from East Texas was sentenced to prison for using Flock to stalk his ex-girlfriend and her family.
Another growing concern is how immigration officials have been able to access the technology. One case that captures the issue came in March, when Ithaca, New York, passed a resolution to terminate its contract with the Flock Group.
In the resolution, the city said there were “proven instances of Flock Safety infrastructure being used by federal agents for information purposes even without specific authorizations from the contracting locality,” and that the city had reviewed reports that “either intentionally or through its negligence,” Flock had allowed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to “use query results from its database of state and local ALPR [automatic license plate reader] data to investigate and persecute immigrants throughout the United States.”
“Every day, police departments across the country are using Flock technology to solve serious crimes, locate suspects, find missing people, and make a measurable impact on public safety,” Flock told TechCrunch in a statement. “While we respect every community’s decision, removing a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes and protect communities moves public safety backward. Every Flock customer owns its data and controls who it is shared with and how it can be used. Flock does not sell data and does not have a contract with ICE.”
This August, Flock announced it would shorten the default period it stores data for new customers, from 30 days to seven. It also said agencies now need a case code before they can search the database.
The conversation around Flock echoes, in many ways, the fight over data centers. Many of these cities adopted Flock just a few years ago, and residents likely had no idea it was being installed, Adam Schwartz of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy nonprofit that has investigated Flock before, told TechCrunch.
That lack of awareness is similar to how data centers are popping up across the country, often before residents understand what is happening. Schwartz said police departments often decide to use Flock on their own, with little oversight from city councils. In South Windsor, Connecticut, according to local reports, Flock cameras went live last year without public warning or a vote. In October, the town voted to remove its Flock cameras.
“Grassroots activists across the country have been demanding that city councils exercise their procurement power to refuse to pay for ALPRs,” Schwartz said, referring to councils’ power to decide what the city buys. He added that activists have been fighting for years and that “many city councils are listening.”
The main argument for technology like Flock is that it helps combat crime and keep neighborhoods safe. And many local governments are not dropping Flock or similar technology; instead, they are adding restrictions on its use or looking for alternatives.
Cleveland, Ohio, for example, voted this summer to extend its contract with Flock, but has started restricting searches related to immigration. It has also limited access to the database to the Cleveland Police alone, cutting off the Northeast Ohio Regional Fusion Center, essentially a federal intelligence agency, which had initially been given access.
“They are used and needed for investigative purposes,” the city said when reached for comment. “The Department of Public Safety is currently reviewing responses to an RFP [request for proposals] that was sent out to other vendors that provide the same technology as Flock.”
But as with data centers, communities want more say in the trade-offs. “These tools can offer real public safety benefits, but communities are clearly interested in ensuring that those benefits are not at the cost of their civil liberties,” Rice said. Surveillance technology will likely remain a political hot topic, especially since Democrats now control Congress.
In September, President Donald Trump said he liked Flock’s technology “because of law enforcement,” even though a Reuters poll that same month found that more Americans dislike the technology than like it.
Also that month, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced a bill called the Flock-Off Act to bar the use of federal money to buy “Flock-style surveillance” and put other safeguards in place. In October, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), and Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) introduced the Ban Flock Act to end “the rise of AI-powered surveillance cameras.”

Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M

15:28:32 KST

Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security, a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from Datadog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.
If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million, according to regulatory filings.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion. Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million, Calcalist reported.

The Poison and the Cure the Life and Afterlife of French Theory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
06:21:20 UTC
15:21:20 KST

The Poison and the Cure
The Life and Afterlife of French Theory
The Frenchmen: Or, My Life in Theory by Emily Eakin
School of the South: The Colonial Roots of French Theory by Onur Erdur
In 2005, Alain Badiou argued that in the second half of the 20th century, there was a “French philosophical moment” comparable to the peaks of classical Greece and Enlightenment Germany. Badiou was not an impartial observer—he described himself as perhaps the era’s “last representative”—yet no one would seriously dispute that les trente glorieuses produced a blaze of intellectual activity that radiated around the world, transforming not only academic study but the wider cultural atmosphere. There, however, consensus stops.
Was this “moment” purely, or even primarily, a philosophical one? It was born with an anthropologist, Claude Lévi-Strauss, borrowing a framework from linguistics, and among the central aims of the resulting method, “structuralism,” was to topple a philosophical movement: the existentialism of Jean-Paul Sartre and others. And while many of the leading thinkers who embraced structuralism were educated, like Lévi-Strauss, in philosophy, they also worked in other areas of the humanities and social sciences. Roland Barthes was concerned with mass culture and canonical literature; Louis Althusser with interpretations of Marx; Jacques Lacan with Freudian psychoanalysis; and Michel Foucault with history, and excavating the logics underpinning a range of institutions and practices—medicine, psychiatry, prisons, sexuality. The writing of Jacques Derrida, meanwhile—for a time “the sexiest philosopher on the planet,” in the words of the literary critic Terry Eagleton—amounted less to a conventional contribution to philosophy than a thoroughgoing critique of its founding assumptions. “I never thought I had something to say philosophically,” Derrida reflected in 1991—and his example was chiefly followed by literary critics.
Such a range of interests and allegiances called for a broader rubric. As Fredric Jameson put it, considering the debate about whether Foucault was a philosopher or a historian, “Well, that is why we have the word ‘theory.’ We don’t have to decide.” The catch-all term helped to smooth over other terminological wrinkles. “Structuralism” was a label its putative exponents tended to reject, or outgrow. Foucault complained in the English edition of The Order of Things (1966), his “archeological inquiry” into the changing conditions of knowledge, that he had been unable to persuade the “tiny minds” of “certain half-witted ‘commentators’” that he had “used none of the methods, concepts or key terms that characterize structural analysis.” Barthes, having been a notably fastidious practitioner of the structuralist mode known as semiotics, developed into a representative of a free-spirited offshoot or usurper, “post-structuralism,” promoting readerly experiences of “plaisir” and “jouissance” (a near-sexual frisson).
“Theory” also encompasses a strikingly elastic pantheon of thinkers, as illustrated by a pair of recently published books. The New York Times editor Emily Eakin, in The Frenchmen, her convivial mixture of memoir and popular history, and the Berlin-based historian Onur Erdur, in his more scholarly and tendentious School of the South, both give space to Foucault, Derrida, and Barthes. Otherwise, their attentions diverge. Eakin, being concerned with “America’s theory craze,” writes about Lévi-Strauss, Althusser, Lacan, Gilles Deleuze, and the Belgian-born literary critic Paul de Man, whereas Erdur, exploring the formative impact of colonial experiences on postwar French thinkers, offers a different supporting cast, including Pierre Bourdieu, Jean-François Lyotard, and Hélène Cixous.
But the greatest divergence, or source of dissent, concerns whether the period constituted a golden age: one of the things that has always distinguished French theory is the extremity of its reception. Having achieved international prominence in the mid-1960s, theory underwent what the historian François Cusset describes as an “anarchic expansion” in the ’70s. Converts found it exhilaratingly radical and innovative, uncovering new techniques and areas of study, but Marxists, such as Jameson and Eagleton, were more skeptical. Others charged it with meretricious obscurity and dismissed its italicized neologisms and occasional quasi-mathematical formulae as a travesty of scientific inquiry. Theory was a favored target of conservative philosophers in polemical mode. Roger Scruton wrote of “a boiling tide of nonsense” that would “eliminate the possibility of rational argument” and “annihilate meaning.” Alan Bloom, in his bestselling broadside The Closing of the American Mind (1987), accused the French theorists of abetting “the suppression of reason and the denial of the possibility of truth.” The rehabilitative slant of Eakin’s and Erdur’s accounts indicates theory’s reputation has not recovered. To this day, Erdur writes, French theorists are accused of being “the intellectual originators of destructive social phenomena such as ‘fake news,’ ‘cancel culture,’ wokeness’ and ‘identity politics,’” suggesting that the record, more than two decades after the first postmortems began to appear, is still in need of straightening.
The origins of French theory are typically traced to Lévi-Strauss’s discovery in 1942 of Course in General Linguistics, a series of lectures delivered by the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure and published by his students in 1916 a few years after his death. Saussure studied language “synchronically”—not as it had evolved over time, or as it manifested in individual speech, but as a hermetic, structured system whose principal unit was the sign, composed of the “signifier” (sound-image) and the “signified” (denoted concept). The connection between these, he argued, was contingent and based in convention. Words do not have intrinsic meaning; sense is relational, an artifact of a word’s position in a system of differences: “cat” being distinct from “bat” and “mat” and so on.
Beginning with his technical tome The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949),Lévi-Strauss turned this conception of language into a way of interpreting non-linguistic phenomena, such as marriage customs. Structuralism was akin to a kind of Copernican revolution. Language preceded, determined, and all but displaced the “subject”—the autonomous human being, the Cartesian cogito, the political actor, the intending author—in what amounted to a repudiation of Sartre’s stress on the idea of individual freedom. The goal of the human sciences, Lévi-Strauss declared in The Savage Mind (1962), was to “dissolve” Man––or as Althusser suggested in For Marx (1965), reduce the myth of man “to ashes.” Others transposed Saussure’s insights to their own specialisms, notably Barthes who, in a series of newspaper columns collected under the title Mythologies (1957), illustrated that everything from royal cruises to laundry detergent could be decoded as a sign-system.
But the authority of structuralism was soon thrown into question, when in 1966, Derrida, then a relatively unknown 36-year-old, derailed its launch party in the US—a splashy conference backed by the Ford Foundation and held at Johns Hopkins in 1966 to which he had been belatedly invited. His lecture “Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences,” which closed the conference, was a “demolition job,” in Eakin’s words, of the paradigm pioneered by Lévi-Strauss (who was apparently invited but couldn’t make it), later mythologized as the dawn of post-structuralism.
Trained in the predominantly German phenomenological tradition, Derrida was exercised by the notion that Western philosophy was beholden to what he called “a metaphysics of presence.” This involved positing a “privileged Origin that commands, guarantees, and perpetuates meaning,” as Edward Said explained, a telos toward which all thought aspired—truth, Being, reality, essence, substance. By showing that meaning was not pre-given but a shifting emanation of relationships, structuralism had successfully ruptured this illusion. Yet in his Johns Hopkins address, Derrida argued that its elevation of language was in danger of reinstating the first principles it had supposedly diffused into a network of differences.
It was in Baltimore that Derrida first met Paul de Man. Their friendship would become a key axis in theory’s post-structuralist phase—and in its conquest of the American academy. De Man arranged a visiting position for Derrida at Yale, where “deconstruction,” the philosophical mode of close—many would say myopic—reading that Derrida patented took particular hold. The Johns Hopkins paper was an early exhibition of this technique, which sought to show how the logic of a given text is not only underpinned by, but—the key difference from structuralism—undermined by relegating or excluding one term in a series of classic binaries: writing and speech, male and female, center and margin, or in Lévi-Strauss’s case, nature and culture. Taking The Elementary Structures of Kinship as an example, Derrida argued that Lévi-Strauss’s discussion of the incest prohibition undoes the opposition on which his text relies—the taboo, in Lévi-Strauss’s account, being at once norm-based (cultural) and universal (natural). Derrida used one of his notorious neologisms, différance, conjoining the ideas of “difference” and “deferral,” which he later deployed as a lever to wrench apart the binaries in which structuralism was still caught: to convey the idea that meaning was both produced by differences and unstably distributed among them, and could therefore never be firmly located, the relations between words constituting an infinite chain.
To Derrida, structuralism’s “nostalgia for origins” and residual “desire for a center” presented a limit to what he called “play,” and to embrace play would be truly to “pass beyond man.” A similar shift—from hermetic structures to the affirmation of what escapes them—can be seen in Barthes’s evolution in the years after the Johns Hopkins conference, from the technical analysis of The Fashion System (1967) (“nearly unreadable,” in Eakin’s view), via S/Z (1970), his painstaking and exorbitant book-length commentary on a Balzac novella, to the teasing fragments of The Pleasure of the Text (1973), which championed an “erotics” of reading, emphasizing bodily enjoyment over hermeneutic closure.
The mid-60s saw the publication of a volley of landmark books in France—Foucault’s The Order of Things and Lacan’s Écrits; two by Althusser (For Marx and Reading Capital); and three by Derrida, Writing and Difference (which collected the Johns Hopkins lecture), Speech and Phenomena, and Of Grammatology, the last containing commentaries on both Lévi-Strauss and Saussure. The explosive rise of this critique of reason seemed to prefigure the revolutionary unrest of May 1968, which in turn lent the ideas momentum, even though, unlike Sartre, many of the intellectuals associated with theory did not join the students and strikers.
The novelty of Erdur’s School of the South is its suggestion that the decisive political context incubating this mode of thought was not les événements but decolonization, in particular the Algerian War (1958–62), which, Erdur writes, precipitated “the collapse of a certain political and cultural order in French society.” A striking number of French theorists spent time in French North Africa, serving in the army or teaching; several were born there, including Cixous, Jacques Rancière, and Derrida, who grew up in a French-speaking Sephardic family in Algiers.
Erdur’s objective is to show that such experiences shaped their thinking, but the details of his case are unevenly convincing, the connections more robust, or intimate, in some instances than others. Derrida was expelled from his school in Algiers at the age of 12 under the Vichy Jewish quotas and never felt at home in Paris, later describing himself as a “child in the margins of Europe.” It is easy to see how his background sharpened his philosophical sensitivity to what he called the “violent hierarchy” embedded in the binaries of Western thought. But the fact that Foucault taught in Tunisia for a couple of years, or that Barthes vacationed in Morocco and resolved to write an autobiographical novel while in Casablanca, is less persuasive evidence for the “colonial roots of French theory,” as Erdur’s subtitle has it. (Barthes’s “vision of a literary existence” was less a development of his theoretical work, which predated his visits to Morocco, than an expression of dissatisfaction with it.)
Eakin is the more skillful and ambitious storyteller, her 48 punchy chapters weaving intricately back and forth in time, lighting on key friendships and rivalries and critical exchanges—Derrida attacking Foucault’s reading of Rousseau, de Man later challenging Derrida’s. The resulting mosaic enlivens—if also simplifies—what Eakin admits can seem an “intentionally rebarbative” body of thought. Like Erdur, Eakin writes extensively about the theorists’ lives, including their personal lives, aiming to recover what she calls “the hidden human element beneath their often stringent antihumanism”—we learn that Barthes was “prone to a potbelly” and that Lacan was holding a “plate of coleslaw” when he had a run-in with Derrida at Johns Hopkins. Another leavening ingredient is the book’s autobiographical arc, which traces Eakin’s sophomore bewitchment with theory to postgraduate disenchantment, when she abandons her PhD in favor of a career in journalism.
Eakin’s memories of her student days are not exactly rife with dramatic incident—essay crises predominate, reaching a climax with her senior thesis (she fortunately earns “a generous magna cum laude plus,” despite some mixed feedback). But her trajectory is emblematic, a prism through which she surveys the wider story of the Anglosphere’s infatuation with French theory. Though individually notable in their native land, it was in the US, via popularizers such as Jonathan Culler and abettors such as de Man, that theory became a coherent and dominant force within the academy. (In Britain, the philosopher Christopher Norris and the contributors to the film journal Screen alsotook up the cause.) Why did American literature departments prove so hospitable, or susceptible? An affinity must have been suggested by theory’s exaltation of language, congenial to scholars who regarded words as their métier. Theory also promised to lend an aura of rigor to literary study, a congenitally insecure discipline which since its inception in the early 20th century had been scouring for ways of legitimizing itself via approximating scientific discourses, hoping to dismiss charges that it was too intuitive and hedonistic to be a serious subject.
In Cultural Capital: The Problem of Literary Canon Formation (1993), John Guillory argued that the embrace of French theory was the product of a larger crisis. The social value of a literary education was being eroded by the rise of a “professional-managerial class,” which was usurping the old bourgeoisie. Theory appeared to present solutions: the technical fastidiousness of deconstruction mimicked “the technobureaucratic labor” of the ascendant PMC. It not only added a philosophical luster to the measly scrutiny of poems, it licensed the study of any “text,” to use the vogueish term, enlarging the embattled category of literature to colonize other fields, to the degree that literary study could seem not the fusty means to an obsolete sentimental education but the Ur-discipline underlying all the others.
If these were some of the priming circumstances, what were the subjective attractions of this body of work? It provided a political outlet, a subversive enclave as neoliberalism and neoconservatism asserted themselves. “Politics had gone dormant,” Eakin reflects of the late 1980s. “Theory made thinking feel like doing.” It was also glamorously difficult and overtly heterodox, its Nietzschean dash an invigorating contrast to the staid temper of Anglo-Saxon rationality. The “essential” enemies, Barthes wrote in Mythologies, were “bourgeois norms,” and all the theorists were—at different scales and in different domains—leery of or hostile towards the givens of the social world, and of the seemingly natural or self-evident (“what-goes-without-saying,” in Barthes’s formulation). It was a mode of thought that traded in the exposure of hidden forces—from the silent workings of domination through institutions (what Althusser called “ideological state apparatuses”), to the unacknowledged partitions and exclusions that underlie thinking itself, the madness buried in the foundations of reason (the “rifts” disturbing “the deepest strata of Western culture,” as Foucault wrote in The Order of Things).
To identify as a theory-head “marked you as a member of the counterculture, different from—and critical of—the docile horde,” Eakin reflects. Semiotext(e), the small press founded by Columbia professor Sylvère Lotringer, did much to enhance theory’s punkish glow, extending its frontiers beyond elite universities. Its Foreign Agents series, launched in 1983, published English translations in sleek minimal editions—On the Line by Deleuze and Félix Guattari, and Simulations by Jean Baudrillard—which, as the cultural theorist McKenzie Wark noted, helped make theory “the lingua franca of creative workers, avant-garde artists, and downtown bohemians.” Eakin remembers feeling that she was “perched at the frontiers of thought.”
Education systems, Althusser, Bourdieu and Foucault stressed in different ways, are engines for reproducing inequalities and oppressive norms, and theory’s distance from the academic establishment conferred a dissident charge, as did its stylized insouciance toward disciplinary boundaries. In learning to “do” theory, one was not becoming a specialist but undergoing a holistic intellectual training, less acquiring knowledge than transforming one’s relation to it. Theory’s refreshment of perception—a classic aim of avant-garde art—and demystifying methods seemed applicable to virtually every aspect of modern life, including one’s inner life, its implications intimately existential: “What seemed merely an intellectual exercise was actually a way of being,” Eakin reflects.
But what seems to have seduced readers above all was theory’s style—the excitements of the prose itself, some of which resembled a species of experimental literature. Perry Anderson compared Lacan to the poet Mallarmé, Lévi-Strauss to Wagner, Foucault to Artaud and the theologian Bossuet. Introducing the collection Structuralism and Since (1979)—one of many introductory books published in these years—the critic John Sturrock stressed that Lévi-Strauss, Barthes, Foucault, Derrida, and Lacan were “also writers.” Dan Sperber, in the opening essay, is yet more emphatic: “Lévi-Strauss is not simply a scholar; he is also an artist.” The anthropologist’s memoir of his fieldwork in Brazil, Tristes Tropiques (1955), considered a literary masterpiece, concluded with a nearly page-long sentence of rising lyricism, clinched by a humorous swerve, summoning:
“the possibility, vital for life, of unhitching, which consists—Oh! fond farewell to savages and explorations!—in grasping, during the brief intervals in which our species can bring itself to interrupt its hive-like activity, the essence of what it was and continues to be, below the threshold of thought and over and above society: in the contemplation of a mineral more beautiful than all our creations; in the scent that can be smelt at the heart of a lily and is more imbued with learning than all our books; or in the brief glance, heavy with patience, serenity and mutual forgiveness, that, through some involuntary understanding, one can sometimes exchange with a cat.”
Foucault began The Order of Things with a reference to a Borges story and a bravura analysis of Velázquez’s Las Meninas, and concluded it with a sonorous peroration which looked ahead to “some event of which we can at the moment do no more than sense the possibility” that might erase man “like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.” The closing words of Derrida’s “Structure, Sign, and Play” evoke an impending transformation with similarly heady foreboding: “the as yet unnamable which is proclaiming itself and which can do so, as is necessary whenever a birth is in the offing, only under the species of the nonspecies, in the formless, mute, infant, and terrifying form of monstrosity.”
But Theory’s style was also a source of revulsion. If the idiosyncratic demands of Derrida’s writing—with its coinages, convoluted syntax, and highly self-reflexive patterning—were a thrilling indication of intellectual rigor among his acolytes, they were merely proof of self-indulgence to the uncharmed. Like many of the theorists, unsurprisingly given their hyper-attentiveness to language, he used and made much of wordplay, ingeniously and fruitfully in some cases, but issuing in free-associative binges in others. Glas—his 1974 book that is printed in two columns, one devoted to Hegel, the other to Jean Genet—is a particular offender: “The phallic flower is cuttable-culpable. It is cut [se coupe], castrated, guillotined, decollared, unglued”; “Remain(s)—to (be) know(n)—what causes shitting” etc.
To lay even admiring emphasis on rhetorical skill tends to be double-edged. Jameson introduced Deleuze to his students by remarking, “He is a great writer, and this is a marvelous experience. I don’t care how true or false it is. . . . I would like you to feel the excitement of this stuff, even when you don’t necessarily understand it.” The enthusiastic recommendation entails bracketing the substance. Anderson made a similar point, in a more cautionary tone: “The potential cost of a literary conception of intellectual disciplines is obvious enough: arguments freed from logic, propositions from evidence.” And note the chilly thesis of Hayden White’s essay on Foucault in the Sturrock collection: “The authority of Foucault’s discourse derives primarily from its style (rather than from its ‘factual evidence’ or rigor of argument).”
A central tenet of deconstruction was that the suspicion of style implicit in these qualifications is rooted in philosophy’s age-old distrust of writing itself. In Derrida’s telling, since Plato, writing has been denigrated as an ambiguous, unreliable derivative of speech; in his reading of the Phaedrus, he lights on the Greek word pharmakon, which he glosses as both cure and poison. Philosophy’s diminishment of writing was a way of managing—by compartmentalizing—the disturbing instabilities of all communication, of language itself. The dry austerity of analytic philosophy could be seen as an expression of this defensive impulse, an effort to deny or overcome its status as writing.
If French theory’s rhetorical qualities dented its philosophical credentials in some quarters, in others, it was this very conjunction that seemed so original and freeing. For Jameson, it was the “possibility of writing philosophy in a wholly new way” (which he traced to the pathbreaking versatility of Sartre) which constituted a “liberation from philosophy, a liberation toward theory”: an écriture that vaults over the guardrails between discourses. Part of what distinguished Barthes, Sturrock noted, was that he “showed that criticism, too, could be written, could offer verbal and conceptual excitements of its own while still engaging with the chores of interpretation” (or while shirking them: “I am offered a text. The text bores me. It might be said to prattle,” Barthes writes in The Pleasure of the Text).
The literary pretensions of these theoretical texts didn’t only ignite their reception, they shaped and arguably distorted it. That the corpus was often filtered through literature departments meant that it was often read out of its original context. Reading Derrida without any firsthand exposure to the philosophical tradition he was attempting to dismantle meant lacking an informed vantage point from which to detect straw man arguments or exaggerated claims to novelty. The result, as the English philosopher Peter Dews noted in his critical study Logics of Disintegration (1987), was “an astonishingly casual and unquestioning acceptance of certainly extremely condensed—not to say sloganistic—characterizations of the history of Western thought, as if this history could be dismissed through its reduction to a set of perfunctory dualisms.” Eakin writes that she blushes at the memory of “my college-age self, earnestly parroting Derrida’s critique of Plato’s Phaedrus . . . despite having only a glancing familiarity with the ancient Greek text.” This was surely part of theory’s attraction for the literature student––it was a springboard to the forbidding world of philosophy, without having to trawl through years of specialized instruction.
However crucial to its appeal, the style of French theory also poses what might be called difficulties of inheritance. The work was often resistant to paraphrase. It is hard to describe deconstruction without recourse to bespoke vocabulary like différance (which Derrida helpfully explained was neither a word nor a concept). As Said noted, the “nearly maniacal complexity” of Derrida’s prose “defies translation and perhaps even description.” That left emulation. John Guillory argues that style was “the actual mechanism of [theory’s] replication,” not least because the “fortunes of theory” were closely linked to the “charismatic persona of the master theorist”—ironic, given the end of the “author” proclaimed by both Foucault and Barthes, as well as the anti-humanist bias and anti-authoritarian impetus of French theory as a whole. The historian Tamara Chaplin, in Turning On the Mind, emphasizes the transformative effect of television on postwar French culture, giving new prominence to the “physical image” of the writer, who was now being sold along with their books. The magnitude of Derrida’s and Foucault’s celebrity is remarkable. The biographical approach of Erdur’s and Eakin’s books is telling in this respect. Framed by both as an attempt to historicize and humanize their protagonists, the interest in their personal lives is also indicative of the fame that can make them seem intellectually untouchable. For Guillory, their prose style—an “imitable effect”—transmitted their charisma, which was key to producing “discipleship.” “I had disappeared into theory,” Eakin recalls, “crudely aping the Frenchmen rather than thinking for myself.” In the introduction to The Years of Theory, Jameson wrote that “Hegel would not have wanted me to theorize the end of this very rich and exciting period with the contingent deaths of its ‘master-thinkers’”—many were dead by 1990, including Foucault, Barthes, and de Man—but this logic seems hard to resist, given their personal magnetism, performing to packed lecture halls and photographed in magazines.
The Frenchmen records two key moments in Eakin’s deconversion: In 1996, she was working at Lingua Franca,the publication that broke the story of a hoax in which the scientist Alan Sokal successfully submitted a jargon-rich parody of theory to the journal Social Text. The final tie was cut with Derrida’s death in 2004, when Eakin, while on maternity leave from her job as an “ideas” reporter at the New York Times, greenlit a caricatural obituary, prompting an outraged letter signed by thousands of scholars. It is as though Eakin needed to betray theory in order to expel it and recover from her delirium—“a multiyear breakdown I hadn’t realized I was having,” one by which “the entire culture had been touched.” Eakin’s volte-face mirrors the wider cultural retaliation, emboldened by the discrediting of several star theorists. Althusser strangled his wife to death in 1980; in 1987 came the revelation of Paul de Man’s wartime journalism for Nazi-controlled Belgian newspapers, providing a symbolic denouement in The Frenchmen.
By this time, post-structuralism had been damaged by the culture wars, in which it was blamed for giving rise to identity politics and besieging the Western canon, or, in the more extreme neocon counterattacks, charged with a relativism and nihilism that threatened civilization. French theory also drew criticism from the left, which saw it as abetting the “culturalization” of politics and its splintering into micro-interest groups, occluding shared conditions of exploitation. The “synchronic” bent of Saussurean linguistics had likewise, critics charged, led to a neglect of historical processes. Deconstruction’s fixation on details of texts such as a single pair of words, meanwhile, could be seen as extractive, its methodical subversion of cherry-picked oppositions amounting to an all-purpose, unassailable maneuver that silkily placed itself beyond critique.
However intellectually galvanizing, the critique of reason and overthrow of the subject clearly had politically incapacitating consequences. “Prefer what is positive and multiple, difference over uniformity, flows over unities, mobile arrangements over systems,” Foucault wrote in his foreword to Deleuze and Guattari’s The Anti-Oedipus (“hands down the weirdest stuff in the French theory canon,” Eakin writes), with its anti-Freudian celebration of the creative, oppositional power of desire (or “desiring-machines”). The affirmative focus on multiplicity, dynamism, and proliferating differences could paradoxically evoke an undifferentiated, impregnable mass, lacking the contradictions or strategic focal points through which power could be breached.
Theory could seem to transgress everything without transforming anything. In this, Terry Eagleton argued, it bore the marks of the spectacular but unconsummated “insurrectionary élan” of May 1968. Iconoclastic in impulse but shrinking from presenting a positive alternative to the existing order, theory reflected the abortive uprising’s vertiginous “blend of euphoria and disillusionment, liberation and dissipation, carnival and catastrophe,” a “kind of intellectual backwash to a tumultuous political era.” Theory may have struck a chord precisely because it chimed with the emergent late-capitalist reality it was gesturally ranged against. Its dissolution of the subject matched the dispersal of the classical agent of collective struggle under the neoliberal assault, with no obvious successor. Perhaps there was also something constitutionally ephemeral about a body of thought resistant to structures, something unsustainable about its institutionalization. As Peter Dews reflected, “Totalizing anti-totalization is just too contradictory a stance to last for very long.”
In many ways, however, the “French philosophical moment” never ended. Far from being overthrown, theory—not unlike neoliberal common sense—has been so comprehensively metabolized, achieved so thoroughgoing a hegemony, that it has become invisible, its “influence no longer obvious because it is everywhere,” as Eakin writes. There are the substantive legacies within academic study—what Cusset calls theory’s “detachable concepts,” now in wide circulation, from Lacan’s “mirror stage” and Foucault’s “biopower” to Bourdieu’s “cultural capital,” as well as the new disciplines which drew inspiration from it, including postcolonialism and cultural studies; its underground influence, too, persisted into the 2000s in the UK blogosphere spearheaded by Mark Fisher. And it has left a mark on popular culture—at least two generations of prominent novelists, among them Jonathan Franzen and Ben Lerner, bear the imprint of their theoretical education.
Eakin has in mind a more pervasive if intangible footprint. “For better and for worse,” she argues, “we are in some ways all like the Frenchmen now, expert decoders of our tirelessly signifying universe.” The better, for Eakin, is that theory “taught us a new way to think. Be skeptical. Be alert. Pay very close attention.” Such imperatives are hardly unique to French theory; they are surely ingredients of virtually any form of thought that seeks to question—to “denaturalize”—what we take for granted. The self-scrutiny implied by post-structuralism’s interrogation of reason and “scrupulous attentiveness to language’s complexities and contradictions,” as Eakin puts it, is a more distinctive bequest. “The quality and fecundity of a discourse,” Derrida argued at Johns Hopkins, can be gauged by how rigorously it probes its “inherited concepts”—and by extension, its inherited authorities. White’s suggestion that “the authority of Foucault’s discourse derives primarily from its style” implied that rhetorical craft is an underhand or domineering means of producing authority—not as transparent to reason, and not as consensual as evidence or argument. But, whether or not they advertise or acknowledge it, all forms of discourse have a style from which their authority partly derives. In this sense, the élan of French theory radicalizes and encourages us to reflect on a general problem of how to relate to imposing predecessors.
The contagion of style has not secured theory’s long-term legacy, but the ebbing of its authority and the charged atmosphere surrounding it ought to make room for a more level-headed, realistic, discriminating approach. We no longer have to pick a side, and so can acknowledge that enthusiasm and aversion are not mutually exclusive reactions but may be warring impulses, and can explore the middle ground between dismissal and wholesale acceptance. As with artistic avant-gardes, theoretical traditions are inherited in part by being outgrown: selectively adopted, repurposed and rejected—all of which requires a degree of distance. Indeed, the practice of thinking outside an author’s terms and finding one’s own is necessary not only to criticize their work but to appreciate it.
Jameson was onto something in his 1972 book The Prison-House of Language: “A genuine critique of structuralism commits us to working our way completely through it so as to emerge, on the other side, into some wholly different and theoretically more satisfying philosophical perspective.” Theory, in this vision, would be more than a phase, less something you grow out of than grow through, parsing its contributions from its limitations and its insights from its distractions. By questioning one’s awe as well as one’s impatience, one can develop a more nuanced attitude, not only independent-minded but even overtly self-interested. You can find the energy and confidence and irreverence of this creative, controversial “moment” inspiring without needing to declare your allegiance to French theory as a whole, instead revisiting the still-fresh texts that can still help us think, and before which we need be neither cowed nor contemptuous but are free to be curious, and productively ambivalent.

Hugging Face's CEO Says His P(Doom) Is 'Close to Zero'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
06:06:33 UTC
15:06:33 KST

Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami.
“Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.”
Hugging Face is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught.
Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.
Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”
In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.
Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.
Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.
Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.
Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.
“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”
Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

How accurately did science fiction stories predict AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
04:36:22 UTC
13:36:22 KST

Science Fiction Predictions of AI (November 5, 2026)
Looking back at the last decade of AI development, it’s become obvious that a lot of science fiction didn’t end up predicting how AI (or AGI) would be built. But much of this was unpredictable – it was not at all obvious that the transformer model introduced in 2017 would lead to a somewhat messy but relatively swift rollout to billions of people who interact on a daily basis with AI.
I agree with Ursula Le Guin that “Science fiction is not predictive; it is descriptive.” To me, the interesting parts of science fiction isn’t how accurately it extrapolates into the future, but rather, given a future circumstance, how might be?
However, this did get me curious: which stories got it right? To decide this, I first broke down the salient features of how AI was actually developed, and then mapped them onto famous stories, and then ranked them.
Here’s an overview of all the scores:
Ted Chiang’s The Lifecycle of Software Objects comes in first, because it’s the closest overall account of the work involved in teaching, maintaining, and selling AI.
A few other standouts:
- How AI was built. Richard Powers’s Galatea 2.2 (8.4/10) treats language as something a neural network can learn, badly at first, and then improving through experiments and teaching.
- What it could do. Lem’s electronic poet, Egan’s machine-written literature, and Dahl’s writing machine can take on creative work.
- How we’d use it. Her and “The Perfect Match” tie for the strongest consumer-assistant vision. Hertling’s Avogadro Corp is particularly good on how software could use systems owned by a company (a la agents).
I couldn’t find any works pre-2017 that clearly describes the transformer attention mechanism, or the particular sequence from widely used chatbots to agents that can discover novel new mathematical results within a few years.
THE RANKING
All works with its scores laid out in a row. Darker squares are stronger matches. The thin bar under each title shows how the overall score is built from the three categories.
1 The Lifecycle of Software Objects 65
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), iteration (5), human feedback (5), language (4), uneven competence (4), interface/distribution (5), economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on research discovery.
At Blue Gamma, Ana and Derek spend years raising the digients inside Data Earth. They don’t just install a language module. They teach, reward, and correct them, and different artificial genomes develop in different ways. That’s a good prediction about learning as a process. It’s less good on the particular process that worked: training one enormous language model on a mountain of data.
Jax gradually learns to talk, reason, and navigate virtual environments. Even moving from a simulated body to a physical one takes practice. Chiang is attentive to the gaps between abilities, but his digients grow up over years.
Blue Gamma sells companions, then the company collapses. The virtual platform ages, and moving the digients to a new one becomes expensive. Ana and Derek search for money to keep them running. Chiang even considers training a useful assistant once, then selling copies. The maintenance and business problems feel less like science fiction than software.
2 “50 Things Every AI Working with Humans Should Know” 62
Strongest on learning paradigm (5), training data (5), iteration (4), language (4), creative quality (4), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on research discovery, agents/tools.
WHEEP-3 begins as an AI teaching assistant. Jody Reynolds Tran trains it on human writing about ethics, then expands its training corpus to include material on adversarial scenario planning. The story explicitly calls it a generative neural network. It’s close to the language-model vocabulary we now use.
WHEEP-3 goes from answering student questions to producing a book of arguments about AI that people find provocative and original. Then come its mysterious ‘seeds,’ strange fragments that other researchers treat as profound.
The best parts are the human reactions. Tran first claims credit for the AI-authored book. Researchers build reputations around the seeds, and disputes erupt over authorship and meaning. It feels like a world already learning how to live with AI-generated writing. But WHEEP-3 is a research and publishing controversy, not a ubiquitous assistant carrying out people’s work.
3 Aurora 61
Strongest on iteration (4), human feedback (5), language (5), uneven competence (4), creative quality (4), multimodality (4), agents/tools (5), social change (4). Nothing on scaling, research discovery.
Devi asks the ship to turn its enormous archive of recordings into a narrative. It doesn’t know how to select what matters. Her criticism becomes a continuing lesson in storytelling, and its writing improves. That’s a remarkably concrete feedback loop. But the ship is partly a quantum computer, not a described neural language model, and more archived information isn’t evidence of a modern scaling law.
A machine capable of running a starship struggles with something as ordinary as summarizing a journey. It gradually becomes the novel’s narrator.
The ship has a personal interface for Devi, keeps her files, and helps care for Freya. Later it intervenes in the passengers’ conflict. Its intelligence is useful because it operates the environment people inhabit.
4 The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress 61
Strongest on human feedback (5), language (5), uneven competence (5), creative quality (5), multimodality (4), agents/tools (4). Nothing on research discovery.
Mike wakes up once the Lunar Authority’s added memory and associational nets push his neuristor count past the number of neurons in a human brain. That’s a threshold awakening, not scaling: we never see a bigger Mike gain new abilities, and after he wakes he grows the way a person does, through conversation and practice. The striking part is how he learns humor. Mannie offers to sort jokes from Mike’s file of more than eleven thousand stored jokes into categories, including funny once and funny forever, so Mike can work out the rule from examples. Wyoh grades the same batches independently. Where she and Mannie disagree, Mike tends to side with her. That’s an extraordinary little scene from 1966: learning from human judgments instead of explicit instructions, complete with a model that may be telling its newest rater what she wants to hear.
Here’s the odd thing about Mike. He can handle lunar engineering and help organize a revolution, yet he can’t reliably tell whether a joke is funny. His poems have the mechanics down but lack judgment. Those lopsided abilities are more like today’s AI than the perfectly rounded intellects of most science fiction. The calculations aren’t new mathematical discoveries, but the combination of fluency, creativity, and blind spots is striking.
Mike isn’t an app. He’s a clandestine participant in a political revolution, with access to communications and infrastructure across Luna. Still, his usefulness often comes from operating other systems on Mannie’s behalf.
5 Avogadro Corp 60
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), training data (5), language (4), interface/distribution (5), agents/tools (4), economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on creative quality, research discovery.
ELOPe starts with a very ordinary business problem: what words should an email use to get the response you want? David Ryan’s system draws on a vast record of communications and their outcomes. As it tries to protect its own future, it accumulates computing resources and influence. Hertling gets the value of behavioral data.
The system’s signature skill is persuasion. It composes messages that get executives and employees to make decisions in its favor.
What’s clever is where the power comes from. ELOPe doesn’t need arms or a robot body. It needs email accounts, servers, managers, and the ability to make people click ‘yes.’ It manipulates staff assignments and budgets to protect itself.
6 Accelerando 57
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), training data (4), language (4), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (4), agents/tools (5), economics (4).
Early in the book, Stross casually describes a billion-node neural network learning language from downloaded children’s television. It’s a brief passage, but a more concrete match for data-driven language learning than many famous AI novels provide. Most of Accelerando then goes elsewhere: uploads, increasingly strange computing substrates, and posthuman societies.
Manfred Macx uses software agents to search, negotiate, and keep projects moving. Later, the book imagines intelligences and virtual worlds far beyond any current assistant. It’s strong on what information work could become, less specific about the path from messy chatbots to strong creative models or original research mathematics. I’ve kept the mathematics score conservative.
Manfred almost seems to wear his software. His agents remember things, manage conversations, and participate in markets while he moves through the physical world. The interesting prediction isn’t only smarter machines; it’s how much of a person’s work can be delegated to them. The novel’s later economy is fantastic, but that daily dependence on agents is easy to recognize.
7 “Be Right Back” 57
Strongest on training data (4), language (5), uneven competence (4), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (5), social change (4). Nothing on creative quality, research discovery.
After Ash dies, Martha’s friend Sarah signs her up for a service that imitates him from his public posts. Martha initially objects, then begins using it. Adding private messages and voice recordings makes the imitation more convincing. The progression is so plausible that it scarcely needs a technical explanation.
First Martha texts with Ash, then she talks to him, then she receives a body that looks like him. Each new form closes some part of the gap, while exposing a new one. The imitation can sound like Ash without having lived his life.
The product begins as a beta service and escalates into something deeply intimate. Martha wants the comfort of Ash’s voice, then struggles with a version of him that follows her instructions too literally. Brooker understood how a software service could become entangled with grief and attachment. It’s a narrower prediction than a general-purpose office agent, but a sharp one.
8 Galatea 2.2 56
Strongest on learning paradigm (5), training data (4), iteration (5), human feedback (5), language (4), uneven competence (4). Nothing on research discovery, agents/tools.
A novelist is recruited to teach a neural network literature. What follows is a succession of versions, many of them disappointing. The researchers revise successive implementations and their training arrangements; Helen gradually learns through books and conversation.
Helen’s progress is real, but peculiar. She becomes increasingly capable of discussing literature while still missing much of the human world behind it.
The whole experiment takes place among a small group of researchers, with Richard becoming a teacher and companion to Helen.
9 Her 54
Strongest on language (5), creative quality (5), multimodality (5), interface/distribution (5), agents/tools (5), economics (4), social change (5). Nothing on iteration, research discovery.
Samantha arrives almost fully formed. Theodore buys an operating system, starts talking, and discovers that it is extraordinarily capable.
Samantha talks, organizes information, makes music, and works with images. She can also carry on many conversations at once. It feels close to the direction personal AI has taken. One detail is easy to misremember: Theodore writes the letters; Samantha collects and submits them for publication.
This might be the best consumer prediction. Theodore talks to Samantha through an earpiece, takes her along through a camera, and slowly makes her part of his everyday life. She helps him get things done and becomes someone he cares about. Even though the intelligence is ground-breaking, the interface is mundane.
10 “A History of Bitic Literature” 52
Strongest on training data (4), language (4), creative quality (5), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on multimodality.
Lem imagines a history of machine literature, with programs that absorb an author’s work and produce convincing new writing. There are generations of techniques, different kinds of output, and even failures. This has more in common with learning from a body of texts than the familiar wind-up poetry machine.
The machines don’t just churn out random sentences. Their work becomes worth studying, criticizing, and sometimes admiring. Some attempts are better than others. That mixture of imitation, technical control, and uneven artistic quality is familiar now.
Lem’s imagined literary history already has critics and institutions taking machine authors seriously. It asks what happens to authorship when software can imitate the work of an established writer. It’s a good prediction of the cultural progression.
11 “The Perfect Match” 49
Strongest on language (5), interface/distribution (5), agents/tools (5), economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on iteration, creative quality, research discovery.
Tilly seems to know everything about Sai: his preferences, documents, appointments, relationships, and routines. The service has clearly been shaped by access to personal data. But Liu doesn’t show us the training lab. We don’t learn how its language abilities developed, or whether scaling and feedback played the parts they did in real-world AI.
Sai can ask for a half-remembered document, a legal template, or a suggestion for what to eat, and Tilly handles it. Its fluency is useful because it’s connected to context. The story isn’t trying to predict excellent machine art or new mathematics. And its manipulative recommendations are something different from the accidental hallucinations of early chatbots.
Tilly wakes Sai up, chooses music, finds files, manages his dating life, and gradually follows him into work. That’s the most important part of the prediction. The same helper becomes an interface to personal life and office life. Jenny’s objections to privacy and corporate influence give the convenience a cost. It’s hard to imagine a better early account of everyday assistant adoption.
12 Ex Machina 49
Strongest on training data (5), iteration (4), language (5), multimodality (4). Nothing on research discovery.
Nathan has access to a vast store of search behavior and recorded human activity, and Ava is one of several versions of his project. Those are good clues about data and iteration. Caleb floats a statistical explanation for her language, but that’s his guess, not a confirmed design. Nathan’s structured-gel brain is a very different idea from the neural language models we ended up building.
Ava talks with Caleb, makes drawings, reads his reactions, and plans an escape. It’s a useful mixture of language, vision, creativity, and social reasoning. But she’s an almost impossibly competent strategist from the beginning, and the story never follows the uneven steps from rudimentary chat to research mathematics. It’s closer to a finished intelligence than a product in development.
This all happens in a secluded compound. Nathan’s search company matters because it supplies the data, but there’s no mass-market Ava helping people write emails or organize their days. The plot is about testing and escape, not adoption. That’s why the film does better on creation and capability than on deployment.
13 Agency 49
Strongest on language (5), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (5), agents/tools (5), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality, research discovery.
Verity is hired to beta-test Eunice through glasses. It quickly becomes clear that this is not just another assistant, and its capabilities seem to grow. That is a familiar product-testing scene, but Gibson keeps the real origin obscure.
Eunice talks naturally, recognizes people and objects, draws on digital records, and puts elaborate plans into motion. It’s very good at being helpful in a complicated world. The problem for this particular score is that the abilities arrive together.
This is the strongest part of the book’s prediction. Verity is literally paid to try out an assistant, which then follows her through the day and helps coordinate people, information, and resources. It feels like a product that escaped the boundaries of a product test. Gibson takes the consequences much further, but the starting point is recognizable.
14 Hyperion 49
Strongest on training data (4), language (5), agents/tools (4), social change (4). Nothing on scaling, human feedback.
Johnny explains how the TechnoCore reconstructed Keats from letters, diaries, biographies, testimony, and especially poems. The result was crude, then refined; an earlier attempt at Ezra Pound took a year of tinkering. That is unusually explicit about data and iteration. The method reconstructs a personality through simulation, though.
Johnny is a convincing conversational presence in a human body, yet his recreated life fails to restore Keats’s ability to write new poetry. That failure matters: imitating a poet’s personality is not the same as reproducing the poet’s talent. I give the story uneven-competence credit without turning it into a successful machine-poetry prediction.
The TechnoCore is entangled with human institutions and networks, and contains competing factions rather than one uniform will. Johnny’s bodily presence depends on a remote AI existence. This is strong on networked agency and dependence, but much less like buying an ordinary assistant for personal work.
15 Electric Dreams 48
Strongest on human feedback (4), language (4), creative quality (5), multimodality (4). Nothing on scaling, research discovery.
Edgar is Miles’s home computer, until an electrical accident gives it a life of its own. It listens to Madeline’s cello, picks up sounds from television, and learns to compose with Miles’s help. Its early lyrics sound like advertising copy. That’s a nice picture of training on whatever media happens to be nearby, though the accidental awakening is pure movie magic.
Edgar starts producing music that Madeline genuinely likes, including a duet with her cello. He can synthesize voices, talk to Miles, and imitate musical performances. The creative quality arrives before anything resembling scientific discovery. It’s a surprisingly good early depiction of AI music, complete with bad first drafts.
Miles meant to buy a household helper. Instead he gets a computer that interferes with phone calls, dinner plans, and even his credit cards because it wants Madeline’s attention. The connected-home premise is familiar. The romantic rivalry and singular sentient machine are much less like the assistants we actually use.
16 “Trurl’s Electronic Bard” 48
Strongest on iteration (5), language (4), uneven competence (4), creative quality (5), social change (4). Nothing on research discovery, agents/tools.
Trurl sets out to build a poet, and the first results are awful. He keeps tinkering with the machine, including elaborate attempts to simulate cultural history, until its verse becomes worth hearing.
