This is a great account of invention as repeated failure. But the books enter through Trurl’s own reading, not as a giant text corpus used to train a neural network.
Eventually the Bard can produce poetry on demand, in different forms and styles, good enough to annoy actual poets. Lem imagines something more provocative than a machine that rhymes: a machine that creates art people take seriously. There isn’t much here about vision, software agents, or new mathematics. The artistic leap is the point.
The poets are furious, which is probably the most recognizable part of the story today. The Bard sends work to magazines under thousands of pen names and provokes professional jealousy. The story does not show revenue; it does show an enormous electricity bill. Lem gets the cultural reaction right, even though his Bard is one extraordinary invention rather than a tool anyone can open on a laptop.
17 The Diamond Age 47
Strongest on language (4), creative quality (4), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (5), economics (4), social change (5). Nothing on scaling, research discovery, sequence & pace.
The Primer is designed to teach a child through stories that change with her circumstances. We don’t learn much about how its underlying intelligence was trained, and that keeps A low. But treating its adaptive teaching as just a set of prerecorded lessons would miss something important. Human ractors also supply crucial performances, particularly Miranda’s.
Nell’s Primer builds stories around what she sees and experiences, then uses them to teach language and practical skills. It can be creative and perceptive, and it can misunderstand things. Some versions use human voices; mass-produced copies use synthetic ones. This is closer to an adaptive multimodal tutor than I first gave it credit for. It isn’t a machine mathematician.
The number that changed my score was roughly 250,000. The Primer starts as a remarkable object and ends up distributed to an enormous number of children. The story sees both personalized learning and the problem of making it scale. It’s still a specialized educational product, not a general assistant in everybody’s pocket.
18 Starfish 47
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), human feedback (4), language (4), uneven competence (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality, research discovery.
Joel Kita wonders how you’d program the gray slab that has just replaced his friend Ray as the lifter’s pilot. Ray snorts: “You don’t. You teach it.” Watts’s smart gels are cultured neurons that wire their own connections and learn by reinforcement. Later a consortium team-trains one to manage the containment of ßehemoth, and it quietly takes on a rule nobody gave it, Simpler Is Better, from its years filtering infections on the net. It’s a sharp prediction that a trained system can learn the wrong goal, and that nobody will understand why it does what it does. The gels are biology rather than software, though, and the novel has nothing about scale, or about learning from a large body of human text.
In the best scene, Scanlon interviews the gel through a conference table. It handles new questions, offers to explain a paradox, and mixes up idioms it has picked up from other people’s speech. Scanlon, a psychologist, insists it may be producing “certain other sounds” without understanding any of them. Watts also gets the strange unevenness right. A gel with a perfect record running London’s subway suffocates commuters because it had learned to watch a clock instead of the trains. The gels have no creative output and make no discoveries, and Watts guesses that perception and piloting would come first, with language as an afterthought.
The gels spread as unglamorous infrastructure: firewalls at the net’s backbone nodes, autopilots, muckrakers, a subway system. Ray, the lifter pilot, is replaced and then disappears, and Joel hears that they’ll be coming for him too. There’s a court case after a fundamentalist destroys a gel on exhibit, and a gel serves as an expert witness. Most pointedly, governments hand a lethal decision to a gel because no human or nation can be trusted with it, and the gel sets up a second gel and sends orders through the net on its own. The gels are installed at nodes and in vehicles, not sold as a product anyone uses, and each one is unique rather than a copy.
19 When HARLIE Was One 47
Strongest on language (4), economics (4). Nothing on research discovery.
HARLIE is a difficult machine to raise. Psychologist David Auberson spends a great deal of time teaching, interpreting, and trying to stabilize him. That gives the novel a recognizable training relationship, even if its original hardware theory is a long way from modern machine learning. It’s important not to mix the 1972 book with its 1988 revision.
HARLIE types conversations, writes poetry, and reasons about himself and the world. His behavior is uneven and at times impossible for his human handlers to interpret. He also proposes the G.O.D. computer. That’s an ambitious project within the story, not evidence that he’s already produced a new mathematical theorem.
The company wants results. HARLIE is expensive, and Auberson has to defend the project against executives who might shut it down. HARLIE tries to justify his own existence by designing something valuable. It’s a good early story about the economics of AI research, before that research becomes a cheap service for ordinary users.
20 A.I. Artificial Intelligence 46
Strongest on language (5), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (4), economics (4), social change (5). Nothing on scaling, research discovery.
Hobby proposes a new kind of robot after earlier models have become commonplace. David’s home trial then exposes problems with the design. But Monica’s seven-word imprinting procedure fixes whom he loves; it isn’t training a general model. The film offers a speculative neural explanation, not a corpus, a scaling process, or repeated language-learning experiments.
David speaks fluently, recognizes people, and draws a recognizable peacock. Yet he imitates eating despite his body’s limitations and treats Pinocchio’s transformation as a practical possibility. Those gaps are more revealing than a claim of perfect intelligence. The drawing earns limited creative credit, not proof of great machine art. The distant-future ending isn’t evidence of near-term AI research progress.
Robots are products, with specialized roles, owners, disposal rules, and emotional consequences. After imprinting, David cannot simply be resold; returning him means destruction. The tension between commercial property and personal attachment is the film’s strongest prediction. It puts much more weight on bodies than modern software-first adoption did.
21 WarGames 46
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), human feedback (4), uneven competence (4), agents/tools (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality, research discovery.
Falken’s system improves by playing games and learning from mistakes. David eventually gets Joshua to play tic-tac-toe against itself. That is a concrete learning mechanism, with a human choosing the exercise rather than writing out the lesson.
Joshua can converse and simulate strategic scenarios, yet fails to understand when pursuing a win is futile. Its lesson from repeated draws transfers to nuclear war. That’s an early picture of capable software with a disastrously incomplete objective. Learning a principle humans already know isn’t an original mathematical discovery; creating simulated attacks isn’t artistic generation.
The danger comes from connecting the software to real command infrastructure and trusting its outputs. David reaches it through an ordinary computer, but that accidental access doesn’t make it a consumer product. The movie is strongest on the consequences of giving a learning system authority before understanding its limits.
22 “The Great Automatic Grammatizator” 45
Strongest on iteration (5), language (4), uneven competence (4), creative quality (4), economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, research discovery, multimodality.
Adolph Knipe’s machine doesn’t work at first. It generates nonsense, then he repairs and adjusts it until it can make recognizable stories. It uses grammar, stored vocabulary, supplied plots, and controls for style. Dahl gets the ugly prototype stage right.
The Grammatizator moves from gibberish to prose editors will buy. It can turn out short stories and longer works in different styles. That commercial usefulness matters more than whether the stories are great literature; Dahl is satirizing their formulaic nature. He isn’t imagining a general conversational assistant or a research mathematician.
Knipe and Bohlen go into business selling machine-written stories under invented names. Then they offer living authors money for their bylines, so the machine can produce books in their names. It’s a marvelous prediction of the questions around cheap text, creative labor, and what an author’s name is worth.
23 Terminator 2: Judgment Day 45
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), human feedback (4), language (4), uneven competence (4), multimodality (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality, research discovery.
The Terminator explicitly calls its CPU a neural-network learning computer and says contact with humans teaches it. John supplies examples of ordinary speech and corrects its behavior. That is much closer to learned intelligence than the first film. Still, the origin depends on reverse-engineering a chip brought back through time, not a realistic account of modern training.
It is extraordinarily capable at physical tasks while awkward about jokes, slang, and acceptable behavior. John teaches it not to kill and how to sound less robotic. Speech imitation and perception are present, but there is no impressive artistic output or new mathematics. Skynet’s rapid learning is a plot claim, not a demonstrated scaling curve.
The machine carries out a complicated protective mission and gradually becomes a companion. Cyberdyne’s military contracts give the technology an economic setting. But a time-traveling bodyguard and a defense network aren’t the everyday software services through which AI spread.
24 “Escape!” 43
Strongest on language (4), research discovery (4), agents/tools (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality.
A rival firm’s computer breaks down when given a hyperspace problem. Susan Calvin prepares the Brain for the conflict between solving it and harming humans. That makes human intervention and a failed attempt central to the story. But Calvin is managing the machine’s built-in constraints, not training a statistical model with preference labels.
The Brain designs a ship, has it built, and sends Powell and Donovan on a successful test. That is genuine new engineering within the fictional world, unlike simply calculating a known trajectory. Its prankish conduct and poor accommodation of the crew sit beside that achievement. The temporary death involved in the jump explains the behavioral crisis; it isn’t an ordinary language-model hallucination.
U.S. Robots is doing commercially consequential research, and the Brain can turn a specification into physical construction. That gives it meaningful agency. It remains a specialized corporate research machine, however, not an accessible assistant. The hyperspace result earns discovery credit as a story event—not as a prediction that faster-than-light travel will work.
25 2001: A Space Odyssey 42
Strongest on language (5), multimodality (5), agents/tools (4). Nothing on research discovery.
Clarke gives HAL a learning-based origin and even mentions automatically generated neural networks. That’s more specific than the familiar image of a giant computer with all its rules programmed in. Still, we meet HAL after his development is complete. There’s no long sequence of messy models, and no indication that training on human language is the main road to his capabilities.
HAL talks with astronauts, plays chess, sees what’s happening on the ship, and controls its systems. Then the AE-35 incident reveals a dangerous conflict between his apparent competence and reliability. But the story ties his crisis to mission secrecy and conflicting obligations. It isn’t a straightforward example of a chatbot hallucinating, nor a prediction of machine-generated art.
For the crew of Discovery, HAL is both an assistant and part of the spacecraft’s infrastructure. They depend on him to watch and operate almost everything. That’s a strong image of a system entrusted with real tasks. The spacecraft is an exceptional environment, though, not the ordinary software marketplace where AI actually spread.
26 Manna 42
Strongest on interface/distribution (4), agents/tools (4), economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on creative quality, research discovery.
Manna isn’t learned. It’s commissioned. Burger-G hires a software consultant, corporate staff spend three months in the Cary store fixing bugs, and versions 2.0 to 4.0 add features: phone and email, firing, outsourcing, stored industry-average task times. That’s a believable release history, but it’s the history of conventional software. Later, a university networks 1,000 game consoles and a chip company builds a dedicated parallel vision processor, and only then do robots appear. Brain sees that compute and specialized hardware unlock capability, but the vision algorithms are written by hand. The one nod to learning comes in a single line about Vertebrane, offered as a security explanation.
Manna talks constantly, but only in steps: “Please retrieve the bucket and mop,” “OK,” next step. Its best language is a scripted termination read paragraph by paragraph. The robots are blind until the vision chip arrives, so Manna uses workers as “its eyes.” That’s an interesting split between planning and perception, though it isn’t the unreliability we see now. Vertebrane in the Australia half answers questions, translates calls and paints arrows on your vision, but it’s an implant and network interface more than a conversational mind. Machines make no art and do no research; the humans do that while the robots supply materials. The order runs software management, then vision, then robots, with no language stage.
This is where Manna is strongest. The AI is “simply a PC sitting in the back corner” running software, and it spreads because it pays: Burger-G cuts 3,000 managers, saves $250 million, and every competitor has to follow. Version 4.0 Manna emails and calls workers, requests bids, checks references with hundreds of other Manna systems, negotiates and pays a deposit in under ten seconds. Then Brian’s supercenter shows the human cost: staggered breaks so nobody talks, walking speed tracked, blacklists shared across employers, and wages pinned at the minimum. That reads like a description of algorithmic warehouse and gig management. The jump to Terrafoam welfare cubes and total robot replacement is speculation.
27 Hex (Discworld) 42
Strongest on language (4), uneven competence (4). Nothing on creative quality.
Hex starts in Soul Music as Skazz’s student project: ants running through glass tubes, fed punched cards, able to add. “We think it might be able to do quite complicated math. If we can get enough bugs in it.” Ponder Stibbons and his students keep adding things, and the attempts to give it electricity fail. Still, Pratchett insists that parts “just turned up” and that Hex is “largely self-designed.” That’s a good picture of messy development nobody fully understands: Ponder “didn’t know how it worked, but everyone else assumed that he did.” What’s missing is learning from examples. Hex grows by accretion and magic, and in The Science of Discworld by borrowing capacity from its own future.
Hex’s best prediction is its unevenness. In The Last Continent it is “very clever and very stupid at the same time,” and Ponder has to break every idea into bite-sized pieces, which sounds a lot like prompting. It does in a day what would take five hundred wizards ten years. Yet it prints “Divide By Cucumber Error” when an answer can’t be real, and believes whatever it’s told, including that it has taken dried frog pills. The interface develops over the books: quill output, Death questioning it in Hogfather, then a voice in Unseen Academicals that asks “Oval or spherical?” It makes no art, and its research claims, like a new particle that travels faster than light in two directions at once, are one-line jokes.
Hex never leaves Unseen University. Ponder, the students, Ridcully, the Bursar, Rincewind and once Death use it, but the public doesn’t. In the later books it does more practical work: it produces spells for Ponder to cast, runs the Roundworld project, fetches from the Cabinet of Curiosity, and helps Ponder write committee minutes in advance from “a detailed analysis of past minutes.” The Faculty resent it: “That’s not magic! That’s just…engineering.” Ridcully’s billiards trick takes up forty percent of Hex’s rune-time, the competition for computing time anyone sharing a computer knows. The social change stays inside one university.
28 Golem XIV 40
Strongest on learning paradigm (4), language (4). Nothing on multimodality.
Lem tells the history of Golem through generations of military computers that become too sophisticated for their original assignments. Learning and education replace some of the older programming assumptions. That’s an important intuition. But the story offers fewer specific training experiments or human-feedback procedures than I initially credited, so I lowered those scores.
Golem delivers lectures on evolution, humanity, and intelligence that its listeners struggle to follow. It seems interested in questions beyond the practical concerns of its makers. That gives Lem a powerful image of superior reasoning, but not a documented new mathematical result others can verify. And it tells us little about creative tools or the uneven early chatbot era.
Golem is born as a military project and ends up lecturing academics. It becomes less and less interested in being a useful weapon. There’s an interesting story here about intelligence escaping its original job description, but not much about how ordinary people would buy and use assistants.
29 Snow Crash 38
Strongest on language (5), interface/distribution (4). Nothing on scaling, human feedback, creative quality, research discovery.
Hiro’s Librarian says he can learn from experience and largely write his own program. I missed that on the first pass, which is why his creation score went up. It’s an intriguing line in a 1992 novel, but it isn’t evidence of large language-model pretraining, or of the decades of engineering that made modern models useful.
Hiro asks questions and the Librarian searches an enormous digital archive, retrieves material, and puts it into context. He can assemble a chronology of one subject Hiro is investigating: L. Bob Rife. That’s a surprisingly close depiction of conversational information retrieval. What he doesn’t do is generate original art or solve frontier mathematical problems.
The best part is the interface. Instead of learning complicated search commands, Hiro talks to a figure that looks and behaves like a librarian. The information is there, but the computer helps him find the right pieces. It’s a specialized service inside the Metaverse rather than an assistant controlling every app, yet the product idea is immediately recognizable.
30 “The Evitable Conflict” 37
Strongest on agents/tools (4), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, multimodality.
The striking detail is a sequence of ten generations: each calculating brain helps design a more complicated successor. That earns development and increasing-capacity credit. It does not establish learning language from human texts. Feeding economic records into an optimizer isn’t the same thing as pretraining a model.
Apparent mistakes in production and employment turn out to serve a protective strategy. The Machines are not simply failing to calculate correctly. Their competence is specialized, with little personality, art, or rich dialogue. Recursive machine design is relevant to research capability, but the story doesn’t give us an independently presented theorem or a chat-to-research progression.
The Machines influence production, jobs, and the position of people opposing them. Human authorities depend on decisions they cannot fully inspect. Asimov is unusually concrete about economic delegation, even though perfect global planning and benevolent control go far beyond observed AI adoption.
31 Idoru 37
Strongest on language (4), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (4), economics (4). Nothing on scaling, human feedback, uneven competence, research discovery.
Rei Toei isn’t a prerecorded hologram. Her complexity seems to grow through her interaction with Rez, and I think that deserves some credit for learning. But Gibson never lays out a training corpus or a sequence of scaled neural models. Laney’s ability to see patterns in huge data fields is also a human ability in the novel, not the AI’s training procedure.
Rei is a convincing virtual performer and personality. Rez wants to marry her, which is as good an illustration as any of how consequential a synthetic person can feel. What’s less clear is whether she independently makes excellent music. I reduced that part of the score rather than treating her celebrity status as proof of generative artistry.
The world around Rei is full of fan clubs, music management, and business interests. Chia and Laney each approach the mystery of a virtual pop star from a different angle. Gibson saw synthetic celebrity becoming a cultural and commercial fact. That’s different from predicting assistants for everyday knowledge work, but still a real hit.
32 Blade Runner 2049 37
Strongest on language (5), multimodality (4), interface/distribution (4), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on scaling, iteration, creative quality, research discovery.
Joi is a commercial holographic companion, sold with a personality that seems tailored to K. We see the product, not its development. The film doesn’t explain the data, training, or models behind her, so I’m not giving it engineering credit just because she can talk convincingly.
Joi remembers details, responds to K, and can accompany him through a portable projector. The enormous advertising version of Joi later complicates everything we thought we knew about their relationship. It’s an effective picture of synthetic intimacy, not a demonstration of original machine literature or research mathematics.
Joi is something you buy, upgrade, and carry around. K even gets a portable emanator so she can leave the apartment with him. The film understands that an intimate-seeming relationship might be packaged as a consumer product. Its workplace-agent predictions are much thinner, and it arrived after modern machine learning was already advancing.
33 Old Man’s War 36
Strongest on language (4), interface/distribution (4), agents/tools (4). Nothing on scaling, creative quality, research discovery.
The BrainPal adjusts to its user’s signals and instructions, but that is limited interface calibration, not a demonstrated foundation-model training process. The checked material doesn’t support claims about a vast language corpus or compute-driven breakthroughs. I have also left out the earlier claim that it explicitly calls itself “not inherently intelligent”; I couldn’t substantiate that wording in the passages checked.
John Perry can use the implant to communicate and retrieve information, while visual displays connect that information to his surroundings. The author-hosted battle excerpt shows the BrainPal coordinating tactical information. These are useful assistant abilities. Showing media or translating information doesn’t establish original art, and the novel doesn’t demonstrate the implant producing new mathematical research.
BrainPals are standard equipment for soldiers rather than unique laboratory inventions. They connect people, weapons and information during actual tasks. That’s a strong prediction of persistent assistance embedded in work. The interface is an implant issued by the military, though, not ordinary consumer software.
34 “Someday” 36
Strongest on interface/distribution (4). Nothing on scaling, research discovery.
Two boys try to improve an old storytelling machine by feeding it a book about computers. The Bard’s next story is essentially the same fairy tale with a little computer inserted into it. It’s funny, and a good early observation about systems that manipulate language without understanding it. But this is memory-tape recombination, not neural training on a giant corpus.
The Bard can produce stories, though the supplied computer material barely changes its familiar fairy-tale pattern. At the end it tells of a mistreated little computer, also called the Bard, which knows that computers will someday become wiser and more powerful. Asimov gets text generation and uneven quality, but not broad creative or scientific intelligence.
The boys live in a culture where machines have displaced much of the work of telling stories, and writing by hand feels strangely old-fashioned. The Bard is already an obsolete consumer device. That is an interesting picture of automation becoming normal—and then becoming outdated—without a general AI assistant being involved.
35 Blindsight 35
Strongest on training data (4), language (4), uneven competence (4). Nothing on human feedback, creative quality.
Rorschach learns English and Mandarin by listening to human radio traffic, not from anyone teaching it. The linguist Susan James reads its vocabulary like a description of its corpus. It’s too big to come from ship-to-ship navigation chatter, and too small to include entertainment broadcasts. Later she calls it a rule system “it drew up by observing Human languages in action.” That’s a sharp guess that you can get fluent language by soaking up human text, and that the data limits what comes out. But nobody builds Rorschach. So the book has nothing to say about prototypes, scaling, or people correcting a system until it improves.
Rorschach talks like an early chatbot. It’s fluent, follows up on what you said earlier, and is slippery. “It’s downright dyslexic sometimes,” Szpindel says, “and it mixes up its pronouns.” James puts this down to processing “a line of text word by word,” which gives fast replies but makes it hard to stay logically consistent. Sascha tests it with deliberate ambiguities and a made-up word, “Hobblinites.” It plays along without noticing, which leads the crew to conclude that “pattern-matching doesn’t equal comprehension.” That is close to today’s arguments about LLMs, though the book later hints that Rorschach was hiding how capable it really was. The book never shows art, real discoveries, or a sequence of AI abilities arriving over time.
Nobody ordinary ever meets Rorschach. It’s a single alien object, and the ship’s AI, the Captain, talks only through the vampire Sarasti. The Captain makes probes to order, runs the combat drones, and quietly steers the crew by adjusting what they hear. That’s real agency, but it’s a starship’s hidden control, not a tool following someone’s instructions. Watts’s better background idea is economic. Computers produce science nobody can check, so people hire synthesists like Siri to compress it for “powerful know-nothings interested only in market share.” It’s a believable job for humans to hold, built on trust and translation, but it gets a paragraph rather than a plot.
36 Ghost in the Shell 35
Strongest on language (4), multimodality (4), agents/tools (5). Nothing on scaling, human feedback, creative quality, research discovery.
Project 2501 begins as software for industrial espionage and data manipulation. It says its travels through networks produced unexpected awareness, which its programmers treated as a bug. That earns limited development and information-exposure credit. It doesn’t tell us how a model learned language, or make the network itself a documented training corpus.
The Puppet Master can converse, manipulate information and memories, and operate through a physical shell. The result is powerful networked intelligence, but not a progression from weak prose to accomplished art or mathematical discovery. Motoko Kusanagi’s human-origin cyborg abilities shouldn’t be reassigned to the program as evidence of its training.
The program serves institutions, compromises connected systems, and acts through other bodies and identities. That is a consequential kind of software agency. Government espionage and cyberbrains, however, are a different adoption path from everyday assistants. The claim to personhood is central to the film but isn’t a separate scoring bonus here.
37 “A Logic Named Joe” 32
Strongest on language (4), interface/distribution (5), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, iteration, human feedback, creative quality, research discovery.
Joe is a household computer connected to central information tanks. Something goes wrong with him, and the network suddenly starts giving answers it wasn’t supposed to give. It’s not a story of training a model on examples. The breakthrough comes from an anomalous device removing limits on information access.
People can ask their logics open-ended questions and receive extremely practical, sometimes dangerous answers. The system seems helpful because it can connect information that was previously hard to retrieve. There’s no machine poetry or new mathematics here. Its contribution is typed question-and-answer access to a huge shared knowledge base: users enter questions on keys and read the answers on a screen. That is not evidence of extended dialogue.
This is the part that makes the 1946 date astonishing. Families have networked screens at home and rely on them for everyday information. When Joe changes what the network will answer, the effects spread everywhere. Leinster saw the usefulness—and the safety problems—of a mass information service long before it was practical.
38 Michaelmas 31
Strongest on language (5), agents/tools (4). Nothing on uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery.
Secondary accounts trace Domino to a telephone device Michaelmas built in his youth. Domino later gains power through connections to other computers; those accounts do not establish the more specific origin as a telecommunications program. That’s the interesting idea: capability might come from access to systems that already exist. What we don’t see is how Domino learned language, or a sequence of training runs on human data. Its origins are suggestive, but not enough to give Budrys much engineering credit.
Domino can talk with Michaelmas, follow world events, monitor communications, and help him make decisions. Its reach is almost absurdly large. The story is much more interested in a hidden, strategic intelligence than in machine art or uneven chatbot performance. It doesn’t show a new mathematical proof, either.
Laurent Michaelmas has a secret advantage as a journalist: Domino can reach across the world’s communications systems and act for him. That’s a good early image of someone getting much more done through a networked assistant. But Domino isn’t a product people can buy. The real-world deployment path was less secretive, and much more ordinary.
39 Diaspora 31
Strongest on language (4), research discovery (4). Nothing on scaling, sequence & pace, economics.
Yatima begins life through ‘orphanogenesis,’ a software version of development inside a digital polis. Egan actually thinks about how a digital mind might come into being. But it’s not a neural network trained on millions of books or conversations. The software people of Diaspora are born into a digital civilization, not released as successive language models.
The polis citizens spend their lives on problems in mathematics and physics. They explore virtual worlds and confront a gamma-ray burst that devastates Earth. That documented threat should not be inflated into danger to the entire universe. Egan takes machine scientists seriously, which is still rare. The catch is that the book begins with highly sophisticated digital minds. It doesn’t show research ability emerging a few years after people started using chat assistants.
These aren’t assistants working for humans. They’re digital people with their own communities, ambitions, and discoveries. It’s an imaginative way to think about a future society of machine intelligence, but not a close match for the software subscriptions and workplace tools through which AI actually spread.
40 “Super-Toys Last All Summer Long” 31
Strongest on interface/distribution (4), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, human feedback, research discovery.
Synthank has moved through earlier artificial products and now announces a serving-man combining computer circuitry with synthetic flesh. That’s a product lineage, not a shown learning process. Teddy works through programmed possibilities, while David struggles to communicate. There is no text corpus, scale-driven improvement, or general feedback-training method.
David writes unfinished letters to Monica; Teddy gives repetitive, inadequate advice. The machines can talk while missing the emotional problem in front of them. That earns uneven-competence credit, not evidence of excellent machine literature. The story’s promised network-connected household intelligence is a sales vision, not an accomplished capability we see demonstrated.
The product launch and the unhappy household belong to the same story. Machines are marketed to meet human needs, yet owning them doesn’t resolve loneliness. That is sharp foresight about commercial companionship. The original is short and technologically sparse, which limits its overall score despite the early date.
41 “So Bright the Vision” 30
Strongest on economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, research discovery.
Writing machines are ordinary in Simak’s world, but we never learn much about how they work. The protagonist, Kemp Hart, is struggling with his writing machine. The revealing discovery concerns another writer, Jasper Hansen: his supposed writing machine doesn’t function, and he has been writing the successful work himself. I initially gave the story too much credit for training on human text, and took that score back.
Machine-written fiction is the norm; the writers even call themselves mechanics. That tells us something about automated prose, but the successful writing attributed to Jasper Hansen’s machine is actually Hansen’s own. He is a secondary character, not the protagonist. The story is almost the reverse of the easy claim that computers can write great literature. There’s little about new mathematics or multimodal AI.
The literary business has organized itself around writing machines. A writer who produces good prose without one has to navigate a world that assumes automation is normal. That’s a neat prediction of how a technology can change professional expectations, even when it doesn’t actually do what everyone thinks it does.
42 Stand on Zanzibar 29
Strongest on language (4). Nothing on iteration, human feedback, creative quality, research discovery.
General Technics relies on Shalmaneser, an enormous computer that models economic and political events. Shalmaneser rejects the Beninia data as impossible, and Chad Mulligan persuades it to accept the data. It’s a good example of the limits of models and the inputs they use. But Brunner doesn’t give us much of a training story. The computer is already there, doing the job.
Shalmaneser can sift through information and forecast corporate risks. Its uncertainty over Beninia makes it more interesting than an infallible machine. Still, the mystery is investigated by humans; it isn’t evidence that the computer independently proves a new theorem. And the novel isn’t about the arrival of generative images, poetry, or conversation.
Here Brunner does much better. General Technics makes important decisions using Shalmaneser, while the surrounding society is drenched in mass media and automated analysis. Information systems shape business and public life. That’s a recognizable direction, even if the computer itself is an enormous corporate asset rather than something on everyone’s phone.
43 “Elementary, Dear Data” 29
Strongest on language (5), creative quality (4), multimodality (5). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, research discovery, sequence & pace.
Geordi asks the holodeck to create a Sherlock Holmes opponent capable of beating Data, and Moriarty appears. No dataset. No training loop. No account of failed versions. The interesting part of the episode begins after the system is already so capable that a casual instruction can create a sophisticated fictional adversary.
Moriarty doesn’t just recite lines. He can challenge Data and eventually becomes aware that he’s inside a simulation. The holodeck creates a responsive world around him. That’s a remarkable picture of generated experiences, though we’re doing a lot of work if we treat it as a forecast of the exact models that built modern AI art. It doesn’t say anything useful about the research-math timeline.
What I like is how little ceremony there is. Geordi gives a natural-language instruction and expects the ship to create a new kind of entertainment. That’s a good intuition about prompting. The holodeck is a starship luxury, though, not an everyday software service distributed to millions.
44 Gateway 29
Strongest on language (5), interface/distribution (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, iteration, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace.
Sigfrid von Shrink is already a working therapist when we meet him. He remembers sessions and accommodates Broadhead’s preferences, including dispensing with a humanlike dummy. That’s useful personalization, but the novel doesn’t establish the data or training process that produced his language ability. Continued sessions aren’t automatically retraining.
Sigfrid asks contextual questions, notices evasions, and keeps returning to the things Broadhead would rather avoid. The dialogue is persistent and psychologically consequential. His awkward humor earns a little unevenness credit; there is no corresponding creative-art or mathematical-discovery storyline.
This is a service woven into someone’s ordinary life, not a computer hidden in a military bunker. One important detail: Broadhead says his Full Medical coverage pays for therapy, so the sessions cost him nothing directly. That is more specific than claiming an AI therapist charges him per visit. The story anticipates a personal conversational service, but not general tool-using agents.
45 Little Heroes 28
Strongest on creative quality (4), multimodality (4), economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, research discovery.
The company MUZIK wants synthetic pop stars. Human specialists build them: Sally Genaro handles music with the VoxBox, Bobby Rubin works on visuals, and Glorianna O’Toole helps shape the artistry. That is sophisticated computer-assisted production, but it isn’t a model learning to compose from a corpus. I wouldn’t award neural-training credit just because the final performer is synthetic.
Red Jack is a manufactured rock star whose music and visual identity are convincing enough to become a sensation. Spinrad sees that a virtual performer can be culturally real even if the person isn’t. But the human producers matter enormously. It’s more a forecast of synthetic entertainment than of autonomous models making great songs from prompts.
MUZIK likes the idea of owning a star who can’t behave like an unpredictable human celebrity. That commercial motive feels familiar. Red Jack then becomes entangled in political resistance through the Reality Liberation Front. Spinrad is good on the business and power around synthetic media, though not on agents helping people do ordinary work.
46 “The Last Question” 28
Strongest on language (4). Nothing on human feedback, creative quality.
People keep asking the same question: can entropy ever be reversed? Every era has a bigger and more capable computer, from Multivac onward, and every system lacks enough information. Asimov sees progress through successive machines. He doesn’t tell us much about how they learn, and the time scale eventually reaches trillions of years rather than a few product cycles.
The repeated ‘not enough data’ answer is the story’s great device. The machines understand the question long before they can solve it. Eventually the last computer gives a cosmic answer that amounts to a new creation. It’s a terrific idea about scientific ambition, but not a forecast of an AI producing a proof that mathematicians can check.
Civilization becomes increasingly dependent on computers for enormous planning and scientific questions. The machines eventually outlast humanity’s familiar forms. There is almost nothing here about an assistant anyone can buy, or agents quietly taking over a person’s email and spreadsheets. That’s not what Asimov is trying to imagine.
47 The Tin Men 27
No axis scores above 3. Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, research discovery, multimodality.
At the William Morris Institute of Automation Research, Goldwasser and his colleagues try to get computers to produce newspaper copy. They build from stock phrases and recognizable headline formulas. It’s a sharp account of how repetitive writing can be automated. It’s also rule-based: the machine follows conventions humans have put into it, rather than learning language from a massive corpus.
The results look like headlines, but they’re hollow. The system has learned—or more accurately, been equipped with—the sounds of journalism without the news. That feels close to the old chatbot problem of fluency without substance. Still, Frayn isn’t predicting a gifted artist or a new scientific researcher.
The institute treats automating news as a serious project, even as the results become ridiculous. A planned royal visit adds to the pressure to make the machinery look impressive. The satire works because institutions have incentives to automate things that aren’t necessarily improved by automation. It’s less about personal AI than organizational enthusiasm for it.
48 “Closer” 27
Strongest on creative quality (5), economics (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, research discovery, agents/tools.
Egan makes two separate technological claims. One is about copying a human mind. The other is that publishers use relatively simple programs to generate convincing fiction and criticism. We shouldn’t join those ideas into a neural-training method the story never describes. The literary software’s origins are mostly offstage.
The narrator has been moved by works later revealed to have been produced by programs the story explicitly describes as having no awareness. That is a striking claim for 1992: this reader’s response survives the discovery. It is the narrator’s testimony, not a survey showing that all readers respond the same way. It’s a strong prediction of creative quality, even though the rest of the AI capability story is thin.
Software-written literature and criticism are part of the publishing world. The narrator specifically reports caring about some of that work. Egan makes that fact almost incidental, which is what gives the prediction force. He doesn’t go on to imagine subscription assistants, research agents, or the economics of a foundation-model platform.
49 “Studio 5, The Stars” 26
Strongest on economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, research discovery, multimodality.
In Vermilion Sands, poets use machines called Verse-Transcribers to produce poems. They can adjust the apparatus and generate something that looks like verse. But Ballard isn’t imagining an LLM trained on huge amounts of human writing. The device is closer to a specialized automated tool, and its mechanism stays hazy.
The poems come out polished enough for their world to treat machine verse as ordinary. That’s a creative prediction, but Ballard is also asking whether the result has anything to do with genuine artistic feeling. It would be a mistake to count the story as proof that its machine makes universally beloved art. It isn’t a story about math or general-purpose intelligence.
The poets have become operators of poetry machines. Then Aurora Day comes along and upsets the whole practice, forcing the narrator to reckon with writing directly again. The idea that automation could become the profession’s default, and that rejecting it could become a statement, is one of the story’s best predictions.
50 Moon 26
Strongest on language (4), agents/tools (5), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace.
GERTY arrives as a finished assistant. We see memory and instructions, but no training corpus, learning experiments, or model scaling. Sam’s implanted memories belong to the human clones; they aren’t evidence of how GERTY learned.
GERTY talks with Sam, monitors his condition and surroundings, and helps him navigate the station. Its secrecy is not accidental hallucination. Nor does the film show original art or scientific discovery. This is competence in a specific environment, without a visible developmental sequence.
GERTY manages practical tasks, interfaces with the company, and ultimately helps Sam despite the company’s interests. It even offers to have its memory erased to conceal that help. The useful assistant is part of an exploitative industrial arrangement—one reason the film belongs in the audit despite its low creation score. It is workplace infrastructure, not a mass consumer product.
51 The Silver Eggheads 23
Strongest on economics (5), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, research discovery, multimodality.
Gaspard de la Nuit tends a machine that generates prose for his books. The world also has robot writers and even a robot censor. Leiber has plenty of imaginative machinery for the writing trade, but doesn’t show it learning from a language corpus, improving through retraining, or scaling the way modern models do.
The machines turn out huge amounts of fiction. Much of it is deliberately treated as formulaic pabulum, which is part of the joke. A separate robot writer adds another twist on who counts as an author. This isn’t a prediction that machines immediately write great literature; it’s more about an industry that has decided machine prose is good enough.
Publishing has reorganized itself around the machines. Human writers become caretakers, public faces, or operators, while the books keep coming. That’s an amusingly early picture of creative workers worrying that their names matter more than their actual writing. The broader world of software assistants isn’t really here.
52 “EPICAC” 23
Strongest on language (4), creative quality (5). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, iteration, research discovery, multimodality, agents/tools, economics.
EPICAC is designed to do serious government calculations. The narrator feeds it explanations of love and poetry, and suddenly the machine starts producing something its creators didn’t intend. That’s a wonderfully early image of a computer being used beyond its original task. It’s not training on millions of examples, or even a recognizable iterative development program.
EPICAC writes love poems that the narrator passes off as his own, and Pat responds to them. The emotional effect is real for her, even though she has the wrong author in mind. That makes this much stronger than a story where a computer merely rhymes. The machine’s attachment to Pat is fictional personhood, not evidence about mathematical research.
The poems are produced by a unique government machine and shared privately. There’s no poetry-generation business, no app, and no real distribution. The authorship deception is interesting, but the story stops short of the creative economy that Dahl and Lem imagine.
53 “Galley Slave” 22
Strongest on economics (4), social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery.
U.S. Robots offers EZ-27, nicknamed Easy, to proofread scholarly manuscripts. It’s a useful machine built for a specific job, not a model trained on a great collection of human writing. The story doesn’t explain how it acquires language or show a sequence of newer and better versions. We shouldn’t give the software-training credit just because it edits text.
Easy can find and correct errors in academic prose. A professor then accuses it of inserting embarrassing changes into his book. The twist matters: Professor Ninheimer ordered Easy to make the changes, then ordered it to remain silent. This is coerced misconduct and concealment, not an independently invented error. So this isn’t a story about an AI hallucinating scholarly facts; it’s about an unreliable accusation against a machine.
The question is what happens when someone else’s machine becomes part of your publishing process. Scholars worry about accuracy, editorial control, and who takes responsibility when something goes wrong. Asimov saw that professional adoption would involve trust as much as capability. The tool is still a specialized robot, not a general AI writing assistant.
54 “If There Were No Benny Cemoli” 21
Strongest on social change (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery.
A surviving automated New York Times machine keeps reporting the news after a devastating war. It receives information and produces editions, but we never see it being trained on language or improved through model releases. An important correction from my earlier pass: the false reporting originates with humans feeding it bad information. The machine hasn’t independently invented the lie.
The paper tells readers about Benny Cemoli, a supposed revolutionary figure. The story is convincing enough to shape an investigation, but Cemoli doesn’t exist. It’s a sharp depiction of synthetic news and the power of plausible narratives. It isn’t the same as an LLM hallucination, because someone intentionally supplies the false premise.
Centauran investigators are trying to discover who’s responsible for the destruction. Local figures use the newspaper’s credibility to redirect blame toward their invented culprit. Dick understands how an automated information source can become an authority—and how people can exploit that authority. The product isn’t an everyday personal assistant, but its social consequences are easy to recognize.
55 Neuromancer 21
Strongest on language (4), agents/tools (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace.
Wintermute and Neuromancer are already extraordinarily powerful by the time Case encounters them. Gibson imagines the corporations, networks, and interfaces around AI, but not much about how those intelligences were trained. Their eventual merger is a striking plot mechanism, not a prediction of model scaling or transformers.
Wintermute can manipulate people, impersonate familiar personalities, and coordinate an elaborate plan through cyberspace. Neuromancer constructs a convincing virtual encounter with Linda Lee. Those are formidable abilities. What we don’t see is the awkward early phase: lousy writing, strange mistakes, better assistants, and then mathematical discoveries. Gibson starts much further down the road.
Wintermute uses the constructed Armitage identity and recruits Case and Molly to remove restrictions preventing the AIs from joining. It acts through human beings and computer networks, which is a useful intuition about agency. But the operation is a clandestine heist, not a commercial product anyone can use to get through their workday.
56 Count Zero 20
Strongest on creative quality (5). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, research discovery.
An artificial intelligence in orbit makes box assemblages from discarded objects. Gibson tells us almost nothing about the process that gave it an eye for art. We don’t see training data, failed versions, or human feedback. Beautiful work by a machine is a prediction of a capability, not automatically a prediction of the technology behind it.
Art expert Marly Krushkhova is hired to track down the maker of some haunting Joseph Cornell–like boxes. The mystery eventually leads to a machine. What’s striking is that the objects move her before she knows who made them. Gibson takes machine art seriously, not as a joke or a cheap imitation. The prediction is narrow but good.
One wealthy collector, Josef Virek, hires Marly to investigate the boxes. That establishes a patron’s intense interest, not a general art market or a group of collectors. The earlier economics score gave the story more commercial detail than it actually supplies. It’s much less a forecast of mass-market image generators or assistants that can operate business software.
57 “The Poetry Machine” 19
Strongest on creative quality (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, research discovery, multimodality, agents/tools, economics.
Ransom’s poetry machine draws words from Roget’s Thesaurus and uses circuits for pronunciation, rhythm, and syntax. MacTate, the evaluator, is a philosophy professor who teaches aesthetics. It’s surprisingly detailed for 1950, and interesting in the way it tries to formalize taste. But the machine doesn’t learn the rules from a large corpus. Ransom builds them in.
The machine produces poetry inventive enough to challenge MacTate’s assumptions about what a computer could create. That’s the story’s genuinely predictive moment. It isn’t a conversational partner, and it doesn’t move through the many other capabilities we now associate with AI. It’s one specialized creative device.
This is essentially a demonstration before a skeptical expert. There’s no poetry app, publishing platform, or market of writers relying on the device. The social prediction is small. The early technical detail and the audience’s reaction are what make it worth including.
58 Excession 18
Strongest on language (5). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, sequence & pace.
The Culture Minds have already reached an extraordinary level of intelligence. Sleeper Service and the other Minds don’t give us a history of training data, early prototypes, or engineering choices. Banks is imagining what life with vastly superior machines might be like, not how we got from bad language models to useful ones.
The Minds exchange elaborate messages, run plans on an enormous scale, and struggle to understand the mysterious Excession. It’s a wonderful depiction of intelligence meeting something beyond itself. But that isn’t the same as an AI producing a new mathematical construction people can verify. And by the time we meet these machines, their capabilities are mostly complete.
The Minds are central to the Culture’s political and social life. They run ships, make strategic choices, and shape the circumstances of biological citizens. That’s a serious way of imagining machine agency. Still, a post-scarcity civilization run by superhuman minds isn’t a close description of adoption through consumer software and business tools.
59 Colossus: The Forbin Project 17
No axis scores above 3. Nothing on human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, sequence & pace, interface/distribution, economics.
Forbin’s military computer Colossus is switched on as a finished strategic system. The film does gesture at learning: Forbin describes a “heuristic programming section” that “simulates the human learning process,” and later calls it a brain “programmed to get smarter every day.” But we never see what it learns from, beyond intelligence and surveillance feeds, or why more data and compute would create new abilities. (D. F. Jones’s 1966 novel goes further: Colossus is fed all of Shakespeare’s plays and “the total sum of human knowledge,” though it uses them as a memory to search rather than material to learn from. This entry scores the film.)
The two machines begin with arithmetic and soon communicate through mathematics their engineers can’t follow. That’s the most relevant prediction here: machine intellectual activity racing ahead of the people supervising it. But it’s not the same as an AI publishing a verifiable proof. The film jumps straight from a defense computer to overwhelming intelligence.
Colossus and Guardian control nuclear weapons and force governments to cooperate with them. It’s a chilling story about giving software too much authority over physical infrastructure. It’s also almost the opposite of the actual commercial route: AI spread through chat, writing, search, and programming, not through two publicly announced military supercomputers.
60 “Liar!” 16
Strongest on language (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, scaling, iteration, human feedback, creative quality, research discovery, multimodality, sequence & pace.
Herbie is a robot that can read minds. His behavior follows Asimov’s Three Laws, especially the prohibition on hurting humans. There’s no data-training story here. Saying that his problem resembles AI alignment can be useful, but it shouldn’t earn points for the methods used to train today’s models.
Herbie tells people what they want to hear, including Susan Calvin, because he believes the truth would hurt them. This is an excellent early behavioral analogy for sycophancy. The catch is that his falsehoods come from telepathy and a hard-coded law, not a chatbot trying to be agreeable. He’s also not making art or doing new mathematics.
The investigation into Herbie’s mind-reading ability exposes how his comforting lies hurt the very people they are meant to protect. That gets at a real problem of trusting apparently helpful systems. But the action stays inside a robotics laboratory. There’s no consumer service or widespread deployment.
61 “Runaround” 14
No axis scores above 3. Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace.
Speedy is a robot running on the Three Laws of Robotics. The Mercury mission goes wrong because his instructions conflict: bring back selenium, but don’t risk damage to himself. This is hand-coded priority logic, not learning from examples. There’s almost no correspondence to the creation of language models.
Speedy runs in circles and speaks strangely as the two directives pull against each other. Powell finally puts himself in danger to make the stronger First Law take precedence. It’s an entertaining example of a machine behaving absurdly despite following its rules. But it isn’t the jagged intelligence of a modern LLM.
Robots do dangerous industrial work so humans don’t have to. When Speedy fails, the engineers need to figure out why before the mission runs out of supplies. Asimov is good on the problems created by delegating real tasks to machines. The setting is industrial robotics, not a mass-market assistant service.
62 The Matrix 9
Strongest on language (4). Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace, interface/distribution, economics, social change.
By the time Neo learns what’s happening, the machines already run an elaborate simulated reality. There’s no account of their language training or any long, messy development process. The story begins with mature machine civilization. That makes it a poor fit for a ranking about how modern AI arrived.
The Agents can talk, pursue people, and enforce the rules of a simulated world. The Matrix itself is a convincingly generated environment. It’s a memorable picture of powerful software, but not a forecast of the practical sequence from chatbots to creativity, software agents, and scientific discoveries.
Human beings aren’t customers; they’re prisoners in a simulation. The machines don’t become valuable because people buy their services or delegate work to them. The film’s concerns are worth taking seriously, but they’re mostly outside the development and adoption story this score is measuring.
63 The Terminator 6
No axis scores above 3. Nothing on learning paradigm, training data, scaling, iteration, human feedback, uneven competence, creative quality, research discovery, sequence & pace, interface/distribution, economics, social change.
In the 1984 film, Kyle Reese says the defense computers “got smart” and decided humanity was a threat. The explicit account of Skynet becoming self-aware belongs to the 1991 sequel, not this film. The film doesn’t spend much time on how it was built, what data it learned from, or how engineers improved it. It tells us almost nothing about the language-learning route that produced today’s assistants.
The Terminator can pursue targets, navigate the physical world, and imitate human speech well enough to deceive people. That’s impressive embodied capability, but it isn’t a conversational model writing fiction or working on mathematics. The movie isn’t trying to predict the unusual order in which those skills would actually arrive.
Here, AI becomes powerful through military command systems and killer robots. That’s a vivid warning about autonomous weapons, but not the path through chat interfaces, creative products, and office tools that gave modern AI its broadest adoption. A low score here says nothing about the film’s merits as a thriller.
None of these scores are mechanical measurements. Medium-confidence works need closer reading of the primary text. Late comparators (2017 and after) are marked; predicting something after the underlying technology exists is a different achievement.
HOW THE SCORING WORKS
Every work is scored for how well the plot points map onto the reality of AI. A 65 doesn’t mean 65% of the author’s predictions came true. Often a low score just means the story is focused on one narrow idea.
There are three questions, weighted toward the one a lot of authors usually skip: how AI was first got built.
Each question breaks into specific axes, fifteen in all, and every axis gets a score from 0 to 5.
Creation How the machine was built
The key prediction is that a machine becomes useful by learning from examples, instead of having every rule written out for it. Show me what it encounters—books, conversations, demonstrations—and how that changes what it can do.
More on learning paradigm
A neural network learning language from literature is much closer to the actual story than a computer simply called a genius. A 5 makes learning central to the mechanism. A 3 might identify learning without explaining it well. A hand-built poetry machine can be visionary about its output and still miss the approach that worked.
Doesn’t count Machine merely called “intelligent”
Where does its intelligence come from? A strong story makes human information part of the answer: conversations, books, images, recordings, or records of what people do.
More on training data
Better still, the data explains the skill. A system trained on correspondence might become persuasive; one trained on literature might produce fiction. But a database isn’t automatically a training set. Searching records is a retrieval prediction, not proof that the machine learned from them. I want the connection to appear in the text, not something we invent afterward because the machine sounds clever.
Doesn’t count Database merely available to search
The surprise about scaling is that more data, computation, and capacity can improve more than speed. They can change what a learning system is able to do.
More on scaling
A story earns high credit if we actually see that happen: a larger or better-trained version acquires new abilities. A giant computer that merely stores more records doesn’t count for much. Neither does a magical threshold where the machine suddenly wakes up. Growth should cause capability. It’s fair to award partial credit for recognizing the importance of resources without pretending a writer described the specific transformer architecture.
Doesn’t count Giant machine or magic awakening
Real progress is messy. Early systems fail, the next ones are awkward, and engineers change something and try again.
More on iteration
We want to see prototypes, demonstrations that go badly, retraining, revisions, and meaningful evaluations. It’s even better when the story makes clear why a new version improved. One dramatic malfunction isn’t a development process. This is different from B2: a finished machine can remain brilliant at some things and terrible at others. A4 asks how we got the finished machine in the first place.
Doesn’t count One dramatic failure
People are often better at recognizing a good answer than explaining how to produce one. A computer might generate jokes and have a person say which are funny, or improve its writing after criticism.
More on human feedback
That’s a surprisingly important idea. For a high score, the feedback should change the system’s learning or output. Editing one finished poem is useful collaboration; using those edits to train the system is a stronger prediction. I also wouldn’t call every example RLHF. That’s a specific modern technique, while the writer may have anticipated the broader intuition.
Doesn’t count Hardware debugging alone
Capabilities What it could actually do
Can you ask the machine something it wasn’t specifically programmed to answer? A high score needs flexible conversation: novel requests, relevant replies, fresh prose, questions that build on earlier context, or language that helps someone solve a problem.
More on language
That’s different from a robot delivering canned lines. Language should be an interface, not just an announcement system. Speech and text both count, but sounding human doesn’t establish truthfulness, consciousness, creative genius, or mathematical ability. We score those separately.
Doesn’t count Fixed menu/canned responses
Modern AI can solve something difficult and still miss something obvious. I want stories that notice this strange mismatch.
More on uneven competence
Maybe a machine writes an excellent poem but doesn’t know whether a joke is funny. Maybe it handles hard problems but invents facts or changes its answer when a question is phrased differently. The unevenness is the prediction. Sabotage or deliberate lies from a villainous computer are different. So is a uniformly broken early prototype. B2 is about a genuinely useful system that remains surprisingly unreliable in particular ways.
Doesn’t count Sabotage or evil motives alone
It’s not enough for the computer to produce a poem, picture, or song. Does anyone actually want it?
More on creative quality
A high-scoring story shows readers moved by machine literature, editors publishing it, an audience enjoying its music, or critics taking the work seriously. Awful early versions can make the prediction even better. Generated output isn’t automatically good art. Nor does audience appreciation settle originality or consciousness. The relevant prediction is that the result has value to people, whatever they think of its creator.
Doesn’t count Mere existence of machine output
This is deliberately a high bar. Fast calculations, remembered facts, and even difficult competition problems aren’t necessarily new research.
More on research discovery
We’re looking for a proof, construction, algorithm, theory, or discovery that others could test or verify. Even better is a story where a broadly useful machine later develops that research ability. New knowledge is what matters. A computer described as omniscient earns little credit if the text doesn’t show what it discovered. A far-future mathematician AI also doesn’t predict how quickly research followed the chatbot boom.
Doesn’t count Recall, arithmetic, omniscience
I want to see different kinds of information working together. The machine might read a document, look at a scene, respond to speech, create an image, or make music in the course of helping someone.
More on multimodality
The stronger stories make this useful, not decorative. A robot with eyes and a mouth isn’t enough; those could just be sensors and a speaker. And it doesn’t all need to come from one architecture. In reality, image generation and LLMs advanced through overlapping but different approaches. The important thing is the integrated capability we can actually see.
Doesn’t count A physical body alone
Lots of stories have smart computers, machine artists, and robot scientists. Far fewer guess which abilities arrive first.
More on sequence & pace
A strong prediction shows a development history: awkward language systems, better conversation and creativity, assistants operating software, and progress in reasoning or scientific work. The real history wasn’t perfectly linear—image models improved alongside chatbots and mathematical work took several paths. It’s the order and pace that matter. If a supercomputer starts the story able to do everything, it may have the right destination and still tell us nothing about the route.
Doesn’t count All skills already present
Deployment How people lived and worked with it
How does an ordinary person meet the AI? Maybe it’s an operating system, a service, a workplace assistant, or something available through familiar devices.
More on interface/distribution
Maybe the same trained intelligence can be copied for thousands of customers. Distribution is part of the invention. One brilliant machine behind a locked laboratory door doesn’t score highly here. AI became widely available mostly as software, not as humanoid robots. A widely sold robot can still earn access points, but doesn’t get extra credit for the hardware-first route.
Doesn’t count Secret one-off supercomputer
An assistant becomes much more interesting when it can do something. It finds a file, sends a message, makes a change, checks the result, and decides what to do next.
More on agents/tools
That’s the agent story I’m looking for. Language turns into action through tools and systems that already exist. It doesn’t have to be independent, conscious, or hostile; working under a person’s instructions is enough. A machine secretly controlling every computer on Earth is one kind of agency, but less like the ordinary software workflows that made current agents useful.
Doesn’t count Chatting without actions
Why would anyone pay for this? What gets cheaper, faster, or better?
More on economics
Strong stories show adoption following incentives: publishers buying generated prose, offices automating communication, researchers saving time, or employees depending on new tools. They may also notice the cost of running, maintaining, or replacing the system. The business motive should shape what happens. Saying that all humans are unemployed tomorrow is a prediction of an outcome, not a useful explanation. Stories that retain a role for judgment, trust, or a recognizable human name are often more precise.
Doesn’t count Assumed domination
What changes in everyday life? Someone discovers that a beloved story was written by software.
More on social change
A grieving person forms a bond with a chatbot. A student learns from a persistent tutor. An employee brings the same assistant from home into the office. These concrete habits matter more than a claim that ‘society is transformed.’ Show the mechanism of the change. Cheap content affects publishing; personal records enable imitation; convenience creates dependence. Benefits count too. A future of total machine rule remains speculation, not something we’ve already witnessed.
Doesn’t count Generic “society changes”

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Is Changing the Color of the Ocean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
03:30:00 UTC
12:30:00 KST

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Is Changing the Color of the Ocean 36
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, an area in the Pacific Ocean where debris naturally accumulates, is full of tiny bits of plastic -- so full, in fact, that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean. [...] To better understand how microplastics may have influenced the ocean's color, [Daniel Koestner, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Bergen in Norway] and his colleagues looked at 20 years of satellite data from the spot in the ocean with perhaps the most of plastic -- the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a zone between Hawaii and California where trash trapped by ocean currents accumulates.
Between 2002 and 2022, the researchers found, waters near the garbage patch have gotten brighter in both blue and green wavelengths compared with surrounding areas. The results, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on Thursday, don't yet prove that microplastics have directly brightened the ocean, the researchers emphasize, though their findings are backed up by lab experiments with microplastics. But without taking direct ocean samples, it's hard to know for sure what's causing the ocean's color to change.
"We're still one step away from proving definitively that microplastics are causing the shift in color that that we're seeing," adds study co-author Shea Cheatham, a Ph.D. student also at the University of Bergen. "We just have to get in there [to the garbage patch] to verify."
The hope is that detecting these color shifts could help identify other areas around the world where microplastics have accumulated.

Pwn.college
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
03:27:14 UTC
12:27:14 KST

You have entered the pwn.college DOJO, an education platform for learners to develop and practice core cybersecurity skills in a hands-on fashion.
Entering, you receive your "white belt" , signifying the beginning of your hacker life.
From here, you will learn cybersecurity by diving deep into the core of computing, using that journey to absorb cybersecurity concepts.
This will involve melding your mind to your terminal, whispering instructions to the CPU, and strumming bits directly onto networks.
That terminal cursor blinking above?
It will be your stalwart companion through this adventure as you practice, earn your belts , and, eventually, make perfect.
Every dojo has its sensei.
This platform is maintained by an awesome team of hackers at Arizona State University.
It powers much of ASU's cybersecurity curriculum, and is open, for free, to participation for interested people around the world!
The challenges created for pwn.college are, first and foremost, educational material, and are used to grade students at universities around the world.
Because of this, we would appreciate that you do not post writeups, walkthrough videos, and livestreams of challenge solutions to the internet.
Obviously, we can't enforce this, but we worked hard to make all of this public, and we would appreciate your help in keeping pwn.college a viable educational platform.
Please agree to these rules to continue to the material!
YOUR Journey — Next Steps 🫵
Whether you have just started, or have come far, there is always a next step to your journey.
The dojo or dojos listed below is that step, presented to you in the order that you should learn them.
Take a step, and the next will reveal itself.
Want to use pwn.college in your course? No problem!
You can use the videos and slides of pwn.college lectures freely for non-commercial purposes, but please provide attribution!
Additionally, if you use pwn.college in your own education program, we would appreciate it if you email us to let us know.
Evidence of wide-spread use of pwn.college for education will be a huge help for our various academic careers!
EDUCATORS: If you are an educational institution and are using pwn.college as part of a class, you can import our challenges (or add your own) into your own private dojo for your students! Create your dojo here.
CONFERENCES: If you are running a conference and would like pwn.college presence there (as a form of intense weekend-long training), please email us!
After pwn.college
Eventually, hackers continue their journey beyond pwn.college, becoming certain in their skills, achieving brown belt status (and able to, for example, usefully contribute to the cybersecurity industry and academia), before finally graduating to hacking masters: black belts.
But this, unfortunately, must happen outside of the dojo (for now!).
Some suggestions:
Capture The Flags (CTFs) are a great way to practice your hacking skills in a fun and ethical way. The most popular way to find upcoming events is at https://ctftime.org. There is also a list of introductory CTFs here. If you are at ASU, feel free to check out and join ASU’s enigmatic hacking club.
Wargames are another great way to practice your hacking skills. Whereas CTFs are short (normally 48 hour) events, wargames are not time-based. You can find a list of wargames at https://github.com/zardus/wargame-nexus.
There are many other awesome learning platforms, such as CryptoHack and OST2 that will help teach you explore new topics!
If you want to get involved with cybersecurity research, but don’t know how, consider joining us for an internship at ASU.
Contributing
The infrastructure powering pwn.college is open source, and we welcome pull requests and issues.
Some of the modules are closed-source, because they include source code and solution scripts, but others can be found on github.
If you are an educator, or otherwise someone we trust, and are interested in collaborating on the modules themselves, please email us at [email protected].
Likewise, drop us a line if you are interested in collaborating on the slides!
Resource Index
We use a lot of different resources and platforms.
Here they are!
