The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
03:22:14 UTC
12:22:14 KST

It’s a bad time and maybe also a great time to make a new smartphone.
The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
It’s a little phone with a big challenge ahead of it.
Brennan Jordan and Austin Boer are two-thirds of the trio behind the Enough Phone, a small phone that will run your choice of stock Android or the minimalist OdysseyOS. They’re currently seeking funding on Kickstarter, and just a day after launching, the project is over halfway to its $250,000 goal.
The Enough Phone’s target specifications include a 5.3-inch display, 3,500mAh user-replaceable battery, MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, a 50-megapixel Sony sensor in the rear camera, and 8GB of RAM. The dimensions listed on the Kickstarter page suggest an iPhone Mini-ish size; Jordan and Boer also happen to be former iPhone Mini users themselves.
The two of them cofounded a software startup called Sleke, which sells refurbished phones loaded with OdysseyOS, their minimalist, low-distraction version of Android. Putting the software on existing phones is a win for sustainability, but it also helps them get their software to market faster, Boer tells me. The pair offers small batches of Pixel 8 and 9 phones right now through the Sleke website, but the large devices didn’t feel quite right to some customers.
“One of the biggest things that we get is, ‘I don’t want this large of a phone for a minimal operating system,’” says Boer. They’d wanted to make a small phone, and the opportunity arrived when Will Stults approached them about creating one. Stults operates an online store for non-smartphones called Dumbwireless. He also brings familiarity with the smartphone manufacturing process to the mix thanks to some previous work with a “big” phone brand.
But hardware is hard in the best of times, and 2026 has proven extremely challenging for phone companies big and small. The chip shortage has driven prices up and made RAM scarce. Jordan and Boer are feeling the pressures, particularly around pricing. The Kickstarter campaign offers some discounts for early backers, but after that the Enough Phone will sell for $599. “We don’t want to be charging as much as we are,” says Boer, “but as a startup you can only do so much.” They’re a self-funded operation and want to keep it that way, he says, so they can choose their own priorities. Outside funding would change the dynamic and might put pressure on them to shorten their promised five years of software support or cut other costs.
As it stands, the project is on schedule. According to the Kickstarter page, it’s in the production tooling phase, with plans to ship phones to customers in May 2027 — though a footnote says that the RAM shortage’s “ripple effects across the entire electronics manufacturing industry” could still throw a wrench in the works.
Prospects for small phone fans (disclosure: I am one) were bleak even before the chip crisis. Apple’s last Mini was released five years ago, and there’s no indication of another one in sight. Asus’ Zenfone used to be a nice, small-ish Android option before the company made it bigger and quit selling it in the US. Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky made a lot of noise about launching a small phone, but has since shifted priorities. And there’s Unihertz’s Jelly Max — certainly small, but its specs lag behind a modern midrange phone.
Boer sees this gap as an opportunity, even in the midst of a global RAM crisis. “Nobody was doing it, and we’re kind of seeing why — because it’s not the ideal time to start. But that also kind of makes it the ideal time to start, because no one else is doing it,” he says. “Let’s just do it ourselves.” Enough is enough. At least that’s what they’re hoping.

Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)

Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl.
Preview: NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production workloads. See Preview status and known limitations.
Get started · Documentation · Contribute · Get help
The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64, with at least
6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk. It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report Ready.
On macOS, use the local site guide, which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.
For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). NICo is the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The platform and version reference lists validated combinations and pinned dependencies.
- Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE
API or nvkectl; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
clusters with their own control planes.
- Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools, upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.
- Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available per cluster.
- Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.
The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure API authentication and protected access before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest confidentiality. Read the known limitations before choosing an evaluation or installation path.
The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other.
NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters: a throwaway seed cluster stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters on demand.
An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster:
- The management cluster runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure
controllers. nvkectl forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the
management-plane services is a separate step.
- Workload clusters run customer applications. The management plane creates and operates them through NICo, Cluster API and the node agent.
Read What is NVKE for the operator workflow and Architecture for the implementation and data flows.
Use Go 1.27.3, the version pinned in go.work, and GNU Make 4 or later. Public Go modules must be reachable on the first build. Flox is optional and supplies the repository's development tools; on macOS, it also supplies GNU Make 4. See Development for toolchain setup.
git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke.git
cd nvke
make build
This builds the workspace and writes nine binaries to bin/: agent,
updater, controller, nvkectl, capd-reboot-controller,
nvke-os-image-check, management-engine, tenant-api and operator-api. Building does not start a
management plane or create a cluster. The node agent runs on Linux.
The workspace guide explains the modules and outputs.
For local services and test environments, see Local development setup.

make preflight; it selects checks for the modules you changed.

Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl.

Claude was faster and cheaper. We took the scenic route anyway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
02:59:39 UTC
11:59:39 KST

Verify, Then Vote
We gave five small local models the same questions and checked their sources before picking an answer. Our first paper reports what got better, a safety test that failed and how we can rerun decisions without asking the models again.
When five models disagree
We wanted to see how far a few small models could get running on one machine. We gave five of them the same question, let them look things up and compared their answers. They often disagreed. The obvious fix is a vote, but models can share the same mistake and a vote can’t catch that.
So we tried something else: check the sources each model cited, then use a fixed rule to pick the answer. We called the paper Verify, Then Vote. We kept answering, checking and choosing as separate steps and saved the results of each, so we could go back and reuse them.
Five local models and one checker
We used Llama 3.2 3B, Mistral 7B, Gemma 2 2B, Phi-3 mini and Qwen 2.5 3B, running through Ollama on an Apple M3 Pro with 36 GB of RAM. We left it running overnight and it finished in about eight hours.
Each model wrote a search query and got back five passages: Wikipedia for general questions, research abstracts for science claims. It then gave an answer, said how confident it was and cited up to three passages. We saved everything before any answer was picked.
To check sources, we used Claude Sonnet 5.5 as a separate hosted model. It saw only one sentence stating the answer and one cited passage and said whether the passage supported the answer, contradicted it or didn’t say enough. It never saw the correct answer.
A supported answer can still be wrong
If a passage says Sydney is the capital of Australia, it supports the answer “Sydney,” even though the capital is Canberra. Our check asks whether the passage backs up the answer. It doesn’t ask whether the passage is true.
Our rule starts with the answer that got the most votes and breaks ties the same way every time. It only switches to a different answer if the checker says a cited passage supports it. Every switch keeps a record of the passage and the check behind it, so we can see why it happened.
We also proved one thing about the rule using Lean 4, software that checks mathematical proofs: if the rule ever swaps a correct answer for a wrong one, a source check must have backed the wrong answer. That tells us where to look when something goes wrong. It doesn’t prove the source was true or that the checker read it correctly.
91 fixes, 12 new mistakes and a failed test
We tuned the settings on a separate practice set, then ran the rule on 1,000 main questions. Accuracy went from 77.1% with a simple majority vote to 85.0% with our rule.
On 526 of those questions, the models gave a mix of right and wrong answers. There, the rule fixed 91 answers the vote got wrong and broke 12 the vote got right, raising accuracy from 71.5% to 86.5%. One caveat: the vote broke ties at random, while our rule always broke them the same way, so part of the gain came from how ties were handled.
Before we started, we set a limit on how many right answers the rule could break. Of 376 answers the vote got right, the rule made 12 wrong (3.2%). Allowing for chance, the true rate could be as high as 5.5%, above our 5% limit. So the original rule failed our test. We had written down the plan and analysis before collecting data, though we didn’t file them in a public registry.
We also wanted to know whether the checker was really reading the passages. So we ran it again with the cited text removed or swapped for unrelated text. Either way, 76 of the 91 fixes disappeared. The passages mattered, though Sonnet may still lean on what it already knows when the right text is in front of it.
Keep the answer if it’s already backed up
That result suggested a more careful rule: if the starting answer already has a source backing it, keep it. We wrote down that change before collecting answers from five different models on the same questions and reused existing checks wherever the answer and passage were the same.
With the new models, 547 questions had a mix of right and wrong answers. The revised rule fixed 73 and broke three, raising accuracy from 73.1% to 85.9%. Of 400 answers the vote got right, three became wrong (0.75%) and the worst-case rate was 2.2%, well under our 5% limit.
So the revised rule passed with a new set of models. Because the questions were the same and we designed the change after seeing the first results, this shows the rule carries over to other models, not that it works on new questions.
Why not just let Sonnet choose?
We tried that too. Given the same answers and passages, Sonnet picked the right one 93.9% of the time on the first group’s 526 mixed questions, compared with 86.5% for our rule. It was also cheaper: about $0.014 per question, versus $0.021 for checking sources. Neither number includes the cost of the models writing their answers.
So Sonnet is better at making the first call. Our approach helps afterward. Because every check is saved, we can see exactly why an answer was picked and try a different rule without paying for new checks. You can log a judge’s choice too, but asking it to choose again means another call.
Rerun decisions without another model call
Across all 1,100 questions, including a separate set of 100 from TruthfulQA, the models disagreed on 702. To see how much each model mattered, a Python script dropped one model at a time and handed the remaining saved answers to our Rust program to choose again. Five reruns per question came to 3,510 in total.
All of them took 23 seconds with no new model calls. The chosen answer changed 9.4% of the time, which shows how much the outcome depends on which models take part. Rerunning all 1,100 original decisions gave exactly the same output.
This works because answering, checking and choosing are kept separate. We can change how answers are chosen while the saved answers and checks stay the same. New answers or sources would need new checks.
What we want to try next
Next we need new questions, not just new rules. Because we keep every run, we can dig into a decision, change the rule and measure the effect before paying to collect more answers.
The paper, code, proofs and saved runs are on GitHub, with scripts to reproduce our results and try your own rules on the same data.
The record
Sources & methods
These links point to the paper, code and saved experiment records on GitHub.

Closed AI models dominate the price-performance frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
02:49:56 UTC
11:49:56 KST

Closed AI models now dominate the price-performance frontier
Village’s LLM Atlas maps the price-performance frontier: the strongest AI model at every price point.
Closed models hold almost every budget
- An open-weight model is the best buy at 3% of budgets. Nearly all of those are at the cheap end, held by Google’s Gemma 4 E4B and Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Flash.
- In June, it was 41%. DeepSeek V4 Flash alone was the best buy across nearly a third of budgets, with Zhipu’s GLM-5.2 just above it.
- Two OpenAI releases took most of that back. GPT-6 Luna in September and GPT-6.1 Terra in October now cover the budgets open models used to win, alongside Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5.
Open models have led on value before
- Today’s share is the lowest we have measured. At the end of every quarter since 2024, open models held at least 6% of budgets.
- The peaks came from single releases. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp was the best buy at nearly half of all budgets the week it launched in September 2025.
- None of them lasted. After each peak, the open share fell by about half or more by the next quarter as closed labs shipped cheaper tiers.
Open models win on value in bursts: a strong, cheap release, usually from DeepSeek, takes a wide band of budgets until the next closed model undercuts it. The latest closed releases have been both cheaper and stronger than anything open, so the band has shrunk to the very bottom of the price range.
Why closed labs may be winning on value
Three explanations fit the pattern:
- Closed labs can distill their own frontier models. A lab with the strongest model can train cheaper ones on its outputs in-house, and today’s cheap closed tiers followed their flagships within weeks, as Claude Haiku 5.5 did two weeks after Claude Opus 5.5. Open labs have to start from their own, weaker models, since closed labs’ terms generally bar training competitors on their outputs.
- Closed labs release whole families. OpenAI’s GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 models, from Luna and Terra up to Sol and Astra, hold 11 of the frontier’s 21 points between them, so one generation covers nearly every price.
- Closed labs may serve more cheaply. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google run inference at enormous scale, Google on its own chips, which can lower what each task costs; most open-model labs serve far less traffic.
How we built this
This study uses Village’s LLM Atlas, which estimates a capability score for each model and reasoning setting from public benchmark results and, with a separate cost model, its cost per task from evaluators’ runs, described in its methodology. Costs are relative to GPT-5 at high effort. For each date, we take every model released by then and find the most capable one at each of 201 budgets spread evenly on a log scale from 1% to three times GPT-5’s cost. The scores are from October 31, 2026; Atlas updates as new results arrive.
Costs reflect what evaluators paid through hosted APIs, and open models can be cheaper to run on your own hardware. Restricting to models scored on at least 10 benchmark families, or narrowing the budgets to 3% to one times GPT-5’s cost, gives the same pattern; widening them to 0.3% to ten times raises today’s share to 16%, because tiny open models still win at the very cheapest end.

Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420B in combined market cap in the two days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
02:30:25 UTC
11:30:25 KST

The midterm elections have dealt a major blow to Donald Trump and his Republican Party, as well as to one of his biggest backers, entrepreneur Elon Musk. The two major companies controlled by Musk—Tesla and SpaceX—have suffered a sharp stock market correction following the Democrats' unexpected victory in Texas and their majority in the U.S. Congress.
Tesla shares fell 3.3% on Wednesday, and on Thursday the decline accelerated, dropping another 10.77%. SpaceX shares fell 3.8% on the first day and another 9% on Thursday. In total, the market value loss for the two companies is approaching $469 billion, or about €417 billion at the current exchange rate. On Wednesday, the depreciation amounted to €110 billion.
Given that Elon Musk controls 35% of SpaceX and 11% of Tesla, the loss in value of his personal wealth is around $189 billion (€170 billion).
Markets have interpreted the election results as an increase in regulatory risks for the business empire of the South African tycoon, one of the main funders of the Republican Party in the midterm campaign .
Musk's business empire has benefited in recent years from a very lax tax regime in Texas, along with regulations highly favorable to the development of data centers for processing artificial intelligence algorithms, one of his major investments. He has also capitalized on SpaceX's consolidation as the primary supplier to the aerospace agency, NASA.
Analysts consulted by Bloomberg believe that a Democratic-controlled Congress could strengthen oversight of key sectors for Musk, such as AI, and complicate a potential integration between Tesla and SpaceX.
The market reaction has been furious, especially since both companies are headquartered in Texas , a state Musk has made the center of his operations. The entrepreneur moved his residence there in 2020 and relocated Tesla's headquarters the following year, after his clashes with California authorities during the pandemic. He also established his large Tesla car factory near Austin, his largest production facility in the United States.
“Texas becoming a Democratic state creates a new political challenge for Musk, especially considering how much money he has invested in making it the center of his business empire,” notes Ivan Feinseth, chief investment officer at Tigress Financial Partners.
The Democratic victory in Texas also has a symbolic dimension for the entrepreneur. The new governor, Gina Hinojosa , advocated during the campaign for greater control over data centers, essential infrastructure for the development of AI-related projects. The outcome of the Senate elections in the state has also been interpreted by some analysts as a sign of rejection of Musk's growing political influence.
The billionaire has strengthened his political involvement with Donald Trump and the Republican Party in recent years, having donated nearly $450 million to Republican candidates , of which some $205 million went to campaigns in Texas. According to various estimates, he has donated more money in these months than investor George Soros spent on the Democratic Party throughout his lifetime. Furthermore, Musk used his social network X (formerly Twitter) to openly urge people to vote against the Democrats during the election campaign.
After the results were announced, Musk reacted ironically on the same platform. “Guess my space lasers for interfering with the election didn’t work this time,” he wrote. In another message, he stated that “ data centers in space are starting to look pretty appealing.”
The new political landscape could have implications for some of their companies' strategic projects, such as the potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX . Several analysts believe that Democratic control of Congress could increase political and regulatory scrutiny of this deal.
Despite the decline in the value of Musk's companies, other electric vehicle manufacturers reacted in the opposite way. Rivian and Lucid saw their stock prices rise amid expectations that a Democratic majority will push for measures favorable to the energy transition.
One of the most common interpretations among fund investors is that Elon Musk has capitalized on the wave of deregulation championed by Donald Trump in recent years. In the early stages of Trump's presidency, the entrepreneur even served as an external advisor to the administration, heading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), to try to cut public spending, much like Javier Milei's chainsaw campaign in Argentina. Ultimately, a disagreement between the president and Musk led to his temporary departure from the White House.
Beyond the midterm election results , doubts persist about the viability and timeline of several projects that underpin the high valuations of Musk's companies. The potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX remains in a preliminary stage, while initiatives such as robotaxis , humanoid robots, and Mars colonization plans continue to fall short of generating significant revenue.
